name: The Fool
upright: Something is starting, and you don't have all the information yet. The Fool steps out anyway, carrying almost nothing, because the only way to learn this road is to walk it. This is the card of first days and fresh starts, of saying yes while it still feels a little silly. The risk is real and the card knows it. It just trusts that curiosity will carry you further than worry will. The Fool doesn't need a plan yet; he needs a first step and a bit of luck. In a reading it often shows up right before something new begins, when you're excited and a little underprepared, and that's allowed.
reversed: Upside down, the leap either doesn't happen or happens without looking. Maybe you're putting off something new because you're scared of looking foolish, or waiting for a guarantee that isn't coming. The other version is carelessness, jumping into things with no plan and calling it freedom. Either way, the little dog is barking for a reason. Take one honest look at the edge before you decide. Upside down, this is often the leap that keeps getting put off until the moment passes. Ask yourself honestly whether you're waiting for a sign or waiting for an excuse.
sitWith: What would you try if you were allowed to be bad at it for a while? What's the smallest version of that leap you could take this week?
inASpread: Where the Fool lands tells you a lot. In the first position, the situation is brand new and nothing is settled yet; as the outcome, it's a clean slate rather than a tidy ending. Next to careful cards like the Four of Pentacles or the Emperor, expect a tug between the urge to jump and the need to be sensible. As the first card in a spread about something new, it says the beginning itself is the point.
imagery: A young traveler in bright clothes steps toward the edge of a cliff with a small bundle on a stick, a white rose in one hand and a little white dog jumping at his heels. He's looking up at the sky, not down at the drop, which is both his faith and his blind spot.

waite.upright: Folly, mania, extravagance, intoxication, delirium, frenzy, bewrayment.
waite.reversed: Negligence, absence, distribution, carelessness, apathy, nullity, vanity.
waite.picture: With light step, as if earth and its trammels had little power to restrain him, a young man in gorgeous vestments pauses at the brink of a precipice among the great heights of the world; he surveys the blue distance before him—its expanse of sky rather than the prospect below. His act of eager walking is still indicated, though he is stationary at the given moment; his dog is still bounding. The edge which opens on the depth has no terror; it is as if angels were waiting to uphold him, if it came about that he leaped from the height. His countenance is full of intelligence and expectant dream. He has a rose in one hand and in the other a costly wand, from which depends over his right shoulder a wallet curiously embroidered.
waite.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911)

symbols.meaning: The drop he isn't watching. Every new start has a risk you can't fully see from where you stand.
Innocence and a clean motive. He's going for the love of it, with nothing to prove.
The instinct that barks a warning or cheers him on, depending on how you read it.
Everything he owns fits in one small bag, so he travels light and can't be held back by much.
The sun, Waite writes, knows where he came from and where he's going, even if he doesn't yet.

history: He is Le Mat in the Marseille deck and Il Matto in Italian decks, both meaning the madman. Older versions show a ragged vagabond with a bundle over his shoulder while a dog or cat tears at his trousers, and the card usually carried no number at all. Waite gave him the number zero, yet in his book he still discusses the Fool between Judgement and the World. Pamela Colman Smith turned the beggar into a bright young traveler pausing at a cliff edge in the morning sun.
numerologyAstrology: Zero is the number before anything has been counted, which suits a card of pure beginning. Golden Dawn astrology gave the Fool to elemental Air, open and unformed; the link to Uranus, planet of sudden breaks, came from later astrologers.

upright.love: A new romance, or a fresh chapter in an old one, with more excitement than plans. Let it be light and curious for now; you don't need to know where it goes to enjoy the first steps. Unattached, this is a fun, low-pressure meeting that doesn't need a label yet. Already together, it asks for something new as a pair, a trip or a spontaneous plan, so things don't go stale.
upright.work: You may feel underqualified, and that's fine, because this card rewards the person willing to learn on the way. A new job, a new field, or a side project you'd start just to see what happens. Expect to be the beginner in the room, and a willingness to ask questions will serve you better than pretending to know.
upright.money: Spending on something new, or a gamble on yourself. Keep enough aside that one wrong step at the cliff edge doesn't take everything with it. Small bets are fine; don't hand over savings on a hunch. If you're starting something, give yourself a budget you can afford to lose and then enjoy it.
upright.advice: Say yes to the thing that scares and excites you in equal measure. Pack light, keep your eyes open, and let the little dog bark if it needs to. Let yourself be new at something.
upright.asAPerson: Someone young at heart, spontaneous, a bit unpredictable, and easy to like. As a feeling toward you, it's fresh curiosity with no heavy expectations attached. They make people laugh and rarely hold a grudge.

yesNo.why: The door is open and the card favors taking the first step. Fresh starts are favored, as long as you look where you step.

reversed.love: Either cold feet about starting something or a rush into it without looking. Someone may be treating the relationship like a game, or you may be holding back from a person who's worth the risk. Someone who won't commit, or a flirtation that goes nowhere because nobody takes it seriously. Single and noticing a pattern? Check whether you keep choosing people who are fun and unavailable.
reversed.work: A plan that never leaves the notebook, or a leap made without checking the ground. Before quitting or launching, do the boring homework you've been skipping. Careless mistakes, missed deadlines, or a start that keeps getting postponed. Check details twice before you sign or send anything.
reversed.money: Impulse buys, careless risks, or money lent to someone flaky. The fix is a simple budget and a pause before any big spend. Impulse spending, gambling, or lending money with no plan to get it back. Put a pause between wanting something and buying it.
reversed.advice: Look down once before you step. Courage is still called for, just with a plan attached this time. Ask one person who knows the ground before you set off.
reversed.asAPerson: Someone who avoids commitment and calls it freedom, or who acts first and apologizes later. Toward you, expect interest without much follow-through. Charming, but hard to count on when it matters.

yesNo.why: Something about the timing or the planning is off; check before you jump. A little more planning could turn this into a yes.

waiteNote.upright: Waite's list sounds harsh because in older fortune telling the Fool was simply the madman: folly means foolishness, mania and frenzy mean wild, unthinking excitement, and extravagance means going too far. “Bewrayment” is an old word for giving yourself away or betraying a secret. A reader today usually softens this into a leap taken without looking, and asks whether the leap is brave or just careless.
waiteNote.reversed: Reversed, Waite's words describe a Fool who never jumps at all. Negligence and carelessness mean things left undone, apathy is not caring, and nullity means nothing coming of it. Vanity here is the older sense of emptiness, effort that goes nowhere, so read it as drifting when you should be choosing.

imageryHistory: In the Tarot de Marseille the card is called Le Mat, a ragged, bearded man walking with a stick and a bundle, and in most older decks he has no number at all. Pamela Colman Smith made him a young man in bright clothes stepping toward the edge of a cliff, and gave him the small white dog, the white rose, and the big sun behind him.

mathers.title: The Foolish Man
mathers.source: S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Tarot: Its Occult Signification, Use in Fortune-Telling, and Method of Play (1888)

olderMeanings.note: Mathers calls him the Foolish Man and reads folly, expiation, and wavering, a much gloomier card than the modern fresh start. Today's hopeful reading comes mostly from the occult writers of Waite's circle, who turned the fool into the soul at the very beginning.

name: The Magician
upright: You have what you need to make this happen. All four suit tools sit on the Magician's table, so skill, feeling, thought, and practical means are there for the using. This card is about focus and follow-through, taking an idea out of your head and doing something with it. It often turns up when someone is plainly capable but hasn't started. Pick the one thing and put your hands on it. The shadow side is skill used to impress or mislead, so check your motives and other people's.
reversed: When the Magician flips, the talent is there but it's leaking out sideways. Maybe you're spread across too many plans, or doubting skills other people can clearly see in you. There's an older, sharper meaning too: the smooth talker who uses charm and words to get their way. Watch for tricks, including the ones you play on yourself about why you can't begin yet. Sometimes the reversal is a con, and sometimes it's you doubting abilities you clearly have. Either way, look at who is doing the talking and whether the actions match.
sitWith: What's already on your table that you keep forgetting you have? What would you start today if you trusted what you already know?
inASpread: The Magician makes whatever sits around him more active, so an Ace or Page nearby says the idea is ready to be put to work now. If the Seven of Swords or the Moon shows up too, read him as the con artist and check who is being straight with whom. Early in a spread, it shows the person asking has more power in the situation than they think.
imagery: A figure in a red robe stands at a table laid with a cup, a sword, a wand, and a pentacle, one hand raising a wand to the sky and the other pointing to the ground, an infinity sign floating over his head. Every tool is already on the table, and he's the link between the idea up there and the thing made down here.

waite.upright: Skill, diplomacy, address, subtlety; sickness, pain, loss, disaster, snares of enemies; self-confidence, will; the Querent, if male.
waite.reversed: Physician, Magus, mental disease, disgrace, disquiet.
waite.picture: A youthful figure in the robe of a magician, having the countenance of divine Apollo, with smile of confidence and shining eyes. Above his head is the mysterious sign of the Holy Spirit, the sign of life, like an endless cord, forming the figure 8 in a horizontal position 8. About his waist is a serpent-cincture, the serpent appearing to devour its own tail. This is familiar to most as a conventional symbol of eternity, but here it indicates more especially the eternity of attainment in the spirit. In the Magician's right hand is a wand raised towards heaven, while the left hand is pointing to the earth. This dual sign is known in very high grades of the Instituted Mysteries; it shews the descent of grace, virtue and light, drawn from things above and derived to things below. The suggestion throughout is therefore the possession and communication of the Powers and Gifts of the Spirit. On the table in front of the Magician are the symbols of the four Tarot suits, signifying the elements of natural life, which lie like counters before the adept, and he adapts them as he wills. Beneath are roses and lilies, the flos campi and lilium convallium, changed into garden flowers, to shew the culture of aspiration.
waite.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911)

symbols.meaning: Endless life and a mind that can keep ideas moving. Waite's term is the sign of life, like an endless cord.
What is drawn from above is brought down to earth. The idea becomes a real thing through him.

symbols.symbol: Cup, sword, wand, and pentacle on the table
symbols.meaning: All four suits, meaning every tool you need is already within reach.
The ouroboros, a symbol of eternity and of skill that renews itself.
Desire and pure intent growing side by side in the garden he works.

history: The Marseille card is Le Bateleur, the juggler or street performer, and Italian decks call him Il Bagatto. The Visconti-Sforza painting seems to show him playing a table game like cups and balls. Waite's own list of older names runs from Magus to juggler, caster of the dice, and mountebank, and he and Smith turned the trickster into an adept with all four suit emblems laid before him.
numerologyAstrology: One is the first number that acts, the single point where things begin. Mercury is his planet in the Golden Dawn system, ruler of messages, skill, and quick hands, which is why he can be the master craftsman or the smooth talker.

upright.love: Confidence and good communication make the first move easy now. You can create the relationship you want by saying what you want, plainly, to the right person. Looking for someone? A date set up through a message or a mutual friend is likely to go well. With a partner, plan something new together, a trip or a project, and actually book it.
upright.work: You have the skills and the contacts; now use them. A pitch, an interview, or a launch goes well when you prepare like a pro and speak with conviction. Pitching, presenting, launching, and closing a deal all go well. Your skills are the selling point, so show them instead of describing them.
upright.money: A good time to start a side hustle, negotiate, or put your talents to paid use. Money comes from what you do with your hands and your head. Price your work properly, since undercharging is the usual leak with this card. Make the move while you're focused.
upright.advice: Pick one goal and put every tool you have toward it. Stop waiting for more resources; you already have enough to start. Use the tools you already own.
upright.asAPerson: Clever, charming, capable, often the one who makes things happen in a room. When they want you, they say so and act on it. They make hard things look easy and like being in charge of their own time.

yesNo.why: Everything needed for success is on the table. You have what it takes to make this happen.

reversed.love: Charm with nothing behind it, or games of words. Someone may be saying all the right things without meaning them, so watch actions over promises. Watch for smooth talk that doesn't match behavior, especially early on. In a settled couple, notice whether one of you is managing the other instead of being honest.
reversed.work: Talent wasted on too many half-projects, or a colleague who spins facts. Check contracts and claims carefully, including your own sales pitch. Scattered focus, a plan that sounds better than it is, or someone taking credit for your work. Get agreements in writing and keep your own records.
reversed.money: Schemes that sound brilliant and aren't, or skills you're underpricing out of doubt. Be wary of schemes, get-rich-quick pitches, or anyone rushing you to decide. Your own plans may also need more work before you put money in.
reversed.advice: Gather your scattered focus back into one place. Be honest about what you can deliver and ask others to do the same. Match your words with actions this week.
reversed.asAPerson: A manipulator or con artist in the worst case, or a gifted person who doubts themselves in the mildest. The feeling may be calculated rather than sincere. Clever and persuasive, and not always honest about their motives.

yesNo.why: Something isn't what it's presented as, or the skill isn't being used well yet.

waiteNote.upright: Waite gives a mixed list here. Skill, diplomacy, and address (an old word for smooth, clever handling of people) are the heart of it, along with subtlety, self-confidence, and will. The darker words, sickness, pain, and “snares of enemies”, reflect older fortune telling where this card could warn of trickery, so a modern reader keeps the skill and notes the risk of someone using it against you.
waiteNote.reversed: Reversed, Waite names the physician and the magus, people who work with hidden knowledge, and then mental disease, disgrace, and disquiet, which means unease. In practice it reads as talent turned sour: nerves, manipulation, or a clever plan that falls apart. It can also mean you have the skill and aren't using it.

imageryHistory: The oldest painted version of this card, from the fifteenth-century Italian decks, shows a conjurer playing with cups and balls at a table. The Tarot de Marseille kept him as Le Bateleur, a juggler or showman with his tools spread out. Smith and Waite turned him into a robed magician with one hand raised and one pointing down, with a wand, cup, sword, and pentacle on the table and an infinity sign over his head.

mathers.title: The Juggler
mathers.reversed: Will applied to evil ends, Weakness of Will, Cunning, Knavishness.
mathers.source: S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Tarot: Its Occult Signification, Use in Fortune-Telling, and Method of Play (1888)

olderMeanings.note: Mathers calls him the Juggler and lists will, willpower, and dexterity, very close to the modern reading. His reversal is sharper: will applied to evil ends, cunning, and knavishness, which means dishonest trickery.

name: The High Priestess
upright: Some things can't be figured out by thinking harder. The High Priestess sits still and simply knows, and she's pointing you toward the part of you that notices before it can explain. Dreams, gut feelings, and the odd sense that something isn't quite as it looks all belong to her. More often than not she's a card for waiting and watching. What you need to know will come clearer once you stop pushing for it. Not everything has to be solved today, and some answers only come when you stop pushing for them. Pay attention to dreams, gut feelings, and small signs that keep repeating.
reversed: Here the inner voice is being drowned out or brushed aside. You might be collecting everyone else's opinion and skipping your own, or ignoring a feeling you've had for weeks. Secrets belong here too: someone keeping information back, or things going on behind closed doors. Sometimes it's simpler: you've been too busy to hear yourself think. Waite's reversed meanings add passion and surface knowledge, so strong feelings or a shallow read of things may be crowding out what you actually know. Give yourself real quiet before you decide anything.
sitWith: What do you already know that you haven't said out loud? If you trusted that feeling completely, what would you do next?
inASpread: She quiets a spread down. With the Moon or the Seven of Swords close by, something hidden hasn't surfaced yet, and among a lot of Swords she can mean your head is arguing with what your gut already knows. Don't expect a plain yes or no from her as an outcome; the answer is still forming. Near a question about a person, she can mean there's more going on with them than they've shared.
imagery: A woman in blue sits calmly between a black pillar and a white one, a crescent moon at her feet and a half-hidden scroll marked TORA in her lap, with a veil of pomegranates hanging behind her. She guards what's behind the veil, and the partly covered scroll suggests some things are only learned by being quiet.

waite.upright: Secrets, mystery, the future as yet unrevealed; the woman who interests the Querent, if male; the Querent herself, if female; silence, tenacity; mystery, wisdom, science.
waite.reversed: Passion, moral or physical ardour, conceit, surface knowledge.
waite.picture: She has the lunar crescent at her feet, a horned diadem on her head, with a globe in the middle place, and a large solar cross on her breast. The scroll in her hands is inscribed with the word Tora, signifying the Greater Law, the Secret Law and the second sense of the Word. It is partly covered by her mantle, to shew that some things are implied and some spoken. She is seated between the white and black pillars—J. and B.—of the mystic Temple and the veil of the Temple is behind her: it is embroidered with palms and pomegranates.
waite.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911)

symbols.symbol: Black and white pillars marked B and J
symbols.meaning: Boaz and Jachin from Solomon's temple. She sits between opposites and holds the balance.
Waite says it's covered by her mantle to show some things are implied and some spoken.
Intuition, cycles, and the part of the mind that works at night.
What lies behind the veil stays hidden until you're ready; the fruit hints at hidden abundance.
A moon crown, linking her to the waxing, full, and waning phases.

history: La Papesse, the Popess, is her Marseille name, and the figure is often linked to the legend of Pope Joan. Historians have connected the Visconti-Sforza Papessa to Sister Manfreda, a relative of the Visconti elected pope by a small heretical sect in Lombardy. Waite rejected the Pope Joan idea, and he and Smith remade her as a High Priestess seated between the temple pillars with the scroll of the Law in her lap.
numerologyAstrology: Two is the first pairing, the number of reflection and balance between opposites, like the two pillars behind her. Her Golden Dawn planet is the Moon, which rules instinct, dreams, and things that change in the dark.

upright.love: Attraction that runs deeper than words, or a connection still forming quietly. Pay attention to what you sense about this person rather than what they say. Early dating may involve someone holding back, so let things unfold before you push for answers. In a long relationship, it's a quiet phase where what isn't said matters more than what is.
upright.work: Hold your cards close and don't rush a decision. Research, listen, and trust the quiet read you have on a situation or a colleague. Keep plans private for now and listen more than you talk in meetings. Research, study, and behind-the-scenes work are favored over public moves.
upright.money: Something hasn't come to light yet, so wait before signing or investing. Your gut is a better advisor than a hurried spreadsheet right now. Don't act on tips or rumors, and wait for full information before a big decision. Quietly reviewing your accounts is a good use of this card.
upright.advice: Get quiet and listen inward before acting. Keep some things private until they've had time to settle. Trust what you notice before anyone explains it.
upright.asAPerson: Private, perceptive, calm, sometimes hard to read; the one who notices everything. Real interest may be there, kept to themselves for now. They listen closely and remember everything you've told them.

yesNo.why: The answer is still hidden behind the veil; wait for more to show. The answer isn't fully visible yet, so wait for it.

reversed.love: Secrets, mixed signals, or ignoring what your gut already told you. There may be something you haven't been told, or something you aren't admitting to yourself. When you already sense something is off, give that feeling some weight.
reversed.work: Office gossip, hidden agendas, or information being withheld. Double-check what you're hearing before you act on it. An instinct you dismissed at work may turn out to have been right. Stay out of office politics and keep notes.
reversed.money: Poor instincts from being rushed or stressed, or financial details kept from you. Ask the direct question you've been avoiding. Hidden fees, fine print, or information someone left out. Read every document before signing.
reversed.advice: Turn the noise down and hear yourself again. If something feels off, give that feeling weight instead of talking yourself out of it. Get quiet before you decide.
reversed.asAPerson: Someone cold, secretive, or emotionally unreachable, or someone ruled by surface feelings. The interest may be there but tangled in things left unsaid. Hard to read, and sometimes cold when they feel exposed.

yesNo.why: Too much is hidden to give a clear yes right now. Something important hasn't come to light yet.

waiteNote.upright: Waite's words point to what isn't known yet: secrets, mystery, and “the future as yet unrevealed.” Silence and tenacity mean keeping quiet and holding on, and science here is the old word for knowledge of any kind. He also uses her to stand for a woman in the question, or for the woman asking, which is how older readers picked out people in a spread.
waiteNote.reversed: Reversed, Waite swaps her calm for passion and ardour, which means strong heat or eagerness, whether moral or physical. Conceit is thinking you know more than you do, and surface knowledge is exactly that. Read it as a moment when feelings or pride are drowning out the quiet inner voice.

imageryHistory: In the Tarot de Marseille this card is La Papesse, the Popess, a woman in a papal crown with a book in her lap and a curtain hanging behind her. Waite renamed her the High Priestess and had Smith seat her between two temple pillars marked B and J, with a veil of pomegranates behind her and a crescent moon at her feet.

mathers.title: The High Priestess
mathers.source: S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Tarot: Its Occult Signification, Use in Fortune-Telling, and Method of Play (1888)

goldenDawn.title: The Priestess of the Silver Star
goldenDawn.printed: The Priestess of the Silver Star
goldenDawn.source: Golden Dawn "Book T", printed as "Liber LXXVIII: A Description of the Cards of the Tarot" in The Equinox I:8 (1912)

olderMeanings.note: Mathers gives science, wisdom, knowledge, and education, so the older card was about learning more than intuition. The modern emphasis on inner knowing and secrets grew out of Waite's own mystical reading of her.

name: The Empress
upright: Things are growing. The Empress is abundance in the plainest sense: good food, a comfortable home, beauty, creativity, and care that actually nourishes. She can point to pregnancy or motherhood, but just as often to a project, a garden, or a relationship coming into bloom. She's also about enjoying your body and your senses without guilt. Let yourself be looked after, and look after what you love. This is growth that comes from care and time, the kind you can't rush. It often points to comfort, creativity, the body, and the pleasure of making something grow.
reversed: When she's reversed, the garden is being neglected, and usually it's yours. Perhaps you're pouring care into everyone else and running on empty, or feeling creatively dry and cut off from things that used to bring you pleasure. The fix tends to be basic and physical: rest, a real meal, time outside, making something for no reason at all. Care can turn into smothering, too, when caring for others leaves nothing for you. Check whether you've been giving from a full cup or an empty one.
sitWith: What in your life needs feeding right now, and what would feed you? Where could you let something grow at its own pace?
inASpread: Surrounded by Cups or Pentacles, the Empress turns up the comfort, love, and material plenty. Put her beside the Ten of Wands or the Four of Swords and the question becomes where caregiving has tipped into exhaustion. When she closes a reading, growth is coming at nature's pace, not yours. With the Ace of Cups or the Ten of Pentacles, it can point to a pregnancy, a new home, or family news.
imagery: A woman lounges on soft cushions in a ripe field of wheat, a forest and waterfall behind her, wearing a crown of twelve stars and a gown printed with pomegranates, a heart-shaped shield with the sign of Venus at her side. Everything around her is growing, which is what happens when living things are cared for.

waite.upright: Fruitfulness, action, initiative, length of days; the unknown, clandestine; also difficulty, doubt, ignorance.
waite.reversed: Light, truth, the unravelling of involved matters, public rejoicings; according to another reading, vacillation.
waite.picture: A stately figure, seated, having rich vestments and royal aspect, as of a daughter of heaven and earth. Her diadem is of twelve stars, gathered in a cluster. The symbol of Venus is on the shield which rests near her. A field of corn is ripening in front of her, and beyond there is a fall of water. The sceptre which she bears is surmounted by the globe of this world.
waite.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911)

symbols.meaning: Waite's text names a diadem of twelve stars; many readers link it to the months and to the woman crowned with stars.

symbols.symbol: Heart-shaped shield with the sign of Venus
symbols.meaning: Love, beauty, and the pleasures of the body.
Harvest and abundance that comes from patient growth.
Life flowing freely and nature left to thrive.
Fertility and fruitfulness, echoing the veil behind the High Priestess.

history: In older decks the Empress sits enthroned with a sceptre and a shield bearing an eagle, the emblem of the Holy Roman Empire. Waite noted that she is sometimes drawn full face while the Emperor is in profile, and said the difference carried no inner meaning. The starry crown, the shield of Venus, the wheat field, and the waterfall are additions by Waite's circle and Smith.
numerologyAstrology: Three is what two creates: the child, the growth, the result. Venus, planet of love, comfort, and beauty, is her Golden Dawn attribution, which is why she speaks of pleasure and plenty.

upright.love: Warmth, affection, and a relationship that feels nourishing. It can point to pregnancy or family plans, and at the very least to feeling cared for and desirable. You're magnetic when you feel good in your own skin, so start there if you're looking. Between partners, this is affection, sensuality, and sometimes talk of a family or a shared home.
upright.work: A nurturing boss or a team that feels like a family may be part of it. Creative projects flourish, and work that nurtures people or grows something slowly does well. Give a project the time it needs instead of forcing a quick result.
upright.money: Comfortable, with room for some beauty and pleasure. Investments in your home, your garden, or your craft pay back over time. Steady abundance, good food on the table, and comfort that comes from care. It's a good time to put money into things that grow slowly, like savings or a garden.
upright.advice: Feed yourself as well as you feed others. Slow down enough to enjoy what's already growing. Take care of your body and your comfort first.
upright.asAPerson: Warm, generous, sensual, maternal in the best sense, the friend whose kitchen is always open. What they feel for you is tender and affectionate. They make a room feel like home and notice when you're hungry.

yesNo.why: Things are growing well and will come to fruit.

reversed.love: Giving too much and getting little back, or care that turns clingy and controlling. It can also be a dry spell where you feel unattractive or overlooked. Neglecting yourself for a partner, or a relationship that feels more like caretaking than love. For anyone single, fill your own life before looking for someone to fill it.
reversed.work: Creative block, burnout, or a project that isn't getting the attention it needs. You may be mothering everyone at work and neglecting your own role. Deadlines may slip because the work has stopped being enjoyable. Rest and play may unstick it faster than effort.
reversed.money: Overspending on comfort, or money worries that come from putting others first every time. Check whether generosity has become a leak. Buying comfort after a hard week can add up faster than you notice. Look at where the money goes and whether it's feeding you back.
reversed.advice: Care for yourself first this week: sleep, food, fresh air. Let someone else carry some of the load. Give yourself the same care you give everyone else.
reversed.asAPerson: Someone smothering, dependent, or neglectful of themselves, or a caretaker running on empty. The feeling toward you may come with strings. Warm, but smothering or needy when they feel unappreciated.

yesNo.why: The ground needs tending before anything more can grow. Growth has slowed and needs tending first.

waiteNote.upright: Waite's main words are fruitfulness, action, initiative, and “length of days”, an old way of saying a long life. The strange second list, the unknown, clandestine (done in secret), difficulty, doubt, and ignorance, comes from older fortune-telling traditions he was collecting. Most readers keep the growth and abundance and treat the rest as a caution that some of what's growing isn't visible yet.
waiteNote.reversed: Reversed, Waite oddly gives mostly good words: light, truth, the unravelling of involved (tangled) matters, and public rejoicings. He adds vacillation, which means wavering back and forth. A modern reader usually reads the reversal as growth that's stalled or care that's been overdone, and notes that the truth coming out can be part of that.

imageryHistory: The Tarot de Marseille Empress sits on a throne cradling a shield with the imperial eagle in one arm and holding a sceptre topped with an orb and cross in the other. Waite and Smith made her a fruitful mother in a garden, with ripening wheat at her feet, pomegranates on her gown, a heart-shaped shield with the Venus sign, a crown of stars, and a waterfall behind her.

mathers.title: The Empress
mathers.upright: Action, Plan, Undertaking Movement in a matter, Initiative
mathers.reversed: Inaction, Frittering away of power, Want of Concentration Vacillation.
mathers.source: S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Tarot: Its Occult Signification, Use in Fortune-Telling, and Method of Play (1888)

goldenDawn.title: The Daughter of the Mighty Ones
goldenDawn.printed: The Daughter of the Mighty Ones
goldenDawn.source: Golden Dawn "Book T", printed as "Liber LXXVIII: A Description of the Cards of the Tarot" in The Equinox I:8 (1912)

olderMeanings.note: Mathers reads action, plan, undertaking, and initiative, so the older Empress was about getting things moving. The modern focus on motherhood, fertility, and nature comes from Waite's picture of the fruitful mother.

name: The Emperor
upright: The Emperor brings structure. He's the father figure, the boss, the one who sets the rules and keeps things running, and sometimes that person is you. This card favors plans, boundaries, discipline, and taking charge of a situation instead of hoping it sorts itself out. His power works because it's steady and you can count on it. If life feels chaotic, he says build a frame and stick to it. He brings order where things have been messy. A clear rule, a boundary, or a plan with steps is exactly what the situation needs.
reversed: Authority goes wrong in one of two ways when he flips. There's too much of it, the parent or boss who won't bend, or you gripping a plan so hard it cracks. Or there's too little, with no follow-through, no routine, and your power handed to someone else by default. Look at who is really in charge here and whether that's working for anyone. Rules may be applied to everyone except the person making them. It can also show you avoiding the structure you know would help.
sitWith: Where would one clear rule or boundary make your life easier? What rule are you ready to set for yourself?
inASpread: The Emperor and the Empress together make a picture of care and structure working as a team. Near the Five of Wands or the Knight of Swords, he often points to a clash with someone who wants control. In the final position, stability comes from taking responsibility and making the call yourself. Next to the Empress, he completes a picture of a stable home or partnership.
imagery: A bearded ruler in armor under a red robe sits on a stone throne carved with ram heads, holding a scepter and an orb, with bare orange mountains behind him. It's order built on hard ground, steady and protective, and not especially soft.

waite.upright: Stability, power, protection, realization; a great person; aid, reason, conviction; also authority and will.
waite.reversed: Benevolence, compassion, credit; also confusion to enemies, obstruction, immaturity.
waite.picture: He has a form of the Crux ansata for his sceptre and a globe in his left hand. He is a crowned monarch—commanding, stately, seated on a throne, the arms of which are fronted by rams' heads.
waite.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911)

symbols.meaning: Aries, the sign of this card, and the drive to lead and push forward.
A form of the Crux ansata, as Waite describes it: life and power held in one hand.
Rule over the world, and responsibility for keeping it in order.
He's ready to defend what he's built, even while sitting still.
A hard, dry place where only discipline and structure hold things up.

history: The Emperor has been in the deck since the earliest Italian cards, including the Visconti-Sforza, usually as a crowned ruler on a throne with a shield. Waite remarked that he was sometimes drawn wearing the stars or ribbons of an order of chivalry, which he took as proof that the cards mix old and new emblems. The rams' heads on the throne, pointing to Aries, came with the Golden Dawn attributions that Waite and Smith followed.
numerologyAstrology: Four is the square and the foundation: four walls, four corners, stability. His Golden Dawn sign is Aries, ruled by Mars, so this is order backed by the will to lead.

upright.love: Stability and commitment from someone who shows love by providing and protecting. A relationship built on clear roles and reliability rather than big romance. A single reader may be drawn to someone older or more settled, and that stability feels good.
upright.work: Leadership, structure, and taking charge. It's a good card for promotions, management, starting a business with a real plan, or dealing with authority. Dealing with a landlord, a manager or an official goes better if your facts are in order. Write the plan and the deadlines down so others can follow them.
upright.money: Budgets, long-term plans, and financial discipline. Security comes from rules you set and stick to. Paying bills on a fixed day and checking accounts weekly will do more than any clever scheme. A good time to organize accounts and set clear limits.
upright.advice: Take responsibility and set some structure. Decide, plan, and follow through like the person in charge, because you are. Make a plan and stick to it.
upright.asAPerson: Authoritative, steady, protective, sometimes stern; a father figure, boss, or someone used to making the call. Their regard for you is serious and loyal. They keep promises and expect you to keep yours.

yesNo.why: With a firm plan and steady effort, this holds. Stability and control are on your side.

reversed.love: It can also show the opposite, someone with no backbone who won't commit to anything. Control, jealousy, or a partner who makes all the decisions. If this is you, loosen your grip and ask what the other person wants.
reversed.work: A bully of a boss, rules that make no sense, or chaos where there should be structure. Watch for power struggles. Decisions stall because nobody will take responsibility for them. Work out which rules actually help and which just protect someone's ego.
reversed.money: Poor discipline, or a tight grip that turns into stinginess. Either the rules are missing or they've become a cage. Money used as control, or a lack of any plan at all. Set a simple budget and keep your own accounts.
reversed.advice: Check whether you're leading or just controlling. Loosen the grip where it's hurting, and firm it up where things have gone slack. Lead without controlling.
reversed.asAPerson: Domineering, cold, or stubborn, or weak and avoiding responsibility. The feeling may be possessive rather than caring. Stubborn and domineering, or oddly passive when it counts.

yesNo.why: Power is being misused or structure is missing. Power is out of balance right now.

waiteNote.upright: Waite reads the Emperor as stability, power, protection, and realization, which means making a plan real. He adds “a great person”, aid, reason, and conviction, meaning firm belief. A reader uses this as structure: rules, leadership, and someone steady who takes charge.
waiteNote.reversed: Reversed, Waite's words are softer than you'd expect: benevolence, compassion, and credit (trust or good standing), with “confusion to enemies”. Then come obstruction and immaturity, meaning something not ready or someone acting childish. Read it as authority that's too rigid, too weak, or not yet grown up.

imageryHistory: In the Tarot de Marseille the Emperor sits in profile on his throne with his legs crossed, and a shield with the imperial eagle rests on the ground beside him. Smith faced him forward on a stone throne carved with ram heads for Aries, the sign the Golden Dawn gave him, and set him against bare mountains.

mathers.title: The Emperor
mathers.source: S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Tarot: Its Occult Signification, Use in Fortune-Telling, and Method of Play (1888)

goldenDawn.title: Sun of the Morning, Chief Among the Mighty
goldenDawn.printed: Sun of the Morning, chief among the Mighty
goldenDawn.source: Golden Dawn "Book T", printed as "Liber LXXVIII: A Description of the Cards of the Tarot" in The Equinox I:8 (1912)

olderMeanings.note: Mathers reads realisation, effect, and development, with a reversal of stoppage, check, and things immature or unripe. That fits the modern card closely, since both see him as the force that makes a plan happen.

name: The Hierophant
upright: The Hierophant stands for schools, churches, mentors, families, and any group with shared rules and rituals. In a reading it often means learning from someone who's been there, or choosing the conventional route: the degree, the wedding, the proven method. There's real comfort in that. You don't have to invent everything from scratch. Ceremonies belong here too: weddings, graduations and religious rites that mark a change in front of others. It's also a card of learning a practice properly from someone who knows.
reversed: Upside down, the rules start to chafe. Maybe you're questioning something you were raised to believe, or feeling boxed in by a family expectation, a workplace, or a group that doesn't make room for difference. That can be healthy, a sign you're finding your own way. That questioning can turn into rebellion for its own sake, though, tossing out what's useful just because it's old. Sort out which beliefs are actually yours. Waite's reversed list includes overkindness and weakness, the kind of going along to keep the peace that leaves you unheard. Take your time deciding what to keep and what to let go.
sitWith: Which rule do you follow because you believe in it, and which because you were told to? Who has taught you something you still rely on?
inASpread: Beside the Lovers or the Two of Cups, the Hierophant often means marriage or another formal commitment. A spread full of Wands, or the Fool nearby, sets up a tug between doing things by the book and striking out alone. If it's the outcome, look for the answer in a teacher, a community, or a method that's already been tested. Beside the Devil, it can show a group or a rule that has become controlling.
imagery: A religious leader in red robes and a triple crown sits between two gray pillars, raising a hand in blessing over two kneeling monks, with crossed keys at his feet. The keys and the students point to knowledge that gets handed down through an institution.

waite.upright: Marriage, alliance, captivity, servitude; by another account, mercy and goodness; inspiration; the man to whom the Querent has recourse.
waite.reversed: Society, good understanding, concord, over-kindness, weakness.
waite.picture: He wears the triple crown and is seated between two pillars, but they are not those of the Temple which is guarded by the High Priestess. In his left hand he holds a sceptre terminating in the triple cross, and with his right hand he gives the well-known ecclesiastical sign which is called that of esotericism, distinguishing between the manifest and concealed part of doctrine. It is noticeable in this connexion that the High Priestess makes no sign. At his feet are the crossed keys, and two priestly ministers in albs kneel before him.
waite.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911)

symbols.meaning: Authority over three worlds, a sign of high religious office.
The keys of heaven: access to knowledge that's passed down through an institution.
Students or followers receiving teaching, the passing on of tradition.
This is the ecclesiastical sign, in Waite's account, that separates the open and hidden parts of doctrine.
The outer temple, unlike the High Priestess's black and white ones.

history: In the Marseille deck he is Le Pape, the Pope, and Waite notes the card was sometimes also called the Abbot. The name Hierophant goes back to Court de Gebelin in the eighteenth century, who took it from the chief priest of the Eleusinian Mysteries while wrongly believing the tarot came from ancient Egypt. Smith kept the papal tiara, the crossed keys, and the two kneeling ministers from the traditional design.
numerologyAstrology: Five follows the stability of four with something that disrupts or adds; here it adds a teacher who explains the rules. His sign in the Golden Dawn scheme is Taurus, a steady earth sign, which fits a card of custom and staying with what's proven.

upright.love: Commitment in the traditional sense: marriage, engagement, meeting the family. Shared values and doing things properly matter here. Someone unattached may meet a partner through a class, faith group, or community they belong to.
upright.work: Institutions, training, mentors, and doing it by the book. A good card for school, certification, or joining an established company. Established companies, training programs, and mentors. Learn the system before you try to change it.
upright.money: Conventional, safe choices: pensions, banks, sound advice from a qualified professional. Not the time for wild experiments. A mortgage adviser, an accountant or a bank's standard product suits this card better than a hot tip. Stick with tested options.
upright.advice: Learn from someone who knows the ground, or follow the method that's already been tested. Tradition exists for reasons. Find a good teacher and listen.
upright.asAPerson: A teacher, counselor, priest, or rule-follower; someone who values tradition and belonging. Toward you they're serious, conventional, and loyal. They like rules, rituals, and doing things properly.

yesNo.why: Following the established path leads to a good result. The traditional route will work here.

reversed.love: Pressure from family or culture to be a certain kind of couple, or a relationship that breaks the rules. It can mean resisting convention or feeling boxed in by it. Pressure to follow a script, or a relationship that doesn't fit what family expects. Decide what you want before you worry about what's proper.
reversed.work: Red tape, rigid bosses, or outgrowing the institution you're in. You may want to learn your own way rather than follow the manual. Pushing back against outdated rules, or a boss who hides behind policy. Question the system carefully and bring a better idea with you.
reversed.money: Bad advice from an authority, or rules that no longer suit your situation. Question the fee, the fund, or the expert. Unconventional choices, or bad advice from someone with a title. Get a second opinion before you trust authority.
reversed.advice: Keep the parts of tradition that help you and put down the rest. You're allowed to question what you were taught. Talk to someone who left the same path and ask what they kept.
reversed.asAPerson: Dogmatic, preachy, or a rebel for the sake of it. The feeling may be tied up in duty or in what other people will think. A rebel, or someone rigid who follows rules they don't understand.

yesNo.why: The usual route isn't working here. The usual way won't get you what you need.

waiteNote.upright: Waite names marriage and alliance, but also captivity and servitude, meaning being bound by duty. Mercy and goodness come from another tradition he was quoting, and “the man to whom the Querent has recourse” means the person you turn to for advice, such as a priest, teacher, or counselor. In practice this card is about tradition, formal commitments, and wise guidance.
waiteNote.reversed: Reversed, Waite gives society, good understanding, and concord, which means agreement, and then over-kindness and weakness. A modern reader takes it as rules followed too blindly or rejected too quickly, or being so agreeable that you lose your own view.

imageryHistory: In the Tarot de Marseille this card is Le Pape, the Pope, a bearded figure in a triple crown and red cloak holding a triple cross. The name Hierophant came from the eighteenth-century French writer Court de Gébelin, who wanted a less Christian title, and Smith still drew a robed churchman with two kneeling clerics and crossed keys at his feet.

mathers.title: The Hierophant or Pope
mathers.reversed: Over-kindness, weakness, Foolish exercise of generosity.
mathers.source: S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Tarot: Its Occult Signification, Use in Fortune-Telling, and Method of Play (1888)

goldenDawn.title: The Magus of the Eternal
goldenDawn.printed: The Magus of the Eternal
goldenDawn.source: Golden Dawn "Book T", printed as "Liber LXXVIII: A Description of the Cards of the Tarot" in The Equinox I:8 (1912)

olderMeanings.note: Mathers reads mercy, beneficence, kindness, and goodness, with a reversal of over-kindness and foolish generosity. So the older card was about charity, while the modern one leans toward tradition and institutions.

name: The Lovers
upright: Love is part of this card, and so is choice. On the love side, it's a relationship with real closeness and honesty, where two people truly see each other. On the choice side, it's a decision that says something about who you are and what you value. Waite himself read it as a card of trial as much as attraction. Whatever the question, choose with your whole heart and not just half of it. In a reading about work or home, it can mean a partnership where each side brings what the other lacks. Two people, or two parts of your life, come together because they genuinely fit.
reversed: In a relationship, the reversed Lovers can mean the two of you have drifted, one is giving more than the other, or you want different things. Temptation is another reading, or a choice made for the wrong reasons. Inside yourself, it may show a gap between what you say you care about and what you're actually doing. Honesty is the way back, and it starts with being honest with yourself. Often it's a choice you keep avoiding, hoping someone else will make it for you. Name what you actually value, and the decision gets clearer.
sitWith: What choice in front of you says the most about who you want to be? What would you choose if no one else's opinion counted?
inASpread: Cups around the Lovers, especially the Two or the Ten, make this a romance reading. The Devil or the Seven of Cups nearby tilts it toward temptation, a choice that needs a harder look. At the end of a spread, it hands the decision back to you rather than promising a result. With the Two of Cups, it strongly confirms a real partnership.
imagery: A naked man and woman stand under a huge angel in the sun, a tree of flames behind him and a fruit tree with a serpent behind her, a mountain rising between them. It echoes Eden: closeness, trust, and a choice that carries weight.

waite.upright: Attraction, love, beauty, trials overcome.
waite.reversed: Failure, foolish designs. Another account speaks of marriage frustrated and contrarieties of all kinds.
waite.picture: The sun shines in the zenith, and beneath is a great winged figure with arms extended, pouring down influences. In the foreground are two human figures, male and female, unveiled before each other, as if Adam and Eve when they first occupied the paradise of the earthly body. Behind the man is the Tree of Life, bearing twelve fruits, and the Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil is behind the woman; the serpent is twining round it.
waite.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911)

symbols.meaning: A great winged figure pours down influences, and many readers take it to be Raphael.
Adam and Eve before the Fall: honesty with nothing hidden between them.

symbols.symbol: Tree with the serpent behind the woman
symbols.meaning: The Tree of Knowledge and the pull of temptation.

symbols.symbol: Tree of flames behind the man
symbols.meaning: Waite's Tree of Life, bearing twelve fruits.
An obstacle or height that the pair face together.

history: The Marseille card is L'Amoureux, the Lover, and it shows a young man standing between two women with Cupid aiming an arrow from above. Waite describes an eighteenth-century form showing married life, father and mother with a child, under a flying Cupid. For the Rider-Waite-Smith deck he replaced these with Adam and Eve in the garden beneath an angel, which cut the human figures from three to two.
numerologyAstrology: Six is the number of harmony and exchange between two sides. Its Golden Dawn sign is Gemini, the twins, ruled by Mercury, so this is a card of pairs and of choices talked through.

upright.love: It can also mark a big decision about a relationship that you make with your whole heart. Deep attraction and real compatibility, the kind that feels easy and right. A new person who shares your values could appear, and a couple can use this time to choose each other again.
upright.work: A partnership that clicks, or a choice about work that should follow your values. Look for collaboration where you share the same goals. A partnership, a collaboration, or a career choice that reflects who you are. Pick the path that matches your values over the one that only pays.
upright.money: Joint finances or a financial choice that reflects what you truly care about. Decide together and be open about numbers. Shared finances go well when you're honest about what matters. Talk openly with a partner before you combine money.
upright.advice: Choose what you actually value, even if something else is easier. Be honest with yourself and with the other person. Choose with your heart and stand by it.
upright.asAPerson: Loving, open, and attractive, often someone who feels like a mirror of you. As a feeling toward you, it's strong mutual attraction. Warm and loyal, and willing to talk about the hard stuff.

yesNo.why: A wholehearted yes, if the choice matches your values. The heart and the choice line up.

reversed.love: Imbalance, mixed feelings, or temptation from outside the relationship. One person may be more invested, or values have started to pull apart. Mixed values, temptation, or two people who want different things. On your own, notice whether you're choosing from loneliness.
reversed.work: A partnership that's lost its shared purpose, or a choice made for money that bothers your conscience. Communication has broken down somewhere. A partnership that isn't working, or a decision you keep putting off. Get clear on your values before you commit to anything.
reversed.money: Disagreements about spending, or a decision that's out of line with what you believe in. Talk it through before signing anything jointly. One of you may be spending in secret, or saving in secret, and it needs to come out. Get on the same page before a big purchase.
reversed.advice: Be honest about where your heart and your choices have split apart. Make the harder, truer choice. Name what you value, then decide.
reversed.asAPerson: Someone indecisive, unfaithful, or unsure what they want. The feeling toward you may be strong but conflicted. Torn, indecisive, or hiding how they really feel.

yesNo.why: The choice is split or the match isn't sitting right.

waiteNote.upright: Waite's upright meaning is short and happy: attraction, love, beauty, and trials overcome, meaning tests you've come through. The simplest reading is love, and the deeper one is a choice made from the heart. Readers use it for relationships and for any decision that says something about who you are.
waiteNote.reversed: Reversed, Waite gives failure and foolish designs, which means plans that were never wise. Another tradition he quotes speaks of marriage frustrated and “contrarieties of all kinds”, an old word for things going against you. Read it as a mismatch, a hard choice avoided, or values pulling apart.

imageryHistory: The Tarot de Marseille card, L'Amoureux, shows a young man standing between two women while Cupid aims an arrow at him from above, a scene often compared to the old story of Hercules choosing between Vice and Virtue. Waite and Smith replaced it with Adam and Eve in the garden, the tree of fruit and the tree of flames behind them, and a great angel over them in the clouds.

mathers.title: The Lovers
mathers.reversed: Unwise Plans, Failure when put to the test.
mathers.source: S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Tarot: Its Occult Signification, Use in Fortune-Telling, and Method of Play (1888)

goldenDawn.title: The Children of the Voice; the Oracles of the Mighty Gods
goldenDawn.printed: The Children of the Voice; the Oracles of the Mighty Gods
goldenDawn.source: Golden Dawn "Book T", printed as "Liber LXXVIII: A Description of the Cards of the Tarot" in The Equinox I:8 (1912)

olderMeanings.note: Mathers reads wise dispositions, proof, and trials surmounted, which means a test passed. His reversal is unwise plans and failure when put to the test, so the older card was about sound choices more than romance.

name: The Chariot
upright: Here comes a push forward. The Chariot is about drive, determination, and winning through self-control. Two sphinxes want to go in different directions and the driver keeps them on course without reins, which is what this card asks of you: pull your mixed feelings together and go. It's good news for competitions, travel, big goals, anything that needs you to stay on track. You can get there if you don't let yourself get pulled off course. A literal trip, a move, or a new car fits this card too. Focus, discipline, and a clear destination are what move things forward now.
reversed: The wheels are stuck or the whole thing is swerving. You might feel pulled between two goals, or unsure where you're even headed, so you end up going nowhere. Or the problem runs the other way: forcing things through, pushing people aside, winning the argument and losing the point. There can also be a plan that has simply got away from you. Work out which way you want to go before you push harder. Sometimes it's a win you're pushing too hard for. Check whether you're driving or just being dragged.
sitWith: Which two parts of you are pulling in different directions? Where do you need discipline more than speed?
inASpread: Paired with the Eight of Wands or the Six of Swords, the Chariot can mean literal travel or a fast move. When the Two of Swords or the Seven of Cups sits next to it, a direction has to be chosen before any progress happens. In the outcome spot it's a win, earned by effort and focus. In an outcome position, it says the effort will pay off if you stay on course.
imagery: An armored driver stands in a chariot under a canopy of stars, pulled by two sphinxes, one black and one white, and he holds no reins at all. He steers by willpower, keeping two opposite forces moving the same way.

waite.upright: Succour, providence; also war, triumph, presumption, vengeance, trouble.
waite.reversed: Riot, quarrel, dispute, litigation, defeat.
waite.picture: An erect and princely figure carrying a drawn sword and corresponding, broadly speaking, to the traditional description which I have given in the first part. On the shoulders of the victorious hero are supposed to be the Urim and Thummim. He has led captivity captive; he is conquest on all planes—in the mind, in science, in progress, in certain trials of initiation. He has thus replied to the sphinx, and it is on this account that I have accepted the variation of Éliphas Lévi; two sphinxes thus draw his chariot.
waite.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911)

symbols.meaning: Opposing forces pulling in different directions; he steers them by will, with no reins.
Protection from above and a sense of destiny behind the drive.
They are supposed to be the Urim and Thummim, Waite notes, oracle stones of the high priest.
What he's leaving behind to go out and win.
Earthly strength and solid purpose under the armor.

history: Le Chariot, the Marseille version, shows a crowned figure in a car drawn by two horses. Waite notes that eighteenth-century decks yoked white horses to it, and that other animals such as a lion and a leopard were also used in some versions. The two sphinxes came from Eliphas Levi, and Waite says outright that he accepted Levi's variation.
numerologyAstrology: Seven is the number of challenge and testing, the point where you have to push past what's comfortable. Cancer, a water sign with a hard shell, is the card's sign in Golden Dawn astrology, so this is will protecting something tender underneath.

upright.love: Taking charge of your love life, or pushing through obstacles together. A relationship that moves forward because both people are determined. Looking for love, go after what you want instead of waiting to be found.
upright.work: Drive, ambition, and winning. You can beat the competition, meet the deadline, or get the role, if you stay focused and disciplined. Ambition, a hard-won promotion, or a project you steer to success. Stay focused on the finish line and don't get pulled into side battles.
upright.money: Progress through hard work and control. A goal you've been chasing is within reach if you don't let spending wander. Financial goals reached through discipline. Stick to your plan and don't let one expense throw you off course.
upright.advice: Decide where you're going and hold the course. Keep your feelings in check long enough to finish. Pick a direction and don't let go.
upright.asAPerson: Determined, competitive, confident, sometimes a bit guarded; someone who gets things done. Once they decide on you, they pursue it directly. Driven and competitive, and fiercely loyal to their own.

yesNo.why: Determination wins this one. Willpower and focus win this one.

reversed.love: Trying to force a relationship forward, or two people pulling in opposite directions. Control may be standing in for trust. Arguments over where the relationship is heading can stall it altogether. Chasing someone who keeps running is part of this card, too.
reversed.work: Losing direction, stalled progress, or aggression that backfires. You might be pushing hard and getting nowhere because the aim isn't clear. Burnout from pushing too hard, or conflict with coworkers over direction. Step back, regroup, and choose one goal.
reversed.money: Impulsive spending, or a plan that stalls because nobody is steering it. Waite's reversed card is riot, quarrel, and defeat, so take the reins again with a written budget before costs run off in two directions. Reckless spending to prove a point, or plans that crash from lack of control. Slow down and review.
reversed.advice: Stop and choose a direction before pushing harder. Force without focus just spins the wheels. Take back the reins.
reversed.asAPerson: Aggressive, controlling, or scattered and aimless. The feeling toward you may be intense but pulling in two directions. Aggressive when crossed and sometimes careless of others.

yesNo.why: Too much force or too little direction right now. Things are out of control and need steadying first.

waiteNote.upright: Waite starts with succour (help in time of need) and providence, meaning care from above, then war, triumph, presumption (overconfidence), vengeance, and trouble. Put together, it's victory that has to be fought for. A reader takes it as willpower and drive, with a warning not to get arrogant once you're winning.
waiteNote.reversed: Reversed, Waite gives riot, quarrel, dispute, litigation (lawsuits), and defeat. In practice this is the drive going out of control or turning into conflict. It can also mean a push that stalls because you're fighting everyone at once.

imageryHistory: In the Tarot de Marseille a crowned charioteer stands in a square cart under a canopy, pulled by two horses seen from the front, a design that stayed almost the same for nearly four hundred years. Waite followed the French occultists in using sphinxes instead of horses, and Smith set the charioteer in a square stone chariot under a canopy of stars, with a walled city behind him.

mathers.title: The Chariot
mathers.reversed: Overthrown, Conquered by Obstacles at the last moment.
mathers.source: S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Tarot: Its Occult Signification, Use in Fortune-Telling, and Method of Play (1888)

goldenDawn.title: The Child of the Powers of the Waters; the Lord of the Triumph of Light
goldenDawn.printed: The Child of the Powers of the Waters; the Lord of the Triumph of Light
goldenDawn.source: Golden Dawn "Book T", printed as "Liber LXXVIII: A Description of the Cards of the Tarot" in The Equinox I:8 (1912)

olderMeanings.note: Mathers gives triumph, victory, and overcoming obstacles, the same as today. His reversal is being overthrown or conquered by obstacles at the last moment, a vivid picture of a win that slips away.

name: Strength
upright: Strength is quiet courage. The woman handles a lion with her bare hands and a calm face, and that's the kind of strength this card means: patience, gentleness, and steady nerve. It can point to handling your own temper, fear, or cravings with kindness instead of harshness. The same goes for dealing with a difficult person without losing your cool. You're tougher than you feel right now. It's also a good sign for health and recovery, with the body finding its steadiness again. It says you can handle this, and that patience will work where force wouldn't.
reversed: Self-doubt tends to take over when Strength flips. You may feel weak, anxious, or at the mercy of feelings you can't manage. Sometimes the lion wins, and that looks like snapping at people, giving in to urges, or letting frustration run the day. Other times the woman is pressing too hard, pushing feelings down until they come out sideways. Find the small bit of courage you still have and start there. Waite also lists abuse of power, so it may be someone else bullying where they should be gentle. It can also be anger you've been holding in too long.
sitWith: What would change if you treated your hardest feeling with patience instead of force? What would kindness toward yourself look like right now?
inASpread: Strength steadies harder cards around it; beside the Nine of Wands or the Five of Pentacles, it says you have more staying power than things suggest. Compare it with the Chariot if both appear, since one pushes and the other persuades. Landing last, it means getting through with patience and heart. Next to the Chariot, it contrasts gentle strength with forceful drive, and gentle usually wins.
imagery: A woman in white, with an infinity sign above her head and a belt of flowers, gently closes the jaws of a lion with her bare hands. There's no fight here; the lion has been calmed by her patience.

waite.upright: Power, energy, action, courage, magnanimity; also complete success and honours.
waite.reversed: Despotism, abuse of power, weakness, discord, sometimes even disgrace.
waite.picture: The only point in which this design differs from the conventional presentations is that her beneficent fortitude has already subdued the lion, which is being led by a chain of flowers.
waite.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911)

symbols.meaning: Gentle strength that tames wild instinct without a fight.
The same sign of life as the Magician's: endless patience and spiritual strength.
Waite says it signifies the sweet yoke and light burden; control that works through love rather than force.
Purity of intent and a calm heart.
Passion, anger, fear, and desire: the wild parts that need a kind hand.

history: Historically the card was called Fortitude, one of the cardinal virtues. In the Marseille deck La Force is number XI and Justice is VIII; Waite swapped them to match the Golden Dawn attributions of Leo to the eighth card and Libra to the eleventh, saying only that his reasons satisfied himself. He notes that in the version printed by Court de Gebelin the woman is plainly opening the lion's mouth, while most show her closing it.
numerologyAstrology: Eight is the number of power and mastery, and here the power is inner. Its Golden Dawn sign is Leo, the lion, ruled by the Sun, which gives the card its warmth and courage.

upright.love: Kindness wins more than pressure, especially with someone who's been hurt. Patience, compassion, and staying steady through a rough patch. Confidence makes you attractive when you're dating, and you don't need to chase anyone.
upright.work: Quiet confidence and self-control carry you through a hard situation. A difficult client or colleague responds to calm firmness. Handling a difficult person or situation with grace. Staying calm under pressure gets you respect and results.
upright.money: Steady discipline and restraint, especially with impulse spending. You're stronger than the urge to splurge. Self-control around spending, and steady progress. Resist impulse buys and let patience build savings.
upright.advice: Be gentle with yourself and with others, and don't back down. Courage can be quiet. Be gentle and stay steady.
upright.asAPerson: Warm, brave, patient, and emotionally strong; someone who stays calm in a crisis. Their care for you is steady and protective. They're calm in a crisis and kind to animals and children.

yesNo.why: Patience and courage bring this home. You have the strength to see this through.

reversed.love: Insecurity, jealousy, or anger breaking through. You may doubt your worth in the relationship, or someone's temper is getting the better of them. Jealousy, insecurity, or losing your temper with someone you love. Work on self-trust before looking to a partner for reassurance.
reversed.work: Self-doubt, burnout, or losing your cool under pressure. The inner lion is either roaring or cowering. Feeling overwhelmed, or letting frustration show at the wrong moment. Take a breath before you reply.
reversed.money: Giving in to a craving, whether a spree, a gamble, or comfort shopping, or making money choices out of fear. Small, patient wins rebuild the confidence to handle it calmly. Impulse spending when stressed, or feeling helpless about money. One small step back in control helps.
reversed.advice: Find your nerve again with small, kind steps. Treat your fears the way the woman treats the lion. Remember you're stronger than this feeling.
reversed.asAPerson: Someone insecure, short-tempered, or overbearing. The feeling toward you might be strong but not well managed. Anxious or quick-tempered when they feel unsure.

yesNo.why: Confidence needs rebuilding before this goes well. Fear or doubt is getting in the way.

waiteNote.upright: Waite calls this card Fortitude in his list, an old word for courage that lasts. He names power, “energy”, action, courage, and magnanimity, which means a generous, big-hearted spirit, plus complete success and honours. Readers apply it as strength that comes from patience and kindness more than force.
waiteNote.reversed: Reversed, Waite gives despotism (ruling like a tyrant), abuse of power, weakness, discord, and sometimes disgrace. In practice this is strength that's gone wrong, either bullying or collapsing. It can also mean losing your temper or your nerve.

imageryHistory: In the Tarot de Marseille the card is called La Force and numbered XI, a woman calmly prying open a lion's jaws. The Golden Dawn and Waite moved it to number VIII to fit their astrology, swapping places with Justice, and Smith drew the woman closing the lion's mouth with an infinity sign over her head.

mathers.title: Themis, or Justice
mathers.reversed: Bigotry, Want of Balance, Abuse of Justice, Over-severity, Inequality, Bias.
mathers.source: S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Tarot: Its Occult Signification, Use in Fortune-Telling, and Method of Play (1888)

goldenDawn.title: The Daughter of the Lords of Truth: the Ruler of the Balance
goldenDawn.printed: The Daughter of the Lords of Truth: the Ruler of the Balance
goldenDawn.source: Golden Dawn "Book T", printed as "Liber LXXVIII: A Description of the Cards of the Tarot" in The Equinox I:8 (1912)

olderMeanings.note: Mathers reads power, might, force, strength, and fortitude, with a reversal of abuse of power and want of fortitude. That's close to today, though the modern card stresses gentleness more than raw might.

name: The Hermit
upright: Time to step back. The Hermit is about solitude, reflection, and looking for answers inside yourself instead of in the noise around you. It can mean taking a break from socializing, going on a retreat, or just spending more evenings alone thinking things through. He's also the wise teacher or guide who has walked this way before. His lantern only lights a few steps ahead, and that's enough. Stepping back from the noise is how answers come now. Time alone, study, or a long walk will show you what all the advice couldn't.
reversed: Solitude has soured into isolation, or it's being avoided altogether. One version is cutting yourself off from people who care about you and calling it independence. Or you could be so uneasy being alone with your thoughts that you keep yourself busy every minute. Now and then it simply means coming back out after a long quiet stretch. Ask yourself whether you're pulling away to heal or to hide. There may be loneliness in it, the kind you didn't choose. If you've been cut off too long, reach out to one person.
sitWith: What would you hear if you gave yourself a whole evening of quiet? What have you been too busy to notice?
inASpread: Where the Hermit sits with the Four of Swords or the Eight of Cups, rest, retreat, or walking away for a while is strongly marked. Among busy Wands or the Three of Cups, there's a pull between a full social life and a need for quiet. Answers from this card come from within, and slowly. Reversed near the Five of Pentacles, it can show isolation that has gone on too long.
imagery: An old man in a gray cloak stands alone on a snowy peak, holding up a lantern with a six-pointed star inside and leaning on a long staff. He's climbed away from everyone to find his own light, and he holds it up for whoever is coming behind him.

waite.upright: Prudence, circumspection; also and especially treason, dissimulation, roguery, corruption.
waite.reversed: Concealment, disguise, policy, fear, unreasoned caution.
waite.picture: The variation from the conventional models in this card is only that the lamp is not enveloped partially in the mantle of its bearer, who blends the idea of the Ancient of Days with the Light of the World. It is a star which shines in the lantern. I have said that this is a card of attainment, and to extend this conception the figure is seen holding up his beacon on an eminence.
waite.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911)

symbols.meaning: Waite says it is a star that shines in the lantern: wisdom lighting the next step.
Discretion and withdrawal from the noise of daily life.
Support on a hard path, and the authority of experience.
He has already climbed; the height itself is attainment as well as search.
Humility and inward attention.

history: Waite lists his older names as the Capuchin and, more philosophically, the Sage. On the fifteenth-century Visconti-Sforza card the old man carries an hourglass, which ties him to Time, while later decks gave him a lantern; the Marseille card is L'Hermite. Waite says his only change was that the lamp is no longer half hidden inside the cloak, and he describes the Hermit as holding up his beacon on a height.
numerologyAstrology: Nine is the last single digit, the point near the end where you step back to reflect. Virgo, a careful earth sign ruled by Mercury, belongs to him in the Golden Dawn system, which suits patient study and discernment.

upright.love: Time alone to work out what you want, or a quiet, slow-building relationship. If you're single, this can be a healthy break from dating. Time alone before you're ready for someone, or a partner who needs space. Respect the quiet and don't read it as rejection.
upright.work: Research, study, expertise, and working independently. Take time to think before your next career move. Independent work, research, or a pause to rethink your direction. A mentor or quiet expert may give the advice you need.
upright.money: Cautious, private planning, done away from the noise of other people's tips. Avoid flashy moves and trust the careful decisions you reach alone, lamp in hand. Careful spending, reviewing your finances alone, and saying no to pressure. Take your time before a decision.
upright.advice: Step away from the crowd and listen to yourself for a while. The answer comes in quiet, one lamp-lit step at a time. Give yourself some quiet.
upright.asAPerson: Wise, reserved, introspective, maybe a mentor or someone who keeps to themselves. The feeling toward you may be real but slow to show. Thoughtful, private, and wise when you finally get them talking.

yesNo.why: More time and reflection are needed first. Wait and reflect before you act.

reversed.love: Loneliness, or pushing people away when you actually want closeness. It can also mean avoiding time alone by staying busy with others. Loneliness, withdrawal, or shutting someone out. Isolation may be keeping you from people who'd welcome you.
reversed.work: Isolation at work, or refusing advice when you need it. Too much solitude can turn into stubbornness. Working in isolation too long, or avoiding feedback. Share your work with someone you trust. A team that never hears from you starts making choices without you.
reversed.money: Hoarding out of fear or avoiding looking at your finances. Ask a trusted expert for input. Cash kept in a drawer or an account that pays nothing may be losing value while you wait. Face them with someone you trust. Avoidance usually costs more than the bill you're hiding from.
reversed.advice: Come out of the cave for a bit. Share what you've learned and let someone in. Reach out to one person today.
reversed.asAPerson: Withdrawn, cold, or bitter; someone who has cut themselves off. Whatever they feel may be buried under distance. Withdrawn or suspicious, and hard to get close to.

yesNo.why: Isolation or avoidance is blocking the way. Reaching out for advice would change the answer.

waiteNote.upright: Waite gives prudence and circumspection, which both mean careful caution and looking all around before acting. Then, surprisingly, he adds “treason, dissimulation, roguery, corruption”, which means betrayal, hiding the truth, and dishonesty. A modern reader keeps the careful, solitary wisdom and treats the rest as a sign that too much secrecy can go bad.
