waiteNote.reversed: Reversed, Waite names concealment, disguise, policy (clever self-interest), fear, and unreasoned caution, which means being careful for no good reason. In practice it's isolation that has become hiding, or caution that has turned into fear.

imageryHistory: In fifteenth-century Italian decks this figure was an old man standing for Time, holding an hourglass, and by the end of that century the hourglass had been replaced by a lantern. The Tarot de Marseille Hermit is an old seeker with a lantern and staff, and Smith set him alone on a snowy peak with a six-pointed star shining in his lantern.

mathers.title: The Hermit
mathers.source: S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Tarot: Its Occult Signification, Use in Fortune-Telling, and Method of Play (1888)

goldenDawn.title: The Magus of the Voice of Power, the Prophet of the Eternal
goldenDawn.printed: The Magus of the Voice of Power, the Prophet of the Eternal
goldenDawn.source: Golden Dawn "Book T", printed as "Liber LXXVIII: A Description of the Cards of the Tarot" in The Equinox I:8 (1912)

olderMeanings.note: Mathers reads prudence, caution, and deliberation, and reversed, over-prudence, timorousness (timidity), and fear. That's close to today's reading, though the modern card leans more toward solitude and soul searching.

name: Wheel of Fortune
upright: The wheel is turning. This card is about luck, cycles, and turning points that come from outside your control. Most often it shows up as a change for the better: a lucky break, good timing, a door opening when you didn't expect it. It also carries the old truth that nothing stays the same, good times or bad. Pay attention to what's shifting and be ready to move with it. Change is coming whether you plan for it or not, and this time it's in your favor. It's a card of timing and lucky breaks, and of noticing patterns in your life.
reversed: Luck seems to have turned against you, or things are going round in the same loop. A setback may feel unfair, or you keep repeating a pattern and wondering how you ended up here again. Bad runs end too. Work on what's in your hands to change and loosen your grip on the rest. Often you're resisting a change that's already happening. Ask what you'd do if you accepted the turn instead of fighting it.
sitWith: What keeps coming back around in your life? What cycle keeps repeating, and what would break it?
inASpread: The cards near the Wheel tell you which way it's turning. The Sun or the Star beside it means luck coming your way, while after the Tower or the Ten of Swords it says a hard change is part of a cycle that will turn again. In the final position, change is coming, often sooner than planned. Surrounded by Majors, it shows big life changes moving quickly.
imagery: A great wheel marked with letters and symbols turns in the sky, with a sphinx sitting on top, a snake sliding down one side and a red jackal-headed figure rising on the other, while four winged creatures read books in the corners. What goes up comes down, and the wheel keeps turning.

waite.upright: Destiny, fortune, success, elevation, luck, felicity.
waite.reversed: Increase, abundance, superfluity.
waite.picture: I have, however, presented Typhon in his serpent form. The symbolism is, of course, not exclusively Egyptian, as the four Living Creatures of Ezekiel occupy the angles of the card, and the wheel itself follows other indications of Lévi in respect of Ezekiel's vision, as illustrative of the particular Tarot Key. With the French occultist, and in the design itself, the symbolic picture stands for the perpetual motion of a fluidic universe and for the flux of human life. The Sphinx is the equilibrium therein. The transliteration of Taro as Rota is inscribed on the wheel, counterchanged with the letters of the Divine Name—to shew that Providence is implied through all.
waite.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911)

symbols.symbol: The great wheel with TARO and the Divine Name
symbols.meaning: Waite says the letters show Providence is implied through all; it also spells ROTA, wheel.
The equilibrium, as Waite has it: stability amid constant change.
Typhon in serpent form, the downward turn and loss.
Hermanubis, lifting with the wheel as things turn upward.
The angel, eagle, lion, and bull in the corners, standing for the fixed signs and steady order.

history: The image comes from the medieval Wheel of Fortune, turned by the goddess Fortuna, with people rising and falling on its rim. Waite says eighteenth-century cards showed odd animals climbing and falling, one with a human head, under a crowned winged beast at the top. For his version he followed Eliphas Levi's reconstruction, with a sphinx above, Hermanubis rising, Typhon as a serpent descending, and the four living creatures of Ezekiel in the corners.
numerologyAstrology: Ten ends one cycle and starts another, which is exactly what a turning wheel does. Jupiter, planet of luck and expansion, is its Golden Dawn planet, so the turn is often a fortunate one.

upright.love: A turning point, often a lucky one: meeting someone unexpectedly or a relationship moving to the next stage. Fate seems to be playing a part. Someone from the past may cross your path again at an odd moment. Go out more, because luck needs you to show up.
upright.work: A break arrives, a new opportunity or a change in direction. Be ready to catch it when it comes around. A restructure or a new manager can open a door that was shut last year. Say yes when the door opens.
upright.money: An upswing, a windfall, or a fortunate change in circumstances. Enjoy it and plan for the next dip. A financial upswing, unexpected money, or a good time to act. Save some of the windfall for the next turn.
upright.advice: Go with the change instead of fighting it. What goes around is coming around in your favor.
upright.asAPerson: Lucky, adaptable, easygoing; someone who seems to arrive at the right time. Feelings for you may arrive suddenly and feel fated. They tend to thrive on change that would rattle other people.

yesNo.why: The wheel is turning in your favor. Luck and timing are turning your way.

reversed.love: Bad timing, repeated patterns, or a setback in a relationship. You may be stuck in the same cycle with different faces. When you keep dating the same kind of person, this is the card that points it out.
reversed.work: Delays, plans falling through, or the feeling that luck has turned. It won't stay down forever. A contract, a launch or a hiring decision may slip into next quarter. Focus on what you can control and wait for the next turn.
reversed.money: An unexpected cost or a lean stretch that arrives through no fault of yours. The wheel keeps turning, so tighten up, cover the essentials, and ride it out. Unexpected expenses, a downturn, or bad luck with money. Build a cushion and avoid risky bets.
reversed.advice: Notice the pattern that keeps repeating and change your part in it. Hard turns pass. Ride it out; this turn won't last.
reversed.asAPerson: Someone unreliable or stuck in the same mistakes. Affection may come and go with the weather. They may blame bad luck for choices they made.

yesNo.why: The timing isn't right; the wheel has to turn again.

waiteNote.upright: Waite's words are all good fortune: destiny, fortune, success, elevation (rising up), luck, and felicity, which means happiness. In practice the Wheel says things are turning in your favor, often through events you didn't plan. A reader also remembers the wheel keeps turning, so enjoy the good turn while it's here.
waiteNote.reversed: Reversed, Waite oddly gives increase, abundance, and superfluity, which means more than enough. Modern readers usually take the reversal as a downturn, delay, or bad luck, so Waite's words are best read as too much of a good thing, or plenty that doesn't last.

imageryHistory: Medieval Wheels of Fortune showed Fortune turning a wheel with figures climbing, sitting on top, and falling off. The Tarot de Marseille kept a wheel with animal figures rising and falling and a crank that no one is turning. Smith followed later occult designs, with a sphinx on top, a snake going down, the letters T A R O around the rim, and four winged creatures in the corners.

mathers.title: The Wheel of Fortune
mathers.source: S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Tarot: Its Occult Signification, Use in Fortune-Telling, and Method of Play (1888)

goldenDawn.title: The Lord of the Forces of Life
goldenDawn.printed: The Lord of the Forces of Life
goldenDawn.source: Golden Dawn "Book T", printed as "Liber LXXVIII: A Description of the Cards of the Tarot" in The Equinox I:8 (1912)

olderMeanings.note: Mathers reads good fortune, success, and unexpected luck, reversed as ill-fortune, failure, and unexpected ill-luck. That straightforward luck reading is still how most people read it today.

name: Justice
upright: In practical terms it shows up around legal matters, contracts, and big decisions where you need to weigh things honestly. The result tends to be fair, which is good news if you've acted with integrity. Tell the truth and own your part. Justice cares about truth more than feelings, and things work out fairly when you've been honest. Cause and effect is clear here: what you've done comes back to you.
reversed: Something isn't fair, or someone isn't owning up. You may be on the wrong end of a biased decision, or dodging responsibility for a mistake of your own. Watch for dishonesty, legal delays, or facts being bent to suit someone. A quieter version is being harder on yourself than you'd ever be on a friend. Look for avoided responsibility too, or blaming others for what's partly yours. Own your part and you'll get further.
sitWith: Where do you need to be honest about your own part in this? What decision would you make if you knew you'd have to explain it honestly?
inASpread: Justice beside the King of Swords or Judgement leans toward courts, contracts, and official decisions. Around the Five or Seven of Swords, it asks whether someone is slipping away from the truth. When it's the outcome, you'll get what's fair, which depends on what's been put in. Near a legal or contract question, it points toward a fair and clear result.
imagery: A figure in red sits between two pillars, holding an upright double-edged sword in one hand and balanced scales in the other, one white shoe peeking out from under the robe. The sword cuts both ways and the scales weigh everything, so this fairness applies to you too.

waite.upright: Equity, rightness, probity, executive; triumph of the deserving side in law.
waite.reversed: Law in all its departments, legal complications, bigotry, bias, excessive severity.
waite.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911)

symbols.meaning: Clear decisions and the cutting away of what isn't true.
Weighing both sides fairly before the verdict.
Action tempered with compassion; the law applied by a person with a heart.

symbols.symbol: Two grey pillars with a purple veil
symbols.meaning: Like the High Priestess, she sits between pillars; Waite says hers open onto a different world.
A foot about to step forward: justice leads to consequences and action.

history: Justice is one of the cardinal virtues and has been in the trump series since the early Italian decks. Marseille decks number La Justice VIII, and Waite moved her to XI to match the Golden Dawn's placing of Libra there. Waite says the woman on the older card was said to be Astraea, and he pointed out that the tarot has Justice, Temperance, and Fortitude but no card for Prudence, the fourth virtue.
numerologyAstrology: Eleven is one step past a completed cycle, a new start that has to answer for the last one, which fits cause and effect. Its sign is Libra, the scales, ruled by Venus: fairness and balance built into the card.

upright.love: Honesty and fairness decide how things go. A relationship with equal give and take thrives now, while one built on half-truths gets called to account. You'll be drawn to people who treat you well, and a couple can use this time for honest talks.
upright.work: Contracts, legal matters, and fair evaluations lean your way if you've done your part. Expect an objective decision based on the facts. An interview panel or a review judges on evidence, so bring it. Be honest in your dealings and document everything.
upright.money: Settlements, taxes, and paperwork come out even. What you're owed arrives, and what you owe must be paid. Fair deals, settlements, and taxes getting sorted. Pay what you owe and check that others pay you.
upright.advice: Tell the truth and take responsibility for your share. Decide with your head, then act on it.
upright.asAPerson: Fair-minded, logical, principled; a lawyer, judge, or the friend who won't take sides without facts. Their regard for you is honest and measured. Fair and principled, with no patience for lies.

yesNo.why: If you've acted fairly, the outcome will be fair to you. Fairness is on the side of whoever is honest.

reversed.love: Unfairness or dishonesty in the relationship, or blame going only one way. Someone may be avoiding accountability for how they've behaved. An apology may be owed, and it may be yours. Look at whether old hurts are making you judge new people too harshly.
reversed.work: Legal delays, biased decisions, or being treated unfairly by a system. Keep records and get advice before challenging it. Unfair treatment, a biased decision, or office politics. A decision may go against you because the paperwork was incomplete.
reversed.money: Disputes, back taxes, or a deal that isn't balanced. Read the fine print and check the numbers yourself. Disputes, unpaid debts, or an unfair deal. Read contracts carefully and get advice if needed. Keep receipts and dates in one place.
reversed.advice: Own your part honestly, even the uncomfortable bits. Where someone else won't, keep facts and dates.
reversed.asAPerson: Biased, dishonest, or harshly judgmental. Score-keeping may be replacing fair weighing. Judgmental, or quick to blame others.

yesNo.why: Something about this isn't balanced or fully honest. The scales aren't balanced yet.

waiteNote.upright: Waite gives equity, rightness, and probity, which all mean fairness and honesty, plus executive, meaning the power to carry out decisions. “Triumph of the deserving side in law” means whoever is in the right wins. A reader applies it to legal matters, contracts, and any situation where the truth and fair treatment matter.
waiteNote.reversed: Reversed, Waite gives “law in all its departments”, legal complications, bigotry, bias, and excessive severity, which means punishments that are too harsh. In practice it's unfairness, a biased judge, or a decision that doesn't go your way. It can also mean being too hard on yourself or someone else.

imageryHistory: In the Tarot de Marseille Justice is card VIII, a seated figure with a sword in one hand and scales in the other, and in some of the earliest French decks she even has wings. Waite moved her to XI, swapping places with Strength, and Smith built the card much like the High Priestess, seating her between two pillars in red robes with the sword and golden scales.

mathers.title: Strength, or Fortitude
mathers.reversed: Abuse of Power, Overbearingness, Want of Fortitude.
mathers.source: S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Tarot: Its Occult Signification, Use in Fortune-Telling, and Method of Play (1888)

goldenDawn.title: The Daughter of the Flaming Sword
goldenDawn.printed: The Daughter of the Flaming Sword
goldenDawn.source: Golden Dawn "Book T", printed as "Liber LXXVIII: A Description of the Cards of the Tarot" in The Equinox I:8 (1912)

olderMeanings.note: Mathers reads equilibrium, balance, and justice, and reversed, bigotry, want of balance, abuse of justice, over-severity, inequality, and bias. That's almost word for word how Waite and modern readers see it.

name: The Hanged Man
upright: Things are on hold, and that might be the point. The Hanged Man is about waiting, surrender, and seeing a situation from a completely different angle. You may not be able to push this forward right now, and trying will only wear you out. What you can do is loosen your grip on how you thought it would go. Stuck moments like this often bring the clearest insights. Sometimes the best move is no move. Letting go of control for a while shows you what you couldn't see while you were struggling.
reversed: Now the pause drags on with no purpose. Perhaps you're stalling, putting off a decision, or making sacrifices nobody asked for and that don't help anyone. Or the opposite: dodging a needed rest by staying busy. In a kinder reading, it marks the end of a waiting period, the moment you're finally ready to move. Notice whether you're resting or just stuck. Stalling is the other risk, waiting for something that won't come without your action. Ask whether this pause is still teaching you anything.
sitWith: What would you notice if you stopped trying to fix this?
inASpread: Put the Hanged Man near the Four of Swords or the Hermit and the need to stop is hard to miss. Next to the Eight of Wands or the Chariot, you'll feel the tension between wanting speed and being made to wait. The result is usually a delay that changes how you see the whole thing. In a spread full of action cards, it says to slow down before choosing.
imagery: A man hangs upside down by one foot from a living T-shaped tree, his other leg bent behind his knee and his hands behind his back, a glowing halo around his calm face. He isn't in pain, and he seems to have chosen this, a way of seeing the world from a new angle.

waite.upright: Wisdom, circumspection, discernment, trials, sacrifice, intuition, divination, prophecy.
waite.reversed: Selfishness, the crowd, body politic.
waite.picture: The gallows from which he is suspended forms a Tau cross, while the figure—from the position of the legs—forms a fylfot cross. There is a nimbus about the head of the seeming martyr. It should be noted (1) that the tree of sacrifice is living wood, with leaves thereon; (2) that the face expresses deep entrancement, not suffering; (3) that the figure, as a whole, suggests life in suspension, but life and not death.
waite.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911)

symbols.symbol: Hanging upside down by one foot
symbols.meaning: A voluntary pause that turns your view of things upside down.
Waite stresses that the tree of sacrifice is living wood, still in leaf: life held in suspension.
Insight and calm understanding that come from surrender.
Waite describes the figure as forming a fylfot cross; stillness and a new angle.
Deep entrancement shows in the face, Waite notes, with no sign of suffering.

history: Early Italian decks called this card Il Traditore, the Traitor, since hanging upside down by one foot was a punishment and a public shaming for traitors. Waite noted that the eighteenth-century fortune-tellers' version showed a youth standing on one foot, loosely tied to a stake. He rejected the older labels of prudence and martyrdom, and Smith's figure hangs from a living tree with a glowing halo and a peaceful face.
numerologyAstrology: Twelve is a number of completion in cycles of time, twelve months and twelve signs, and this card stops the clock inside that cycle. The Golden Dawn assigned it to elemental Water, the element of surrender; Neptune was added by later astrologers.

upright.love: A pause in the relationship that helps you see it differently. Letting go of control or old expectations may be what moves things forward. Seeing it from your partner's side may change what you thought the problem was. Time alone may change what you're looking for in a partner.
upright.work: A project on hold, a waiting period, or a sacrifice now for a gain later. Use the delay to rethink your approach. A colleague's view, or a step back from the daily rush, may show you the job differently. Learn a skill while the project is paused.
upright.money: Not the moment to push. Hold off on big decisions until you can see the situation from a new angle. Investments may be slow to pay back, so plan for a longer wait. Sometimes a small sacrifice now saves more later.
upright.advice: Stop struggling and look at it upside down. Sometimes the fastest way through is to wait. Let go of how you think it should go.
upright.asAPerson: Unconventional, patient, spiritual, maybe a bit detached; someone who sees things others miss. Their interest in you may come with a long pause before any move. They often put others' needs ahead of their own, sometimes too far.

yesNo.why: A pause is needed before the answer shows itself. Things are paused, so wait for the answer.

reversed.love: Stuck in limbo, or making sacrifices nobody asked for. Someone may be stalling to avoid a decision. A relationship stuck in limbo, or one person sacrificing too much. If you're waiting for someone to change, ask how long you're willing to wait.
reversed.work: Delays that drag on because nobody will act, or resisting a change that's needed. Busy work may be covering up indecision. Stalling, indecision, or a project that won't move. Make a decision, even a small one, to get things going.
reversed.money: Money tied up with no movement, or giving too much and resenting it. Decide what you're actually waiting for. A refund, a sale or a transfer that's been stuck may need a phone call to move. Look at what's holding you back. Pick one stuck account or plan and move it this week.
reversed.advice: Stop waiting for someone else to decide for you. Make a move, even a small one, and see how it feels to be upright again. Set a date by which you'll decide, and keep it.
reversed.asAPerson: A martyr, a staller, or someone stuck in their own head. They may care but won't commit either way. Stuck, or a martyr who sacrifices for attention.

yesNo.why: The stalling itself is the problem right now. Nothing will move until something is let go.

waiteNote.upright: Waite gives wisdom, circumspection (careful watching), discernment (seeing clearly), trials, sacrifice, intuition, divination, and prophecy. In practice it means giving something up for a bigger insight, or seeing things differently after a period of waiting. A reader treats it as a pause that teaches.
waiteNote.reversed: Reversed, Waite gives selfishness, the crowd, and “body politic”, which means society or the public at large. In practice this is refusing to let go, or getting carried along with what everyone else thinks. It can also mean a delay with no lesson in it because you're resisting it.

imageryHistory: The earliest Hanged Man cards show a man hung upside down by one ankle, the kind of shaming picture Italian cities painted of traitors. The Tarot de Marseille hangs him between two posts with lopped-off branches. Smith hung him from a living tree shaped like a T, calm-faced, with a halo that Waite called the nimbus of the martyr.

mathers.title: The Hanged Man
mathers.source: S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Tarot: Its Occult Signification, Use in Fortune-Telling, and Method of Play (1888)

goldenDawn.title: The Spirit of the Mighty Waters
goldenDawn.printed: The Spirit of the Mighty Waters
goldenDawn.source: Golden Dawn "Book T", printed as "Liber LXXVIII: A Description of the Cards of the Tarot" in The Equinox I:8 (1912)

olderMeanings.note: Mathers reads self-sacrifice, sacrifice, devotion, and bound, and reversed, selfishness, unbound, and partial sacrifice. Both he and Waite focus on sacrifice, while modern readers add the idea of a new perspective.

name: Death
upright: Death almost never means a physical death. It's about endings: a chapter closing, a relationship finishing, a way of life that has run its course. These endings are often necessary and they make room for something new, even if that's hard to see yet. The card asks you to let go of what's already over. Something is finishing, and trying to keep it alive only drags out the pain. What comes next can't start until this is over.
reversed: An ending is being resisted. A job, a relationship, or an old version of yourself might be finished, and you're holding on because the unknown feels worse. The result is a kind of limbo where nothing new can start. Or the change is happening, just slowly and painfully instead of cleanly. What would happen if you let it end? Usually you already know it's over and just haven't said it out loud. The change you're resisting is usually lighter to carry than the waiting.
sitWith: What in your life has already ended that you're still carrying? What are you ready to let finish?
inASpread: Death and the Tower together mean big, unavoidable change arriving fast. With the Eight of Cups or the Six of Swords, the ending is quieter, more of a walking away. If Death closes the spread, the situation will end, and whatever follows will look different. With the Six of Swords, it describes a clean break and a move on to calmer waters.
imagery: A skeleton in black armor rides a white horse carrying a black flag with a white rose, while a king lies fallen, a bishop pleads, and a child looks up, and far off a sun rises between two towers. Everyone meets it no matter their rank, and that rising sun says something comes after.

waite.upright: End, mortality, destruction, corruption; also, for a man, the loss of a benefactor; for a woman, many contrarieties; for a maid, failure of marriage projects.
waite.reversed: Inertia, sleep, lethargy, petrifaction, somnambulism; hope destroyed.
waite.picture: The mysterious horseman moves slowly, bearing a black banner emblazoned with the Mystic Rose, which signifies life. Between two pillars on the verge of the horizon there shines the sun of immortality. The horseman carries no visible weapon, but king and child and maiden fall before him, while a prelate with clasped hands awaits his end.
waite.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911)

symbols.symbol: Skeleton in black armor on a white horse
symbols.meaning: Death rides slowly; Waite notes he carries no visible weapon, yet all fall before him.

symbols.symbol: Black banner with a white rose
symbols.meaning: The Mystic Rose, Waite explains, signifies life: endings make room for new growth.
Everyone meets change, no matter their rank or innocence.
It is the sun of immortality in Waite's reading: a new day after the ending.
Crossing over, as in the old image of a ferry to the other side.

history: In the Marseille deck card XIII usually carries no name, which led to it being called the card with no name. The older design shows a skeleton with a scythe mowing a field where heads and hands stick up from the ground, one of them crowned. Waite called that picture crude and had Smith draw an armored rider on a white horse carrying a black banner with a white rose, taken from the visions of the Apocalypse.
numerologyAstrology: Thirteen breaks past the tidy twelve, which is why it has long felt unsettling; one plus three makes four, the structure that follows the clear-out. Its Golden Dawn sign is Scorpio, the sign of endings, secrets, and renewal.

upright.love: A chapter closes: a relationship ends, or an old way of relating dies so a new one can begin. Grieve it honestly, then let the next thing grow. Moving in together, marrying or separating can all be this kind of ending. Letting go of an old love leaves room for someone new.
upright.work: A job, role, or project reaches its natural end. Restructuring or moving on clears space for better work. A contract ending or a team being folded into another are typical. It's hard, and it opens room for something that fits better.
upright.money: An old financial habit or source of income ends. Close accounts and patterns that no longer serve you. Cancelling old subscriptions and closing an unused account are small versions of this card. Let go of what isn't working.
upright.advice: Let go of what's already over, whether a role, a habit, or a relationship. Fighting a finished thing only drags out the pain and delays whatever grows next. Let the ending happen.
upright.asAPerson: Someone intense, deep, and unafraid of hard truths, often going through a major life change. Toward you, it can be a bond that changes both people.

yesNo.why: What you're asking about is ending, so a fresh start isn't on offer yet. Something has to end first.

reversed.love: Holding on to a relationship that's over, or fearing the change it needs. The ending is happening slowly instead of cleanly. Staying friends too soon after a breakup can keep both of you stuck. Old feelings may still be taking up space you need.
reversed.work: Clinging to a job you've outgrown, or refusing to adapt to changes already underway. Stagnation sets in. A restructure may drag on for months with nobody saying what's actually happening. Make a plan to move on.
reversed.money: Keeping a failing investment or habit alive out of fear. Cut the loss before it grows. Clinging to old spending habits or a bad investment. Cut your losses. An old subscription, a losing stock, or a loan you keep extending are all good places to start.
reversed.advice: Let the ending happen instead of propping it up. Change hurts less once you stop pushing against it, and the next season can't start until this one closes. Say out loud what's already over.
reversed.asAPerson: Someone stuck, afraid of change, or unable to move past the past. They may still be tied to an old chapter.

yesNo.why: Resistance to change is keeping things stuck. You're resisting what needs to end.

waiteNote.upright: Waite's words are blunt: end, mortality, destruction, and corruption, meaning decay. The specific lines, the loss of a benefactor (someone who helps you), many contrarieties (setbacks), and failure of marriage plans, show how older readers used it to predict losses. Most modern readers take it as an ending that clears the way, very rarely as physical death.
waiteNote.reversed: Reversed, Waite gives inertia, sleep, lethargy, and petrifaction, which means turning to stone, plus somnambulism, meaning sleepwalking. “Hope destroyed” closes the list. In practice it's an ending that's being resisted, so everything freezes instead of moving on.

imageryHistory: The walking Grim Reaper with a scythe first appears in tarot with the Tarot de Marseille, where the card is numbered XIII and usually left without a name. Smith went back to late medieval imagery: Death as a skeleton in armor on a white horse, carrying a black banner with a white rose, while a king lies fallen and a bishop, a woman, and a child face him.

mathers.title: Death
mathers.upright: Death, Change, Transformation, Alteration for the worse
mathers.reversed: Death just escaped, Partial change, Alteration for the better.
mathers.source: S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Tarot: Its Occult Signification, Use in Fortune-Telling, and Method of Play (1888)

goldenDawn.title: The Child of the Great Transformers: the Lord of the Gates of Death
goldenDawn.printed: The Child of the Great Transformers: the Lord of the Gates of Death
goldenDawn.source: Golden Dawn "Book T", printed as "Liber LXXVIII: A Description of the Cards of the Tarot" in The Equinox I:8 (1912)

olderMeanings.note: Mathers reads death, change, transformation, and alteration for the worse, and reversed, death just escaped, partial change, and alteration for the better. That's closer to today's reading of change than many people expect.

name: Temperance
upright: Temperance is about balance and moderation. The angel pours water back and forth, blending two things until the mix is right, and that's the work this card describes: patience, calm, finding the middle way. It's good for healing, recovery, and any time you're trying to bring different parts of your life together. Don't rush it. Small, steady adjustments add up. Temperance is patience in action, taking the slow, steady route and mixing things carefully. Good health habits, or a calm person who helps others meet halfway, can show up here as well.
reversed: Things have tipped out of balance. Too much work, spending, drinking, or worry all belong here, and so does swinging between extremes. Impatience plays a part too, wanting the result before it's ready. There may be a clash, two people or two parts of your life that just won't mix. Find where you've gone too far and bring it back a notch. Watch for overdoing it in one area to make up for another. Sleep and meals are often the first things to slip, so start there.
sitWith: Where have you been running too hot or too cold lately? What would the middle path look like here?
inASpread: Temperance next to the Two of Pentacles speaks to juggling and finding a pace you can keep. Among heavy Wands or the Knight of Wands, it's a clear call to slow down. The result it promises is calm and balanced, and it takes time. Next to the Four of Swords or the Star, it points to healing and recovery.
imagery: A winged angel with one foot on land and one in a pool pours water from one cup to another, with a path winding up to a glowing crown in the mountains. The steady pouring is about mixing things slowly until the blend is right.

waite.upright: Economy, moderation, frugality, management, accommodation.
waite.reversed: Things connected with churches, religions, sects, the priesthood, sometimes even the priest who will marry the Querent; also disunion, unfortunate combinations, competing interests.
waite.picture: A winged angel, with the sign of the sun upon his forehead and on his breast the square and triangle of the septenary. I speak of him in the masculine sense, but the figure is neither male nor female. It is held to be pouring the essences of life from chalice to chalice. It has one foot upon the earth and one upon waters, thus illustrating the nature of the essences. A direct path goes up to certain heights on the verge of the horizon, and above there is a great light, through which a crown is seen vaguely.
waite.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911)

symbols.meaning: Mixing and blending: the right measure of each thing.

symbols.symbol: One foot in water, one on land
symbols.meaning: Balance between feeling and practical life.

symbols.symbol: Triangle inside a square on the robe
symbols.meaning: Square and triangle together make the septenary, Waite says: spirit held inside matter.
A long, patient road toward a higher goal.
Flowers linked with Iris, messenger of the rainbow, bringing hope after storms.

history: Temperance is one of the cardinal virtues, and the image of pouring from one jug to another stood for watering down wine. It appears in the oldest Italian decks at number VI or VII, and the Marseille deck places it at XIV. Waite says of his version that all the conventional emblems are renounced, and Smith's angel stands with one foot in a pool and one on land, with a path leading up to a crown of light.
numerologyAstrology: Fourteen reduces to five, the number of change, but here change is blended in slowly rather than forced. Sagittarius, ruled by Jupiter, a sign of long roads and steady aim, is its Golden Dawn sign.

upright.love: Harmony, patience, and a relationship that finds its middle ground. Compromise and calm conversation heal old friction. Balance, patience, and a relationship where both people give and take. Newly dating, take things slow and let a connection build naturally.
upright.work: Cooperation, patience, and steady progress rather than big leaps. You're the one who can blend people or ideas into something that works, like the angel mixing water between two cups. Steady progress, teamwork, and finding the right balance between work and rest. Don't rush the results.
upright.money: Moderation: neither splurging nor pinching. A small amount saved regularly does more good here than any clever scheme. Moderate spending, saving a little at a time, and avoiding extremes. Balance your budget.
upright.advice: Find the middle path and take your time. Mix things in small measures until the blend is right.
upright.asAPerson: Calm, patient, and diplomatic, the friend who talks everyone down. Their care for you is gentle and steady, never showy.

yesNo.why: It works out with patience and balance. Don't force the timing.

reversed.love: Imbalance, impatience, or one person doing all the adjusting. Old arguments flare because nobody is meeting halfway. One partner may want more closeness while the other wants more space. Maybe you're rushing things, or holding back too much.
reversed.work: Clashing priorities, overwork, or trying to rush a process that needs time. Things feel out of sync. A team may be mixing people or methods that don't combine well. Find a better balance. Protect your lunch break and your evenings for a week and see what changes.
reversed.money: Swinging between extremes, spending big and then panicking and cutting everything. Disunion and competing interests show up in the reversed meanings, so look for the one habit throwing everything off. Overspending, then overcorrecting. Look for steady habits instead of extremes.
reversed.advice: Pull back from extremes and give yourself a rest. Restore some balance before making any big moves.
reversed.asAPerson: Impatient, excessive, or unable to compromise, all or nothing with no middle. They may swing hot and cold with you. Restless and prone to overdoing it.

yesNo.why: Things need rebalancing before this can work. Things are out of balance right now.

waiteNote.upright: Waite gives economy, moderation, frugality (careful spending), management, and accommodation, which means making room for others and finding a fit. In practice it's balance and patience, blending things in the right amounts. A reader applies it to health, money, relationships, and any situation that needs a middle path.
waiteNote.reversed: Reversed, Waite's list is odd: things connected with churches and priests, even “the priest who will marry the Querent”. Then he gives disunion, unfortunate combinations, and competing interests. In practice most readers take it as imbalance, excess, or two things that won't mix.

imageryHistory: The Tarot de Marseille Temperance, which has barely changed since the seventeenth century, shows a winged figure pouring liquid from one vessel into another. Waite followed the French occultist Éliphas Lévi's description: an angel with the sun sign on the forehead and a square and triangle on the chest, and Smith stood the angel with one foot in the water and one on land, with irises growing nearby.

mathers.title: Temperance
mathers.source: S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Tarot: Its Occult Signification, Use in Fortune-Telling, and Method of Play (1888)

goldenDawn.title: The Daughter of the Reconcilers: the Bringer-forth of Life
goldenDawn.printed: The Daughter of the Reconcilers: the Bringer-Forth of life
goldenDawn.source: Golden Dawn "Book T", printed as "Liber LXXVIII: A Description of the Cards of the Tarot" in The Equinox I:8 (1912)

olderMeanings.note: Mathers reads combination, conformation, and uniting, and reversed, ill-advised combinations, disunion, and clashing interests. That's close to today, since both are about mixing things well.

name: The Devil
upright: The Devil is about the things that hold you: addictions, bad habits, unhealthy relationships, money worries, anything you feel you can't walk away from. Study the chains, though, and you'll see they're loose. That's the uncomfortable truth here, that a lot of what traps us is something we keep choosing. Greed and plain temptation live here too, giving in to appetites you know aren't good for you. Name the chain honestly. The chains in this card are loose enough to lift off, and that's the point. It shows what's holding you, whether it's a habit, a relationship, or money, and that part of you agreed to it.
reversed: The chains are starting to come off. This often means breaking a bad habit, leaving an unhealthy relationship, or seeing through a way of thinking that kept you small. You're finally seeing the pattern for what it is. Be aware the pull can still be strong in private, even while you look fine on the outside. Keep going, and get help if you need it. Upside down, it may be the first step out, the moment you see the chain for what it is. It can also mean the hold is tighter than you want to admit.
sitWith: What are you chained to that you could actually take off? What would you do with the freedom if you took the chain off?
inASpread: Beside the Lovers, the Devil suggests strong attraction with an unhealthy hook in it. When it's surrounded by Swords, especially the Eight or Nine, the trap is mostly in your own head. As the final card, it asks what you're willing to keep putting up with. Next to the Seven of Cups, it warns of temptation dressed up as a dream.
imagery: A horned, bat-winged figure squats on a black pedestal, and chained to it are a naked man and woman with small horns and tails. Look closely and the chains around their necks are loose enough to lift off, so they could leave, and they haven't.

waite.upright: Ravage, violence, vehemence, extraordinary efforts, force, fatality; that which is predestined but is not for this reason evil.
waite.reversed: Evil fatality, weakness, pettiness, blindness.
waite.picture: The Horned Goat of Mendes, with wings like those of a bat, is standing on an altar. At the pit of the stomach there is the sign of Mercury. The right hand is upraised and extended, being the reverse of that benediction which is given by the Hierophant in the fifth card. In the left hand there is a great flaming torch, inverted towards the earth. A reversed pentagram is on the forehead. There is a ring in front of the altar, from which two chains are carried to the necks of two figures, male and female. These are analogous with those of the fifth card, as if Adam and Eve after the Fall.
waite.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911)

symbols.meaning: Waite's Horned Goat of Mendes: appetite, fear, and the material pull at its strongest.

symbols.symbol: Loose chains around the couple's necks
symbols.meaning: The chains are wide enough to slip off; the trap is partly chosen.
Waite says it is a great flaming torch pointed at the earth: passion turned downward.
Matter placed over spirit.

symbols.symbol: Horns and tails on the couple
symbols.meaning: The tails signify the animal nature in Waite's reading; this is the Lovers after the Fall.

history: The Devil is one of the two trumps missing from the surviving Visconti-Sforza deck, alongside the Tower. Waite describes the eighteenth-century devil as a naked winged figure with bird claws standing on a pedestal, with two small tailed demons tied to it by cords. From 1856 onward, he says, Eliphas Levi's Baphomet changed the image into the goat-headed figure with a torch that Smith drew, with a chained man and woman who echo the Lovers.
numerologyAstrology: Fifteen reduces to six, the number of the Lovers, and the chained couple mirror that card in shadow. Capricorn, the sea-goat, ruled by Saturn, planet of limits and ambition, is the sign the Golden Dawn gave it.

upright.love: Intense attraction, obsession, or a relationship built on dependency. Passion can be real here, but so can the hooks. Jealousy and checking up on each other belong here. Notice whether you're drawn to people who aren't good for you.
upright.work: Feeling trapped by a job for the money, or by a culture of overwork. Ask what you're really bound to. A job that pays well and traps you, or feeling chained to your desk. Look at what you're trading for the money.
upright.money: Debt, addiction to spending, or money becoming the only measure. The pull of material things is strong. Buy-now-pay-later plans and gambling apps fit this card closely. Face the habit before it gets worse. Write down what you owe, to whom, and at what interest.
upright.advice: Look at what has a hold on you, honestly. The chain is looser than it feels.
upright.asAPerson: Magnetic, controlling, indulgent, or manipulative. Desire mixed with possessiveness is likely in how they see you. Being around them can feel exciting and draining at once.

yesNo.why: Something unhealthy is driving this. A habit or a person has too much hold on this.

reversed.love: Breaking free of an unhealthy pattern or relationship. Freedom is close, though old habits may tug for a while. You may finally say out loud what has kept you there, whether fear of being alone, money, or habit. Old attachments start to loosen.
reversed.work: Walking away from a toxic situation or finally setting boundaries. It takes effort but you can leave. Leaving a job that felt like a trap, or setting boundaries with a demanding boss. Take the first step out.
reversed.money: Paying off debt, curbing a habit, or getting honest about spending. Relief begins when you face the numbers. Cutting up a card or deleting a shopping app can be the turning point. Keep going, it's working. Each payment loosens the chain a little more.
reversed.advice: Take the chain off while you can see it clearly. Get help if the pull is still strong. Take the first step out, even a small one.
reversed.asAPerson: Someone working to overcome an addiction or unhealthy pattern. Something that bound them is loosening its hold. Waking up to their own patterns and working to change them.

yesNo.why: Freedom is possible if you keep choosing it. You can break free if you choose to.

waiteNote.upright: Waite gives ravage, violence, vehemence (fierce intensity), extraordinary efforts, force, and fatality, meaning fate. His last line matters: “that which is predestined but is not for this reason evil”, meaning something fated that isn't necessarily bad. Readers today use it for anything that holds you: habits, cravings, or situations that feel impossible to escape.
waiteNote.reversed: Reversed, Waite gives evil fatality, meaning bad fate, weakness, pettiness, and blindness. In practice it can mean breaking free, or it can mean the grip is getting worse because you won't look at it. Read the surrounding cards to tell which.

imageryHistory: The Tarot de Marseille Devil has a strange human body, with two small horned minions tied to his pedestal. Smith drew on Éliphas Lévi's Baphomet for the goat horns, bat wings, raised hand, and reversed pentagram, and Waite turned the two minions into Adam and Eve after the Fall, chained loosely at his feet.

mathers.title: The Devil
mathers.source: S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Tarot: Its Occult Signification, Use in Fortune-Telling, and Method of Play (1888)

goldenDawn.title: The Lord of the Gates of Matter: the Child of the Forces of Time
goldenDawn.printed: The Lord of the Gates of Matter: the Child of the Forces of Time
goldenDawn.source: Golden Dawn "Book T", printed as "Liber LXXVIII: A Description of the Cards of the Tarot" in The Equinox I:8 (1912)

olderMeanings.note: Mathers reads fatality for good, and reversed, fatality for evil, meaning fate that falls either way. That's quite different from the modern reading of addiction and bondage, which grew out of later occult writing.

name: The Tower
upright: Sudden, unwanted change. Something you counted on falls apart: a job, a relationship, a belief, a plan. It's shocking and it hurts, and there's no point pretending otherwise. What the Tower knocks down was usually built on something false or unstable, and in time you may see it needed to go. For now, get to safety and let the dust settle. A sudden truth may change how you see a person or situation overnight.
reversed: The collapse is being held off, or it's happening on the inside. You might sense trouble coming and be doing everything to avoid it, which usually just delays it. It can also mean a private upheaval, a shift in beliefs or identity that other people don't see. A narrow escape is possible too, though the warning still stands. What are you propping up that may need to come down? Take it as a warning you still have time to act on. If you see cracks, fix them now instead of waiting for the lightning.
sitWith: What have you already seen cracking that you haven't wanted to name?
inASpread: Alongside Death or the Ten of Swords, the Tower marks a hard ending with no going back. If the Star comes after it, you get the old story of disaster and then recovery. Landing as the outcome, expect a sudden shake-up that clears the ground even as it knocks things over.
imagery: Lightning strikes a tall tower on a rocky peak, blowing off its crown and setting it alight, while two people fall headfirst through the air. Something built on shaky ground comes down all at once.

waite.upright: Misery, distress, indigence, adversity, calamity, disgrace, deception, ruin. It is a card in particular of unforeseen catastrophe.
waite.reversed: According to one account, the same in a lesser degree; also oppression, imprisonment, tyranny.
waite.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911)

symbols.meaning: A sudden flash of truth that breaks what can't stand.
False pride or a false belief knocked loose.
No one stays in the tower when it falls, whatever their rank.
A structure built on unstable ground, or on a lie.
Drops of fire shaped like the Hebrew letter Yod, often read as the twenty-two trumps or divine help falling alongside the ruin.

history: The Marseille card is called La Maison Dieu, the House of God, and Waite lists other old titles for it: the Castle of Plutus, God's House, and the Tower of Babel. Some Belgian decks show a tree struck by lightning instead of a building, and the card is missing from the surviving Visconti-Sforza deck. Smith's version keeps the lightning and falling figures and adds the blown-off crown and the fiery drops.
numerologyAstrology: Sixteen reduces to seven, the Chariot's number, but here the drive has hit a wall. The Golden Dawn gave the Tower to Mars, planet of force, conflict, and sudden action.

upright.love: A sudden break, revelation, or argument that shakes the relationship to its roots. What survives will be more honest. A sudden breakup, a shocking truth, or an argument that changes everything. A surprising revelation may change what you want from love.
upright.work: Job loss, sudden restructuring, or a plan that collapses. It's disruptive, and it clears ground for something sturdier. A merger, a layoff round or a failed launch are typical. Update your CV now, while you remember what you achieved.
upright.money: An unexpected bill, a job loss, or an investment that collapses without warning. Protect what you can, then rebuild on firmer ground than before. Check your insurance and what it actually covers. Build an emergency fund if you can.
upright.advice: Let the false structure fall and get yourself to safety. Once the dust settles, don't rebuild the same tower on the same cracked rock. Ask people you trust for help while things settle.
upright.asAPerson: Explosive, chaotic, or someone whose arrival turns life upside down. Their effect on you is a shake-up that can't be ignored. Unpredictable, blunt, and sometimes explosive.

yesNo.why: Things are coming down before they can be built up. Expect disruption before anything settles.

reversed.love: Avoiding a necessary breakup or confrontation, or a slow-motion collapse. The shake-up is only delayed. Small cracks keep getting papered over, and they widen. Clinging to old patterns keeps the pressure building.
reversed.work: Narrowly dodging a disaster, or ignoring warning signs everyone else can see. Deal with the cracks now, while repairs are still cheap. A narrowly avoided disaster, or a slow decline. Make changes before they're forced on you.
reversed.money: A near miss or a problem you're putting off. Take small losses now rather than a big one later. Avoiding a financial reckoning. Letters marked final notice are easy to leave unopened. Open the statements, list the debts, and call the bank before they call you.
reversed.advice: Face the truth before it forces its way in. Small changes now spare a larger crash. Fix the cracks now.
reversed.asAPerson: Someone in denial or bottling up inner turmoil. They may seem calm while things fall apart inside. Afraid of change, and holding on too tight.

yesNo.why: The collapse is postponed and still coming. Something still has to break before this moves.

waiteNote.upright: Waite's list is heavy: misery, distress, indigence (poverty), adversity, calamity, disgrace, deception, and ruin. He calls it “a card in particular of unforeseen catastrophe”, meaning a disaster no one saw coming. Modern readers take it as sudden upheaval that tears down something that wasn't solid, which hurts and clears the ground.
waiteNote.reversed: Reversed, Waite says it's the same in a lesser degree, and then adds oppression, imprisonment, and tyranny. In practice the reversal is a disaster narrowly avoided, a slow collapse instead of a sudden one, or a shake-up you're resisting. It can also be feeling trapped in a structure that should come down.

imageryHistory: The Tarot de Marseille card was always labeled La Maison Dieu, the House of God, showing a burning tower with its top knocked off, figures falling, and small balls hanging in the air. Smith based her card on that image, crowned the tower, and replaced the floating balls with tongues of flame shaped like the Hebrew letter yod.

mathers.title: The Lightning-struck Tower
mathers.reversed: These in a more or less partial degree.
mathers.source: S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Tarot: Its Occult Signification, Use in Fortune-Telling, and Method of Play (1888)

goldenDawn.title: The Lord of the Hosts of the Mighty
goldenDawn.printed: The Lord of the Hosts of the Mighty
goldenDawn.source: Golden Dawn "Book T", printed as "Liber LXXVIII: A Description of the Cards of the Tarot" in The Equinox I:8 (1912)

olderMeanings.note: Mathers reads ruin, disruption, overthrow, loss, and bankruptcy, and reversed, the same in a more or less partial degree. That's close to Waite and to today, though modern readers stress what the collapse clears away.

name: The Star
upright: It's a card of healing, renewal, and a quiet faith that things are going to be all right. The woman by the water has nothing to hide; she's open and at peace. This is a good sign for recovery of any kind and for dreams you'd started to give up on. Let yourself hope again. After a hard time, the Star is the deep breath. Creative work, study, and anything you do for the long term are favored now.
reversed: Hope is there but hard to reach. You're worn down, and some days it seems like nothing will get better. Sometimes it means you've lost touch with what you used to believe in or dream about. The light hasn't gone out; you just can't see it clearly from where you're standing. Start with something small that feels good and build from there. Maybe you've stopped hoping so you won't be let down again. Try one small thing that used to give you joy.
sitWith: What would you let yourself hope for if you knew you'd survive the disappointment?
inASpread: After the Tower or the Ten of Swords, the Star is healing arriving once the worst is over. Near the Moon, it asks you to keep hoping even when nothing is clear. Few outcome cards are more encouraging.
imagery: A naked woman kneels by a pool under one large star and seven smaller ones, pouring water from one jug into the pool and from another onto the land, while a bird sits in a tree behind her. After the Tower, she's calm and open and giving freely.

waite.upright: Loss, theft, privation, abandonment; another reading says—hope and bright prospects,
waite.reversed: Arrogance, haughtiness, impotence.
waite.picture: A great, radiant, star of eight rays, surrounded by seven lesser stars—also of eight rays. The female figure in the foreground is entirely naked. Her left knee is on the land and her right foot upon the water. She pours Water of Life from two great ewers, irrigating sea and land. Behind her is rising ground and on the right a shrub or tree, whereon a bird alights.
waite.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911)

symbols.symbol: Great eight-pointed star with seven smaller ones
symbols.meaning: A great, radiant star of eight rays in Waite's description: hope and guidance after the storm.

symbols.symbol: Pouring water on land and pool
symbols.meaning: Healing and renewal flowing back into body and spirit.
Openness and vulnerability with nothing left to hide.
Waite mentions a bird alighting on a shrub or tree; many read it as the soul's hope.
The five senses being refreshed.

history: The older card, as Waite describes it, has a large star, seven smaller ones, and a naked woman pouring from two vessels, with a bird perched on a tree near her. He notes that in some later cards a butterfly on a rose replaced the bird, and that the star was sometimes called the Dog-Star or Sirius. Some late fifteenth-century versions show a six-pointed star rather than the eight-pointed one Smith drew.
numerologyAstrology: Seventeen reduces to eight, strength, here as a calm, restored strength after the Tower's shock. Aquarius, the water-bearer, sign of hope and the future, is the card's sign in the Golden Dawn system.

upright.love: Healing and renewed hope. A gentle, honest love, or feeling ready to open your heart again after pain. Healing after heartbreak, or a gentle, hopeful connection. In a relationship, trust starts coming back after a hard season.
upright.work: Inspiration returns and you feel hopeful about your path. A good time for creative work or a fresh start after a setback. Renewed hope, a creative spark, or recognition after a hard stretch. Keep going, it's getting better.
upright.money: Recovery after hard times: debts shrinking, savings slowly refilling. Things improve gradually, and a bit of hope about the future is justified. A small grant, a fair refund or help from a generous person may arrive. Things are improving slowly.
upright.advice: Pour some of the care you give others back into yourself, the way she pours water on both land and pool. Keep hoping, and let yourself heal.
upright.asAPerson: Kind, open, idealistic, a quiet source of inspiration. What they feel for you is sincere and full of hope. Hopeful, kind, and quietly inspiring.

yesNo.why: Hope is justified here. Things are looking up.

reversed.love: Losing faith in love, or feeling too worn down to believe anything good is possible. Waite's reversed words, arrogance and haughtiness, can also show up as coldness that protects a bruised heart. Being closed off protects you for a while and then just keeps you alone.
reversed.work: Creative block, disillusionment, or doubting you chose the right path. The spark is dim and still there, so start with one small piece of work you actually like. Feeling uninspired or discouraged. Reconnect with why you started.
reversed.money: Discouragement about money, or big dreams with no plan underneath them. Pick one practical step toward the hope and take it this week. Pessimism about money, or waiting for luck instead of acting. Discouragement can make you stop checking your accounts at all, which makes it worse.
reversed.advice: Find one small thing to believe in again and start there. Rest, then look up.
reversed.asAPerson: Someone disillusioned, pessimistic, or out of touch with their dreams. Their hope in the connection may have faded for now. Discouraged or cynical, hiding their softer side.

yesNo.why: Hope needs rebuilding before the answer turns.

waiteNote.upright: Waite's first reading is surprising: loss, theft, privation (going without), and abandonment. He then says “another reading says” hope and bright prospects, which is the meaning almost everyone uses today. A reader takes it as hope after a hard time, healing, and quiet faith that things will be better.
waiteNote.reversed: Reversed, Waite gives arrogance, haughtiness (acting superior), and impotence, meaning powerlessness. In practice this is hope that's gone flat, or faith that's turned into pride. It can also mean feeling disconnected from the things that usually lift you.

imageryHistory: The Tarot de Marseille gave tarot this image in the seventeenth century: a naked woman kneeling by water and pouring from two jugs, under one large star and seven smaller ones, with a bird perched on a tree. Smith's Star is closely based on that design, keeping the eight-pointed stars, the two jugs, and the bird in the tree.

mathers.title: The Star
mathers.reversed: Hopes not fulfilled, Expectations disappointed or fulfilled in a minor degree.
mathers.source: S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Tarot: Its Occult Signification, Use in Fortune-Telling, and Method of Play (1888)

goldenDawn.title: The Daughter of the Firmament, the Dweller Between the Waters
goldenDawn.printed: The Daughter of the Firmament, the dweller between the Waters
goldenDawn.source: Golden Dawn "Book T", printed as "Liber LXXVIII: A Description of the Cards of the Tarot" in The Equinox I:8 (1912)

olderMeanings.note: Mathers reads hope, expectation, and bright promises, and reversed, hopes not fulfilled or fulfilled in a minor degree. That matches the modern card, and it's the reading Waite gives as his second option.

name: The Moon
upright: The light is dim, the path winds, and your imagination is filling in the gaps. You might be anxious or confused, or picking up on something you can't quite name. The Moon also rules dreams and intuition, the things that rise up from underneath. Go slowly and don't make big decisions on fear alone. Things aren't what they seem, and the path is only lit by moonlight. It's a time for intuition, dreams, and patience while the full picture takes shape.
reversed: The fog is starting to lift. Confusion clears, secrets come to light, and fears lose some of their grip. What scared you may turn out to be less awful than it looked in the dark. For some, though, the anxiety has gone inward, into the kind of worry that keeps you up at night. Either way, now is the time to sort what's real from what your mind made up. Waite's reversed meanings are milder versions of the upright: instability, silence, and small deceptions or errors, so any trickery here is minor and easier to catch. Keep asking questions and let the truth come out in its own time.
sitWith: Which of your fears is based on something real, and which is just the dark? What would you do if you trusted your instincts over your fears?
inASpread: The Moon and the High Priestess together point strongly to hidden things and trusting your gut. Add the Seven of Swords or the Seven of Cups and it's a warning about deception or wishful thinking. At the end of a reading, it says things aren't clear yet, so wait before acting.
imagery: A full moon with a face hangs between two towers, a dog and a wolf howl up at it, and a crayfish crawls out of a pool onto a winding path. The path leads into the unknown, and the light is dim enough that everything looks stranger than it is.

waite.upright: Hidden enemies, danger, calumny, darkness, terror, deception, occult forces, error.
waite.reversed: Instability, inconstancy, silence, lesser degrees of deception and error.
waite.picture: The distinction between this card and some of the conventional types is that the moon is increasing on what is called the side of mercy, to the right of the observer. It has sixteen chief and sixteen secondary rays. The card represents life of the imagination apart from life of the spirit. The path between the towers is the issue into the unknown. The dog and wolf are the fears of the natural mind in the presence of that place of exit, when there is only reflected light to guide it.
waite.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911)

symbols.symbol: Moon with a face between sun and crescent
symbols.meaning: On the side of mercy the moon is increasing, according to Waite; it shines with borrowed light.
Waite calls them the fears of the natural mind: tame and wild instincts.
Deep fears and hidden things rising from the unconscious.
A gateway into the unknown.
The long road into uncertainty, lit only by moonlight.

history: Older Moon cards, Waite writes, show two towers and a path, two dogs or a wolf and a dog baying, and a crayfish moving out of the water. He notes that some eighteenth-century cards showed the moon waning, the Etteilla deck showed it full in a starry sky, and more recent cards showed it increasing. Smith kept the dog and wolf, the crayfish, and the towers, and drew the moon with a face and falling drops of dew.
numerologyAstrology: Eighteen reduces to nine, the Hermit's number, but here you walk the dark path without his lantern. Its Golden Dawn sign is Pisces, ruled by Jupiter, a water sign of dreams, fog, and deep feeling.

upright.love: Uncertainty, mixed signals, or feelings nobody is saying out loud. Imagination fills the gaps at night, so wait for clearer light before deciding what it all means. With someone new, be careful of anyone who seems too good to be true, and in a long relationship, ask instead of assuming.
upright.work: Confusion, unclear instructions, or something hidden in a deal. Trust your intuition and ask for details in writing. Confusion, hidden agendas, or a situation that isn't clear yet. Wait for more information before you act.
upright.money: Vague promises, unclear terms, or a deal that feels slightly off. Wait for daylight and full disclosure before signing anything. Unclear finances, hidden costs, or scams. Read everything carefully and trust your gut.
upright.advice: Go slowly while the path is dark, and trust your gut about what feels off. The moon's light is borrowed, and so are some of the stories you're hearing.
upright.asAPerson: Mysterious, moody, intuitive, sometimes deceptive or insecure. They may not fully understand their own feelings about you. Dreamy, sensitive, and sometimes hard to pin down.

yesNo.why: Too much is unclear to say yes yet. Things aren't clear enough yet to know.

reversed.love: Confusion clearing or a secret surfacing. Anxiety eases as you see the situation more clearly. A partner may finally explain behavior that worried you. Someone who seemed too good to be true may show their real side. In a relationship, an honest talk now clears up months of guessing.
reversed.work: Misunderstandings get cleared up, or you finally see what was wrong. Fears turn out bigger than the reality. Things becoming clearer, or small lies being exposed. Keep asking questions. Write down what you learn so the story can't shift again.
reversed.money: Hidden costs come to light, or a scam is exposed before it can do more damage. With the facts in hand you can plan properly. A bill you'd been dreading may turn out smaller than feared. Sort out what you owe while it's visible.
reversed.advice: Write down what you're afraid of and check each fear against the facts. Much of what frightened you in the dark shrinks once it's named. Keep asking until the truth comes out.
reversed.asAPerson: Someone confused, anxious, or recovering from deception. They may be starting to see you more clearly. Coming out of a confused or anxious phase.

yesNo.why: Things are clearing, but check before trusting fully. Clarity is coming, and it isn't here yet.

waiteNote.upright: Waite's list is full of things hidden in the dark: hidden enemies, danger, calumny (lies told to damage someone's name), darkness, terror, deception, occult forces, and error. In practice it means you can't see clearly yet, and some of what scares you isn't real. A reader takes it as a warning to go slowly, trust your instincts, and not believe everything you hear.
waiteNote.reversed: Reversed, Waite gives instability, inconstancy (changeability), silence, and “lesser degrees of deception and error”. In practice the reversal is confusion lifting a little, or smaller lies and mistakes coming out. It can also mean you're starting to see through a fear.

imageryHistory: The Tarot de Marseille introduced a whole new Moon scene in the seventeenth century: a moon with rays and falling drops, two dogs beneath it, two towers, and a crayfish in a pool. Waite used Éliphas Lévi's description when designing his version, so Smith drew a dog and a wolf, the crayfish climbing out of the water, and a path winding between the towers, with the moon's face in profile.

mathers.title: The Moon
mathers.source: S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Tarot: Its Occult Signification, Use in Fortune-Telling, and Method of Play (1888)

goldenDawn.title: The Ruler of Flux and Reflux: the Child of the Sons of the Mighty
goldenDawn.printed: The Ruler of Flux and Reflux: the Child of the Sons of the Mighty
goldenDawn.source: Golden Dawn "Book T", printed as "Liber LXXVIII: A Description of the Cards of the Tarot" in The Equinox I:8 (1912)

olderMeanings.note: Mathers reads twilight, deception, and error, and reversed, fluctuation, slight deceptions, and trifling mistakes. That's close to Waite's darker list, while modern readers add intuition and dreams.

name: The Sun
upright: The Sun means success, warmth, confidence, and plain joy. Things are going well or they're about to, and you can see clearly what's in front of you. Whatever you asked about, whether it's love, work, health, or family, the news is good. Let yourself enjoy it. This is one of the happiest cards in the deck. Children, holidays, time outdoors and good health all belong to this card too.
reversed: The sun is behind clouds, but it's still up there. Life feels a bit flat, or good things are hard to enjoy because of doubt or worry. Overconfidence is another possibility, or success that's delayed but still coming. You may also have lost touch with the playful, childlike part of you. The warmth hasn't gone anywhere, and you can step back into it. Too much of a good thing belongs here as well, showing off or burning out from overdoing it. Spend an afternoon outside or with children and notice how much lighter you feel.
sitWith: What's going well right now that you haven't let yourself enjoy? What good thing could you celebrate today?
inASpread: The Sun brightens almost any card around it, turning something like the Five of Pentacles into a passing rough patch. Coming after the Moon, it's confusion giving way to daylight. In the outcome position it's a strong yes. Reversed near the Tower, the good news still comes, only later than hoped.
imagery: A naked child rides a white horse in front of a garden wall lined with tall sunflowers, holding a big red banner under a huge smiling sun. It's joy and openness with nothing to hide.

waite.upright: Material happiness, fortunate marriage, contentment.
waite.reversed: The same in a lesser sense.
waite.picture: The naked child mounted on a white horse and displaying a red standard has been mentioned already as the better symbolism connected with this card.
waite.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911)

symbols.symbol: Naked child on a white horse
symbols.meaning: Joy, innocence, and freedom; Waite calls it the better symbolism for this card.
Energizing life and celebration carried high.
Growth turned toward the light, just past the garden of old limits.
Clarity, warmth, and success that everyone can see.
What's been left behind or climbed over.

history: Waite says older Sun cards showed two children, naked or lightly clothed, playing in a walled enclosure under the sun's rays and drops of dew. He notes that Eliphas Levi mentioned a better symbol, a naked child on a white horse carrying a scarlet standard, and that is the image Smith drew. The sunflowers and the wall stayed as a reminder of the old garden setting.
numerologyAstrology: Nineteen reduces to ten and then to one: a completed cycle that opens right into a new beginning. The Golden Dawn gave the card to the Sun itself, the source of warmth, vitality, and clear sight.

upright.love: Joy, warmth, and a happy relationship. Affection is out in the open, with no games. A wedding, a pregnancy or a family celebration can come with this card. Single, you're glowing and people notice. Couples find it easy to laugh together again, and a new romance can feel openly joyful.
upright.work: Success, recognition, and the confidence to take on more. Your effort shows, people see you at your best, and it's a good moment to ask for what you want. A presentation, an exam or a public role goes well. Share your wins.
upright.money: Prosperity and good fortune, often after a long wait. Enjoy it openly and share a little of the warmth. Financial success, security, and good fortune. Pay off something small, just for the relief of it. This is a good time for a raise, a sale, or a purchase you've saved for.
upright.advice: Let yourself enjoy this and be seen doing it. Like the child on the white horse, you have nothing to hide. Enjoy what's going well.
upright.asAPerson: Warm, joyful, confident, and generous with praise. They light up when they're with you and don't hide it. Warm, cheerful, and easy to be around.

yesNo.why: A bright, clear yes. This one shines bright.

reversed.love: Happiness clouded by doubt, or joy that's there but not being felt. A small setback, nothing lasting. Plans like a holiday or a move together may be pushed back. Being hard on yourself dims whatever is good.
reversed.work: Delayed success or feeling unrecognized. Keep going; the light is behind a cloud and still shining. Success that's slower or smaller than hoped. Share the credit, since overconfidence can put people off. Praise may come late or quietly, and it still counts.
reversed.money: Gains slower than hoped, or overconfidence leading to waste. Waite keeps even the reversal in the same sunlight, only lesser, so this is still mostly good news. Good fortune, just not as much as you wanted. Be patient and keep what you have safe.
reversed.advice: Find the joy that's still there. Don't let one cloudy day convince you it's winter. Let yourself enjoy it, even if it's small.
reversed.asAPerson: Someone a little dimmed, insecure, or trying too hard to look happy. Their warmth toward you is there but muffled. Usually cheerful, and a little dimmed right now.

yesNo.why: Still a yes at heart, just slower or smaller than hoped. Yes, just not as bright or as soon as you'd like.

waiteNote.upright: Waite's list is short and bright: material happiness, fortunate marriage, and contentment. In practice the Sun means things going well in the everyday, touchable sense: health, home, success, and warmth. A reader treats it as a strong yes and a good sign in almost any question.
waiteNote.reversed: Reversed, Waite says it means the same in a lesser sense, so good things, just smaller or later. Modern readers treat it as happiness that's delayed or dimmed, or a good situation you're not letting yourself enjoy.

imageryHistory: The Tarot de Marseille Sun shows two children standing together under a big sun in front of a low wall. The Golden Dawn's own deck kept a boy and girl before a wall, and Smith changed it to a single naked child riding a white horse away from the wall, holding a red banner under a smiling sun.

mathers.title: The Sun
mathers.source: S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Tarot: Its Occult Signification, Use in Fortune-Telling, and Method of Play (1888)

goldenDawn.title: The Lord of the Fire of the World
goldenDawn.printed: The Lord of the Fire of the World
goldenDawn.source: Golden Dawn "Book T", printed as "Liber LXXVIII: A Description of the Cards of the Tarot" in The Equinox I:8 (1912)

olderMeanings.note: Mathers reads happiness, content, and joy, and reversed, the same in a minor degree. It's one of the few cards where old and new readings agree almost exactly.

name: Judgement
upright: Judgement is about waking up. You're hearing a call to look back over your life, forgive yourself or others, and step into a new stage. It often arrives when you finally see something important about where you've been heading. In practice it can mean a long-awaited result, like an exam grade, a legal decision or a medical all-clear. You're ready to rise to something bigger. Judgement is the moment you hear the call and answer it. Family members or old friends may come back into your life for a fresh start.
reversed: The call is being ignored or doubted. Being too hard on yourself is a common version, self-criticism that keeps you from moving on. Avoiding an important decision fits here too, or refusing to learn from the past. Sometimes it's plain self-doubt, hearing the trumpet but not believing it's meant for you. Listen anyway. Harsh self-judgment can be the block, so harsh you can't move forward. Forgive yourself and make the decision.
sitWith: What part of your life is asking you to wake up? What would you do differently if you got to start this again?
inASpread: Judgement with Justice deepens the sense of reckoning. With the Eight of Cups or Death, it marks a big ending that opens into a fresh start. Drawn last, it points to a new chapter and a clearer sense of purpose. Next to the World, it points to the end of one big chapter and the start of another.
imagery: An angel blows a trumpet from the clouds, and below, pale naked figures rise from coffins with their arms raised, answering the call. It's a wake-up moment, people rising to meet a new stage of life.

waite.upright: Change of position, renewal, outcome. Another account specifies total loss though lawsuit.
waite.reversed: Weakness, pusillanimity, simplicity; also deliberation, decision, sentence.
waite.picture: The great angel is here encompassed by clouds, but he blows his bannered trumpet, and the cross as usual is displayed on the banner. The dead are rising from their tombs—a woman on the right, a man on the left hand, and between them their child, whose back is turned.
waite.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911)

symbols.symbol: Angel blowing a trumpet with a cross banner
symbols.meaning: The call to rise, answer, and be counted.
Renewal, awakening, and a second chance.
Waite notes all the figures share one wonder and adoration: a response to the call.
The old life left behind in the deep.
Hard truths and the high ground of clear judgment.

history: The card is Le Jugement in the Marseille deck, and Waite calls the design essentially invariable in all tarot sets: an angel sounds a trumpet and the dead rise. He notes that the Etteilla deck left out the angel altogether. Older cards show a family of three rising, and Waite says Smith's version deliberately adds more figures than that.
numerologyAstrology: Twenty reduces to two, the High Priestess's number, where an inner voice now calls out loud. Elemental Fire, the fire of the spirit, is its Golden Dawn attribution; Pluto was added by later astrologers.

upright.love: Renewal, forgiveness, or a relationship reaching a new level of honesty. You may be called to make a clear decision about it. A second chance, a reconciliation, or seeing a relationship clearly. You may finally understand what you want.
upright.work: A calling, a big decision, or a second chance at something you care about. Answer it. Old skills you'd set aside may suddenly be what's needed. Say yes to the role that fits who you've become. A review, interview, or audition tends to go your way.
upright.money: A reckoning with past money choices, and the chance to make better ones. Old accounts get settled, sometimes through a refund, a claim, or a debt finally cleared. Settling accounts, a review of your finances, or a fresh start. Make the decision.
upright.advice: Answer the call you keep hearing. Forgive what needs forgiving, including yourself, and rise to the next stage.
upright.asAPerson: Thoughtful, self-aware, ready for change; someone who has woken up to something important. With you, they may be ready to start fresh.
