numerologyAstrology: Ten ends the suit's cycle, and here completion is heavy. Saturn in Sagittarius, restriction weighing on big plans, governs the decan.

upright.love: One partner carrying the whole relationship, or love squeezed flat by jobs, kids, and caregiving. Say out loud what you're carrying and ask for a share of it back. Newly dating, check that you're not treating the other person like one more job to manage.
upright.work: Overwork, too many projects, burnout close behind. Success brought this load, as Waite notes, and now some of it has to be handed off. Managers and team leads see this when every task lands on their desk. List what only you can do and hand off the rest, even if others do it differently.
upright.money: Heavy obligations such as debt, dependents, or a mortgage stretched thin. The finish line is close, so trim whatever you can. Bills, loans, and people depending on you can make every month feel tight. Pick the heaviest debt and set a plan to clear it first.
upright.advice: Put some of it down. You don't get extra credit for carrying everything alone. Ask for help before you have to.
upright.asAPerson: Responsible, hardworking, and overburdened. They may care about you and have no room left right now. Hardworking and reliable, and quietly resentful when nobody offers to help.

yesNo.why: There's too much weight to carry this well. The load makes it hard to do well right now.

reversed.love: Finally setting down a burden, or collapsing under one. Hidden strains, the contrarieties and intrigues Waite mentions, may be part of what makes it so heavy. Letting a partner help, or finally saying you can't do it all. Watch for a hidden problem, a secret or a scheme, adding weight behind the scenes.
reversed.work: Delegating at last, or burnout arriving hard. Decide what to drop before the choice is made for you. Handing off work, a project ending, or burnout forcing a break. Protect your health while you sort out what comes next.
reversed.money: Paying off a debt or getting out of an obligation brings relief. Keep going until it's actually done. A debt paid off, or cutting back to lighten the pressure. Selling something you no longer use can lighten things quickly. Look at whether someone else's costs have quietly become yours.
reversed.advice: Choose one thing to put down today. Relief starts there. Say no to one new task this week.
reversed.asAPerson: Overwhelmed, or learning to share the load. Give it time and they'll be lighter company. Learning to delegate, and not always gracefully.

yesNo.why: Only once some of the weight comes off. Relief is possible if you share the weight.

waiteNote.upright: Waite admits this card has meanings that don't fit together. His main one is oppression, being weighed down, and he adds that it can be fortune, gain, and success, and then the weight of those very things. False-seeming, disguise, and perfidy (betrayal) come from older sources, and “stultified” means made useless: success is cancelled if the Nine of Swords follows. In practice it's being loaded down by responsibilities, often ones that came with success.
waiteNote.reversed: Reversed, Waite gives contrarieties (things going against you), difficulties, and intrigues, meaning schemes behind your back. In practice it's the heavy load plus complications, or the moment the weight finally shifts. A reader looks at whether you're dropping the load or it's being made heavier.

imageryHistory: Marseille-pattern decks drew the Ten of Batons as a plain bundle of batons with no one carrying them. Book T describes angelic hands holding eight crossed wands while another hand holds two more upright. Smith's man bent under ten staves is one of the clearest borrowings from the fifteenth-century Sola Busca deck, whose Ten of Swords shows a figure carrying a bundle in almost the same pose; photographs of that deck reached the British Museum in 1907.

mathers.title: Ten of Sceptres
mathers.source: S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Tarot: Its Occult Signification, Use in Fortune-Telling, and Method of Play (1888)

goldenDawn.title: The Lord of Oppression
goldenDawn.printed: THE LORD OF OPPRESSION
goldenDawn.source: Golden Dawn "Book T", printed as "Liber LXXVIII: A Description of the Cards of the Tarot" in The Equinox I:8 (1912)

waiteAdditional.upright: Difficulties and contradictions, if near a good card.
waiteAdditional.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911), Part III section 4, "Some Additional Meanings of the Lesser Arcana"

olderMeanings.note: Mathers reads confidence, security, honour, and good faith, and reversed, treachery, subterfuge, duplicity, and bar, meaning a barrier. Waite sets the honour reading aside, and Book T calls it the Lord of Oppression, which is how it's read today.

name: Page of Wands
upright: The Page of Wands is the itch to try something. It often arrives as news or a message that gets you excited: a class, a trip, an offer, an idea a friend throws out over dinner. As a person, it's someone young at heart, eager, a bit dramatic, and full of plans that haven't been tested yet. You don't need to know where this goes. Following the curiosity for a while is enough for now. The risk is that the excitement fades after the first week, so pick something small enough to finish. Buy the notebook, sign up for the taster class, and see what happens.
reversed: All spark, no follow-through. You might have five exciting projects on the go and not one of them past the first week, or you keep talking about the idea instead of trying it. There's a sulky, restless side too, the kid who gets bored and starts trouble. Now and then it's news that disappoints or keeps getting pushed back. Choose one idea and give it a fair month before you drop it. Enthusiasm that burns out quickly leaves a trail of half-started things.
sitWith: What have you been curious about lately that you haven't let yourself try? What are you curious enough about to start learning this week?
inASpread: Near the Ace of Wands, the Page shows an idea at its earliest, most exciting stage. With the Seven of Cups beside it, the risk is chasing every shiny thing and finishing none of them. Landing last, it's a message or opening that gets you fired up, and it will need work to become anything. Next to the Eight of Wands, it's news arriving quickly.
imagery: A young man in a tunic printed with salamanders stands in the desert holding a tall sprouting wand and gazing up at it, pyramids far behind him. He looks at the wand like he's never seen one before, all curiosity and no plan yet.

waite.upright: Dark young man, faithful, a lover, an envoy, a postman. Beside a man, he will bear favourable testimony concerning him. A dangerous rival, if followed by the Page of Cups. Has the chief qualities of his suit. He may signify family intelligence.
waite.reversed: Anecdotes, announcements, evil news. Also indecision and the instability which accompanies it.
waite.picture: In a scene similar to the former, a young man stands in the act of proclamation. He is unknown but faithful, and his tidings are strange.
waite.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911)

symbols.symbol: Young man gazing at a tall wand
symbols.meaning: Curiosity and a fresh idea not yet tested.
Creatures of fire: enthusiasm and a creative streak.
A place for exploring, much like the Knight's scene.
Bright spirits and a taste for adventure.

history: Waite pictures a young man in the act of proclamation and gives meanings like a faithful lover, an envoy, or a postman. Marseille packs called this card the Valet, the knave or servant, and Waite used the English word Page. The Sola Busca deck left its knaves unnamed while giving the higher court cards classical names.
numerologyAstrology: The Page opens the court. Golden Dawn court attributions make him Earth of Fire: an eager spark still learning practical use.

upright.love: Flirting, a new crush, or an exciting message from someone. Waite calls him a faithful lover, so the enthusiasm is sincere, if young. Someone younger, or new to dating, may make the first move. Couples may enjoy a fun new activity together.
upright.work: A new idea, an internship, or a chance to learn something bold. Try it out on a small scale. A short course, a trainee post, or a first job in a new field fits this card. Be curious and ask questions.
upright.money: Small earnings from a creative idea, a side gig, or news about money arriving by message. Test the idea cheaply before you invest real savings. A sale of something you made can surprise you. Keep receipts from the start, even for a hobby.
upright.advice: Follow your curiosity and try something new. Beginners get to play. Say yes to one small adventure this week.
upright.asAPerson: Curious, charming, restless, and full of stories, the messenger Waite describes. They're excited about you and happy to show it. They may talk up a big plan and need help finishing it.

yesNo.why: Yes, with youthful enthusiasm. Good news is likely.

reversed.love: Mixed signals, or someone who loves the chase more than the relationship. Indecision and instability, which Waite lists for the reversal, keep things from getting off the ground. Don't take it too seriously yet.
reversed.work: Lots of ideas, no follow-through, or bad news about a plan. Focus on one thing until it's finished. Bad news, delays, or projects that never get finished. Finish one thing before starting another. Write down every idea and then choose just one to try this month.
reversed.money: Impulse buys on the latest craze, or money spent on a plan you'll drop next month. Wait a week before buying and see if the urge survives. News about money may disappoint, like a smaller refund or an offer that falls through. Check reviews before paying for a course or kit.
reversed.advice: Pick one idea and stay with it long enough to learn from it. Enthusiasm needs a direction. Finish what you start.
reversed.asAPerson: Flaky, attention-seeking, or unable to settle on anything, you included. Their interest may be bright and brief. Restless, flaky, and quick to lose interest.

yesNo.why: The idea is too scattered to rely on yet. The news isn't as good as you hoped.

waiteNote.upright: Waite describes the Page as a dark young man, faithful, a lover, an envoy (messenger), and a postman. He'll speak well of a man he's placed next to, and he's a dangerous rival if the Page of Cups follows. “Family intelligence” means news about the family. In practice it's enthusiastic news, a message, or a young, eager person.
waiteNote.reversed: Reversed, Waite gives anecdotes (stories, gossip), announcements, and evil news, meaning bad news. He adds indecision and the instability that comes with it. In practice it's news that disappoints, or a restless person who can't settle on anything.

imageryHistory: The Marseille-pattern Valet of Batons is a standing youth holding a large baton, with little background. Smith's Page stands in a desert landscape with a wand taller than himself, his tunic covered in salamanders, looking at the wand as if it has news for him, the young man making a proclamation that Waite describes.

mathers.title: Knave of Sceptres
mathers.upright: A Good Stranger, Good News, Pleasure, Satisfaction
mathers.source: S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Tarot: Its Occult Signification, Use in Fortune-Telling, and Method of Play (1888)
mathers.remarks: R. Notice between what cards the News falls, which will show whence it comes, and of what nature it is.

goldenDawn.title: The Princess of the Shining Flame; the Rose of the Palace of Fire
goldenDawn.printed: THE PRINCESS OF THE SHINING FLAME; THE ROSE OF THE PALACE OF FIRE
goldenDawn.source: Golden Dawn "Book T", printed as "Liber LXXVIII: A Description of the Cards of the Tarot" in The Equinox I:8 (1912)

waiteAdditional.upright: Young man of family in search of young lady.
waiteAdditional.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911), Part III section 4, "Some Additional Meanings of the Lesser Arcana"

olderMeanings.note: Mathers calls him the Knave of Sceptres and reads a good stranger, good news, pleasure, and satisfaction, and reversed, ill news, displeasure, chagrin, and worry. That's close to Waite's messenger reading.

name: Knight of Wands
upright: The Knight of Wands wants to go, and he wants to go now. This is passion, daring, and throwing yourself into an adventure: a move, a trip, a bold career change, a whirlwind romance. The man himself is charming, fun, restless, and not always around once the excitement wears off. There's real courage here and it can carry you far. He's just much better at starting things than finishing them. He's off, and fast. It's a card of bold action, adventure, and following passion, sometimes before thinking it through.
reversed: The horse has bolted. Impatience turns into recklessness, quick decisions you regret, or a temper that flares up out of nowhere. Plans may keep stalling, which only makes the frustration worse. In love, it's the person who comes on strong and then disappears. Slow down enough to see where you're charging off to. Rushing into things can leave a mess behind. Check the plan before you jump on the horse.
sitWith: Are you running toward something, or away from something? Where do you want to go, and what would it take to get moving?
inASpread: The Knight with the Eight of Wands or the Chariot means fast movement and often a literal trip. Beside the Four of Pentacles or the Four of Swords, the urge to go runs straight into the need to stay put. In the outcome position, expect a sudden, bold change, possibly a hasty one. Reversed beside the Seven of Cups, plans may scatter before any of them lands.
imagery: A knight in armor and a salamander-covered tunic rides a rearing horse across the desert, wand held high, the red plume on his helmet streaming back like flame. The horse is barely under control, which tells you a lot about him.

waite.upright: Departure, absence, flight, emigration. A dark young man, friendly. Change of residence.
waite.reversed: Rupture, division, interruption, discord.
waite.picture: He is shewn as if upon a journey, armed with a short wand, and although mailed is not on a warlike errand. He is passing mounds or pyramids. The motion of the horse is a key to the character of its rider, and suggests the precipitate mood, or things connected therewith.
waite.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911)

symbols.meaning: The precipitate, hasty mood, shown in the horse's motion.
Fire and passion that never quite settle.
Far travel; he's passing mounds or pyramids, Waite notes.
Mailed, though not on a warlike errand.

history: Waite reads this Knight as departure, absence, flight, emigration, and change of residence, a card of leaving more than fighting. The fortune-telling notes he includes call it a bad card, and reversed, for a woman, marriage that is probably frustrated. The Sola Busca deck of the late fifteenth century names its Knight of Batons Apolino.
numerologyAstrology: The Knight is the court card that moves. As Fire of Fire in the Golden Dawn scheme, he's all speed and heat.

upright.love: An exciting, passionate romance that may not last. Someone sweeps in, and you should enjoy it with your eyes open. A partner who loves travel or sport may pull you into their plans. Check over a few weeks whether their words match what they do.
upright.work: Bold moves, travel, or a quick job change. Waite's departure and change of residence fit a move for work. Sales, jobs on the road, and young startups that move quickly suit this card well. Act fast while you're inspired.
upright.money: Fast risks for fast gains, such as a quick flip or a move for a better-paid job. Keep a safety net under you in case the horse throws you. Spending on travel or adventure. Budget for it. A move or a trip may cost more than planned, so keep a cushion.
upright.advice: Go with courage and keep an eye on where you're charging. Passion does more when it has a target. Take the bold step.
upright.asAPerson: Adventurous, charming, impulsive, and hard to pin down, often just arrived or about to leave. They're drawn to you right now, strongly. Expect them to leave as fast as they arrived.

yesNo.why: Momentum is strong and favors moving. Bold action pays off.

reversed.love: Hot and cold, or someone leaving as fast as they came. Rupture and interruption are the reversed meanings, so a sudden break is possible. Someone who rushes in and runs out. Don't expect commitment yet.
reversed.work: Recklessness, plans falling apart from haste, or a sudden break. Slow down and check the route. Rash decisions, projects abandoned, or clashes with coworkers. Cool off before you quit anything. Leaving a job in a temper can burn a bridge you'll want later.
reversed.money: Rash spending, or a risky move that backfires because nobody checked the details. Wait before jumping into the next one. Reckless spending. Think before you buy. Impulse flights, gadgets, and nights out add up quickly, so give yourself a waiting rule.
reversed.advice: Count to ten before charging in. Speed without thought burns out fast and leaves a mess. Look before you leap.
reversed.asAPerson: Unreliable and quick-tempered, prone to storming off mid-argument. They may not stick around long enough to fix things. Hot-tempered and reckless.

yesNo.why: There's too much haste for a solid result.

waiteNote.upright: Waite gives departure, absence, flight (leaving quickly), and emigration, moving to another country. He also describes him as a dark, friendly young man, and adds change of residence, which means moving house. In practice it's travel, a move, or a bold, restless person who acts fast.
waiteNote.reversed: Reversed, Waite gives rupture (a break), division, interruption, and discord. In practice it's plans broken off, or a hot temper causing a split. A reader takes it as action that's too hasty, or a move that falls through.

imageryHistory: The Marseille-pattern Cavalier of Batons is a rider on horseback holding a big baton. Smith put him in armor on a rearing horse in a desert, with salamanders on his tunic and pyramids or mounds behind him, and Waite says the horse's motion tells you the rider's character.

mathers.title: Knight of Sceptres
mathers.source: S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Tarot: Its Occult Signification, Use in Fortune-Telling, and Method of Play (1888)
mathers.remarks: This card is not to be read singly; it means the Departure of the card which follows it. R. Again, notice the card which follows it; if a Woman, Quarrel with a Woman; if Money, then Loss of Money, &c.

goldenDawn.title: The Lord of the Flame and the Lightning; the King of the Spirits of Fire
goldenDawn.printed: THE LORD OF THE FLAME AND THE LIGHT- NING; THE KING OF THE SPIRITS OF FIRE
goldenDawn.source: Golden Dawn "Book T", printed as "Liber LXXVIII: A Description of the Cards of the Tarot" in The Equinox I:8 (1912)

waiteAdditional.upright: A bad card; according to some readings, alienation.
waiteAdditional.reversed: For a woman, marriage, but probably frustrated.
waiteAdditional.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911), Part III section 4, "Some Additional Meanings of the Lesser Arcana"

olderMeanings.note: Mathers reads departure, separation, and disunion, and reversed, rupture, discord, and quarrel, very close to Waite. Mathers adds, from Etteilla, that this card shows the departure of whatever card follows it.

name: Queen of Wands
upright: She's the one who walks into a room and people turn to look. The Queen of Wands is confident, warm, busy, and completely herself. She juggles work, friends, and a dozen side projects, and somehow makes it look fun. When she appears, it's time to be bold about what you want and stop apologizing for taking up space. She can also be a real woman in your life who is generous, lively, and a little fierce. She's the life of the party and gets things done. Confidence, warmth, and independence are on your side.
reversed: Her fire can turn inward or go sour. Self-doubt creeps in, you shrink back, or your spark seems to have gone out after giving so much to everyone else. On the other side is the jealous, demanding queen who needs to be the center of attention and bristles when she isn't. Burnout is common here, too much on the calendar and nothing left for you. Clear some space and let the fire build back up. Confidence can tip into jealousy or bossiness when she feels unappreciated. Look at where your effort is going and whether it's coming back.
sitWith: Where have you been making yourself smaller than you are? Where could you show up more boldly this week?
inASpread: With the Sun or the Six of Wands, the Queen shines, and success comes through confidence and being seen. The Five of Cups or the Nine of Swords nearby dims her warmth with worry or grief. If she's the final card, this situation needs you to show up boldly.
imagery: A queen sits on a throne carved with lions, a wand in one hand and a sunflower in the other, with a black cat sitting squarely at her feet. The sunflower is warmth and cheer, and the black cat hints at a sharper, independent side.

waite.upright: A dark woman, countrywoman, friendly, chaste, loving, honourable. If the card beside her signifies a man, she is well disposed towards him; if a woman, she is interested in the Querent. Also, love of money, or a certain success in business.
waite.reversed: Good, economical, obliging, serviceable. Signifies also—but in certain positions and in the neighbourhood of other cards tending in such directions—opposition, jealousy, even deceit and infidelity.
waite.picture: The Wands throughout this suit are always in leaf, as it is a suit of life and animation. Emotionally and otherwise, the Queen's personality corresponds to that of the King, but is more magnetic.
waite.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911)

symbols.meaning: Warmth, joy, and life turned toward the light.
Intuition and independence, the part of her that can't be tamed.
Courage and a strong heart.
Life and animation; the wands of this suit are always in leaf.

history: Waite's description of this Queen is brief and never mentions the black cat at her feet, which seems to have been Smith's own addition. He reads her as a friendly, loving, honourable countrywoman, and notes she may show love of money or success in business. Palas, for Pallas Athena, is the name on the Sola Busca Queen of Batons.
numerologyAstrology: Queens hold the suit's element inside themselves. As Water of Fire in the Golden Dawn scheme, she is warmth that can nurture as well as burn.

upright.love: Confident, magnetic, and warm. You attract people by being fully yourself, and Waite says she is well disposed toward the one she's interested in. A night out with friends may introduce you to someone. People are drawn to you right now, and couples feel passionate and playful.
upright.work: Leading with charisma, warmth, and creativity, the colleague whose enthusiasm lifts the room. Take the stage and let people see what you can do. Leadership, confidence, and getting things done. Take charge of the project.
upright.money: Good business sense and a generous hand. Waite mentions love of money and a certain success in business, so trust your instincts on a venture you believe in. A home business or anything with your name on it can do well. Keep your pricing confident.
upright.advice: Be bold and warm at the same time. Confidence is catching, and yours can bring others along. Take up space in the meeting.
upright.asAPerson: Vibrant, sociable, independent, and big-hearted, the one who remembers everyone's name. She's openly interested in you and doesn't play coy. Warm, confident, and magnetic.

yesNo.why: Confidence carries this. Your enthusiasm makes it a yes.

reversed.love: Jealousy, insecurity, or a temper that flares. Waite warns of opposition, jealousy, even deceit in certain positions. Build your own confidence. Comparing yourself to an ex or a rival only feeds the fire in the wrong direction.
reversed.work: Burnout from running everything, or bossiness when she feels threatened. Pull back, delegate, and refuel before the fire turns on people. She may feel threatened by a talented newcomer. Delegate and rest.
reversed.money: Spending to keep up appearances, or money tied up in someone else's drama. Budget with care and keep your own accounts separate. Paying for everyone at dinner may be more about pride than kindness. Budget carefully. Keep one account for bills that nobody else can touch.
reversed.advice: Refill your own reserves before giving more. Let go of jealousy, since comparing yourself to others only dims your light. Look after your own fire first.
reversed.asAPerson: Demanding, jealous, or self-absorbed when insecure. Waite's reversed card is also good, economical, and obliging, so her better side is still there.

yesNo.why: Insecurity or jealousy is in the way. Wait until the heat dies down.

waiteNote.upright: Waite describes a dark woman, a countrywoman, friendly, chaste (faithful), loving, and honourable. If she's next to a man's card she's fond of him, and next to a woman's card she's interested in you. He adds love of money or a certain success in business. In practice she's warm, confident, and good at making things happen.
waiteNote.reversed: Reversed, Waite gives good, economical (careful with money), obliging, and serviceable, meaning helpful. Only near certain cards does it mean opposition, jealousy, deceit, and infidelity. In practice the reversal is her confidence turning into jealousy or control, or her warmth spread too thin.

imageryHistory: The Marseille-pattern Queen of Batons is a seated queen holding a baton. Smith seated her on a throne carved with lions, holding a wand in one hand and a sunflower in the other, with a black cat at her feet, and Waite notes that the wands in this suit are always in leaf.

mathers.title: Queen of Sceptres
mathers.upright: Woman living in the country, Lady of the Manor, Love of Money, Avarice, Usury
mathers.reversed: A good a virtuous Woman, but strict and economical, Obstacles, Resistance, Opposition.
mathers.source: S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Tarot: Its Occult Signification, Use in Fortune-Telling, and Method of Play (1888)

goldenDawn.title: The Queen of the Thrones of Flame
goldenDawn.printed: THE QUEEN OF THE THRONES OF FLAME
goldenDawn.source: Golden Dawn "Book T", printed as "Liber LXXVIII: A Description of the Cards of the Tarot" in The Equinox I:8 (1912)

waiteAdditional.upright: A good harvest, which may be taken in several senses.
waiteAdditional.reversed: Good-will towards the Querent, but without the opportunity to exercise it.
waiteAdditional.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911), Part III section 4, "Some Additional Meanings of the Lesser Arcana"

olderMeanings.note: Mathers reads a woman living in the country, a lady of the manor, love of money, avarice (greed), and usury, and reversed, a good, virtuous woman who is strict and economical. Waite keeps the love of money and softens it.

name: King of Wands
upright: Vision, with the drive to back it up. The King of Wands is the founder, the coach, the boss people actually want to follow, because he knows where he's going and makes others want to come along. He can be someone like that in your life, or you stepping up to lead your own project. He takes risks, but they're calculated ones. Think bigger than you have been, then take charge of making it happen. Waite describes him as honest and conscientious, a good person to have on your side. It's a strong card for starting a business or leading a team through change.
reversed: His boldness curdles. He can be bossy, hot-tempered, impatient with anyone who can't keep up, or so sure of his vision that he stops listening. Watch for the leader who promises big and delivers little. For you, it may mean expecting far too much of yourself or of the people around you. Good leadership needs some humility, so look at where that has gone missing. A strong vision can become bullying when nobody's allowed to question it. Listen to others and slow down.
sitWith: What vision would you pursue if you trusted yourself to lead it?
inASpread: Beside the Emperor or the Three of Wands, the King points to strong leadership and a plan or business taking off. Next to the Knight or Five of Wands, his drive can tip into bullheadedness and conflict. At the end of a reading, you'll need to lead rather than wait for someone else to.
imagery: A king sits on a throne decorated with lions and salamanders, holding a flowering wand and leaning slightly forward as if about to stand, a small live salamander at his feet. He's a leader who is always thinking about the next move.

waite.upright: Dark man, friendly, countryman, generally married, honest and conscientious. The card always signifies honesty, and may mean news concerning an unexpected heritage to fall in before very long.
waite.reversed: Good, but severe; austere, yet tolerant.
waite.picture: The physical and emotional nature to which this card is attributed is dark, ardent, lithe, animated, impassioned, noble. The King uplifts a flowering wand, and wears, like his three correspondences in the remaining suits, what is called a cap of maintenance beneath his crown. He connects with the symbol of the lion, which is emblazoned on the back of his throne.
waite.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911)

symbols.meaning: Vision that still grows.

symbols.symbol: Lions and salamanders on his throne
symbols.meaning: Courage and creative fire mastered.
A living symbol of fire at his command.

symbols.symbol: Cap of maintenance under his crown
symbols.meaning: A mark of rank and duty worn by all four Kings.

history: Waite describes him as dark, ardent, animated, and noble, and says the card always signifies honesty. He also notes that the King wears a cap of maintenance beneath his crown, like the Kings of the other three suits. Levio Plauto is the name lettered on the Sola Busca King of Batons.
numerologyAstrology: Kings govern their element from outside, through leadership. In the Golden Dawn court scheme he is Air of Fire, vision spread by persuasion.

upright.love: A passionate, loyal partner who knows what they want. Old fortune-telling notes in Waite's book even promise a good marriage. Shared plans, like a move or a business, can bind you closer. A confident, take-charge person may catch your eye.
upright.work: Visionary leadership, entrepreneurship, and bold, honest decisions. Take charge of the big picture and let others handle the details. A founder or a coach may offer you a role. People will follow a clear direction, so say plainly where you're headed.
upright.money: Smart, bold investments and a real head for business. Waite even mentions news of an unexpected inheritance before long. Backing your own venture is favored. A business plan with real numbers turns a big idea into income.
upright.advice: Lead with vision and honesty, and people will follow. Say where you're going and why.
upright.asAPerson: Charismatic, honest, and a natural leader, often married or settled according to Waite. He respects you and makes his interest plain.

yesNo.why: Take the lead and it goes your way. Strong leadership will make this work.

reversed.love: A domineering or impatient partner who expects to be obeyed. Waite puts it mildly as good, but severe, so the heart may be fine even if the manner isn't. Arguments may flare over plans made without asking. Talk about how decisions get made.
reversed.work: A boss who won't listen, or impulsive decisions made to prove a point. Check your own leadership style too. A harsh boss, or rushing big decisions. Ask for input before announcing the plan. Decisions made in anger tend to need fixing later, so sleep on the big ones.
reversed.money: Ego-driven investments or promises made too quickly. Slow down and consult someone with no stake in it. Risky investments or overconfidence. Get advice. Overconfidence about a deal is the risk, so run the figures past someone cautious.
reversed.advice: Lead without dominating. Old notes in Waite's book say the reversed card brings advice that should be followed, so listen to the steady voice in the room. Listen before you lead.
reversed.asAPerson: Overbearing and hot-tempered, yet austere and tolerant underneath, in Waite's words. His interest can turn controlling if he feels challenged. Impatient and domineering.

yesNo.why: Ego or impatience spoils the outcome. Too much force right now.

waiteNote.upright: Waite describes a dark man, friendly, a countryman, usually married, honest and conscientious (careful to do right). He says the card always means honesty, and may mean news of an unexpected heritage, an inheritance, arriving soon. In practice he's a bold, honest leader with big ideas.
waiteNote.reversed: Reversed, Waite gives good but severe, austere (strict and plain), yet tolerant. In practice the reversal is a leader who's too harsh or too impatient. A reader takes it as strength that needs softening.

imageryHistory: The Marseille-pattern King of Batons is a crowned king seated with a large baton. Smith seated him on a throne decorated with lions and salamanders, with a small salamander at his feet, holding a flowering wand, and Waite describes his nature as ardent and impassioned.

mathers.title: King of Sceptres
mathers.upright: Man living in the country, Country Gentleman, Knowledge, Education
mathers.reversed: A naturally good but severe man, Counsel, Advice, Deliberation.
mathers.source: S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Tarot: Its Occult Signification, Use in Fortune-Telling, and Method of Play (1888)

goldenDawn.title: The Prince of the Chariot of Fire
goldenDawn.printed: THE PRINCE OF THE CHARIOT OF FIRE
goldenDawn.source: Golden Dawn "Book T", printed as "Liber LXXVIII: A Description of the Cards of the Tarot" in The Equinox I:8 (1912)

waiteAdditional.upright: Generally favourable; may signify a good marriage.
waiteAdditional.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911), Part III section 4, "Some Additional Meanings of the Lesser Arcana"

olderMeanings.note: Mathers reads a man living in the country, a country gentleman, knowledge, and education, and reversed, a naturally good but severe man, counsel, and advice. Waite's good but severe reversal comes straight from that.

name: Ace of Cups
upright: Your heart is opening. The Ace of Cups is the start of something emotional: new love, a new friendship, a baby, a creative project you care about deeply, or simply a wave of tenderness you didn't expect. The cup is overflowing, which means there's more than enough to go around. Healing belongs here too, a moment of feeling loved and able to love back. Let it spill over. Let yourself receive kindness without explaining why you deserve it.
reversed: The cup is there, but the feeling isn't flowing. Maybe your heart is shut after being hurt, or you're pouring love out to others without keeping any for yourself. There may be feelings you're sitting on, sadness or longing you haven't let yourself have. Sometimes it means love offered and not returned. Start by being kind to yourself, since that's the cup nearest to hand. Waite's reversed meanings include a false heart and instability, so check whether affection offered to you is sincere. Ask what feels unsafe about letting it in.
sitWith: Who or what has made your heart feel full lately? Where could you let someone care for you this week?
inASpread: The Ace of Cups with the Two of Cups or the Lovers is one of the clearest signs of new love in the deck. After the Five of Cups or the Three of Swords, it's healing after heartbreak. Wherever it lands, it brings the heart back into the picture.
imagery: A hand comes out of a cloud holding a golden cup that overflows in five streams into a pond of water lilies, while a white dove drops a small wafer into it. The cup can't hold everything it's given, so it spills over.

waite.upright: House of the true heart, joy, content, abode, nourishment, abundance, fertility; Holy Table, felicity hereof.
waite.reversed: House of the false heart, mutation, instability, revolution.
waite.picture: The waters are beneath, and thereon are water-lilies; the hand issues from the cloud, holding in its palm the cup, from which four streams are pouring; a dove, bearing in its bill a cross-marked Host, descends to place the Wafer in the Cup; the dew of water is falling on all sides.
waite.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911)

symbols.symbol: Hand from a cloud holding a cup
symbols.meaning: Love and feeling offered freely, as a gift.

symbols.symbol: Five streams pouring over the rim
symbols.meaning: Emotion overflowing, more than enough to share.

symbols.symbol: Dove bringing down a wafer marked with a cross
symbols.meaning: The Host descending into the Cup, in Waite's words: grace entering the heart.
Calm beauty rising out of still, deep water.

symbols.symbol: Drops falling like the letter Yod
symbols.meaning: A dew of water falling on all sides, blessing spread everywhere.

history: The Marseille Ace of Cups is a single large ornate chalice with no hand at all. Smith's version, with a dove bringing a wafer down into a cup held by a hand from a cloud, reflects Waite's interest in Grail imagery, and he calls the Host an intimation of what may lie behind the Lesser Arcana. His meanings begin with the house of the true heart, joy, and nourishment.
numerologyAstrology: One is the pure start of the suit of feeling. Golden Dawn writers named it the Root of the Powers of Water, the spring every other cup draws from.

upright.love: New love, a deepening of feeling, or a moment when your heart opens after being shut for a while. The house of the true heart is Waite's phrase, and this is sincere affection, freely given. Single readers may meet someone who feels kind from the first conversation.
upright.work: Work you care about, a warm welcome on a new team, or a creative project that moves you. Kindness in the workplace matters here as much as results. Work that feeds your heart: a caring role, a creative project, or kind coworkers. An offer may come through someone who simply likes you.
upright.money: Money tied to generosity, such as a gift, a kind gesture, or funds for a caring project. Spend a little on what nourishes you and the people you love. Gifts, generosity, or spending on things that nourish you. Money flows best right now toward people and experiences that matter to you, so give and receive freely within your means.
upright.advice: Let yourself feel it and let others see it. An open heart is the whole point of this card. Say yes to what fills you up.
upright.asAPerson: Loving, emotionally open, and generous with affection. Their feeling for you is sincere and may be deeper than they've said so far. Open-hearted, kind, and quick to comfort others.

yesNo.why: The cup is full and being offered to you. The heart is open and the answer is warm.

reversed.love: Feelings held back, love offered and not returned, or affection that comes and goes. Waite's reversed phrase is the house of the false heart, so be honest about whether the warmth is real. A single reader may still be guarding a heart that got hurt, and a couple may need a gentle talk about what's gone unsaid.
reversed.work: A job that has lost its heart, or emotional burnout from caring too much for too long. Protect some time for yourself before resentment sets in. Feeling empty at work, or a job that drains your heart. Look for one small way to bring care back into your day, or begin looking for work that fits better.
reversed.money: Waite also lists instability and mutation, so avoid big decisions made in a low mood. Spending to fill an emotional gap, or money tied up in someone else's needs. Notice what you buy on sad days and try a free comfort instead.
reversed.advice: Refill your own cup before pouring for anyone else. Notice where you've been shutting feelings out. Open the lid a little.
reversed.asAPerson: Emotionally guarded, moody, or saying loving things they don't mean. The affection may be real but blocked by old hurt. They may test you before they trust you.

yesNo.why: Feelings are blocked, so wait for them to open.

waiteNote.upright: Waite calls it the “house of the true heart”, meaning a place where love is honest, and adds joy, content, abode (home), nourishment, abundance, and fertility. The “Holy Table” is a religious image, the altar or communion table, so the cup is full in a spiritual sense as well as an everyday one. In practice it's a new wave of feeling: love, friendship, healing, or a pregnancy.
waiteNote.reversed: Reversed, Waite gives the “house of the false heart”, love that isn't sincere, along with mutation (change), instability, and revolution, meaning things turned over. In practice the cup is tipped or blocked: feelings held back, an offer of love that isn't honest, or emotions changing faster than you can keep up.

imageryHistory: In Marseille-pattern decks the Ace of Cups is a single large ornate cup, sometimes shaped like a castle or fountain, and Book T describes the Golden Dawn card as a hand from the clouds holding a cup on its palm. Smith kept the hand and cloud and added a dove carrying a wafer down into the cup, five streams of water falling into a pond of water lilies.

mathers.title: Ace of Cups
mathers.source: S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Tarot: Its Occult Signification, Use in Fortune-Telling, and Method of Play (1888)

goldenDawn.title: The Root of the Powers of the Waters
goldenDawn.printed: THE ROOT OF THE POWERS OF THE WATERS
goldenDawn.source: Golden Dawn "Book T", printed as "Liber LXXVIII: A Description of the Cards of the Tarot" in The Equinox I:8 (1912)

waiteAdditional.upright: Inflexible will, unalterable law.
waiteAdditional.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911), Part III section 4, "Some Additional Meanings of the Lesser Arcana"

olderMeanings.note: Mathers reads feasting, banquet, and good cheer, and reversed, change, novelty, metamorphosis, and inconstancy. That older sense of a feast is still in the card's overflowing cup, though modern readers put love first.

name: Two of Cups
upright: The Two of Cups is real connection, whether that's a new romance, a close friendship, or a partnership built on trust. Both are giving and receiving in equal measure, and both feel seen. Making up after a quarrel counts too, the moment you look at each other and decide it's worth it. When this card shows up, a bond is forming or getting stronger. This is two people meeting as equals and choosing each other. The feeling is mutual, and that's what makes it strong.
reversed: The give and take has gone lopsided. One person may be doing all the reaching, or you're starting to feel like roommates after being close. It can point to an argument, a breakup, or a loss of trust nobody has talked about yet. Sometimes the imbalance is with yourself, offering others a kindness you never give your own heart. A real conversation, not a polite one, is usually where repair starts. Small misunderstandings can pile up when nobody names them. A calm, honest talk usually does more than a grand gesture here.
sitWith: In your closest relationship, are you both giving about as much as you get? What do you most want the other person to understand about you?
inASpread: A love reading with the Two of Cups and the Lovers or the Ace of Cups is about as clear a yes as tarot gives. Put it beside the Five of Wands and it's two people choosing peace after a clash. If it's reversed and near the Three of Swords, take the hurt seriously. Next to the Lovers or the Hierophant, it strongly suggests commitment.
imagery: A young man and woman face each other and exchange cups, while above them a winged lion's head rises over a staff wrapped by two snakes. It's an even trade between equals, with something larger watching over the bond.

waite.upright: Love, passion, friendship, affinity, union, concord, sympathy, the interrelation of the sexes, and—as a suggestion apart from all offices of divination—that desire which is not in Nature, but by which Nature is sanctified.
waite.reversed: Passion.
waite.picture: A youth and maiden are pledging one another, and above their cups rises the Caduceus of Hermes, between the great wings of which there appears a lion's head. It is a variant of a sign which is found in a few old examples of this card. Some curious emblematical meanings are attached to it, but they do not concern us in this place.
waite.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911)
waite.note: Waite gives no reversed meaning in the main entry for this card; the reversed line is from Part III, section 4, "Some Additional Meanings of the Lesser Arcana."

symbols.symbol: Young man and woman exchanging cups
symbols.meaning: Mutual respect and a pledge made between equals.

symbols.symbol: Caduceus of Hermes rising between them
symbols.meaning: Healing, balance, and a bond that connects two sides.

symbols.symbol: Winged lion's head above the caduceus
symbols.meaning: Passion and desire lifted into something higher.
The home or shared future the two might build.

history: Waite says the caduceus crowned by a winged lion's head is a variant of a sign found in a few old examples of this card, though he declines to explain its meaning. Unusually, he gives no reversed meaning in the card's main entry; the only one he prints, in his list of additional meanings, is the single word passion. Smith turned the Marseille pip's two cups into a couple pledging each other.
numerologyAstrology: Two is partnership, and this is the deck's clearest card for it. Its Golden Dawn title is the Lord of Love, set in Venus in Cancer, affection with a homemaking heart.

upright.love: Waite's list runs love, passion, friendship, union, and concord, so the feeling goes both ways. Mutual attraction, a first date that clicks, or a relationship deepening into partnership. If you're already together, it's a good time to renew promises or plan something as a pair.
upright.work: Working with one trusted person may get further than a whole committee. A strong partnership, a good collaboration, or a contract signed with someone you trust. Working in pairs is favored, so find the right person to team up with.
upright.money: Among the extra meanings Waite passes on, it's favourable in business as well as love. Shared finances, a joint venture, or money that comes through a partnership. Fair terms and honest talk make it work, so agree on who pays what before you commit.
upright.advice: Meet the other person halfway and say what you feel. Equal effort is what keeps this bond steady.
upright.asAPerson: Warm, attentive, and interested in a real connection. Their feeling toward you is mutual attraction with respect underneath it. Warm, loyal, and easy to talk to.

yesNo.why: Two cups are raised together. The feeling is mutual.

reversed.love: Passion running ahead of trust, a relationship out of balance, or a falling-out between people who were close. Waite's single reversed word is passion, and here it may burn hotter than it's steady. A breakup, a falling out, or one person caring more than the other. Singles may find chemistry that isn't backed by real compatibility, and couples may be avoiding a talk about imbalance.
reversed.work: A partnership souring, a contract with uneven terms, or a colleague you no longer trust. Clear conversations now can save the working relationship. A partnership that's gone sour, or disagreement with a colleague. Clear the air or renegotiate terms before resentment grows.
reversed.money: Arguments about shared money, or one person contributing much more than the other. Put the arrangement in writing. A friend or partner may borrow and forget. Talk about money before moving in or going into business together.
reversed.advice: Name the imbalance kindly and ask what the other person needs. Repair starts with one honest conversation.
reversed.asAPerson: Infatuated, possessive, or blowing hot and cold. The attraction is strong, and the respect may be lagging behind. Passionate, and sometimes more intense than steady.

yesNo.why: The balance between you is off right now.

waiteNote.upright: Waite's list is all connection: love, passion, friendship, affinity (a natural pull toward someone), union, concord (agreement), and sympathy. “The interrelation of the sexes” is his formal way of saying romance and attraction. In practice it's a real, two-way bond, whether a romance, a friendship, or a business partnership.
waiteNote.reversed: Waite gives no reversed meaning in his main entry; the single word “Passion” comes from his list of additional meanings. In practice readers take the reversal as a bond out of balance: a falling out, trust broken, or attraction that burns hot without real understanding.

imageryHistory: In Marseille-pattern decks the Two of Cups showed two cups with a decorative flower or scroll between them, and Book T describes the Golden Dawn card as a hand holding lotuses rising above water with two cups. Smith drew a young man and woman pledging their cups to each other, with the staff of Hermes, the caduceus, rising between them topped by a winged lion's head.

mathers.title: Deuce of Cups
mathers.source: S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Tarot: Its Occult Signification, Use in Fortune-Telling, and Method of Play (1888)

goldenDawn.title: The Lord of Love
goldenDawn.printed: THE LORD OF LOVE
goldenDawn.source: Golden Dawn "Book T", printed as "Liber LXXVIII: A Description of the Cards of the Tarot" in The Equinox I:8 (1912)

waiteAdditional.upright: Favourable in things of pleasure and business, as well as love; also wealth and honour.
waiteAdditional.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911), Part III section 4, "Some Additional Meanings of the Lesser Arcana"

olderMeanings.note: Mathers reads love, attachment, friendship, sincerity, and affection, and reversed, crossed desires, obstacles, and opposition. Book T calls it the Lord of Love, so every source agrees on this card's heart.

name: Three of Cups
upright: Here are your people. The Three of Cups shows friends gathering to celebrate, a birthday, a wedding, a reunion, or a long dinner where everyone stays too late laughing. It's about the kind of support that comes from a circle, the women in the card holding each other up as much as their cups. After a hard stretch, it says you don't have to get through everything alone. Call the friend you've been meaning to call. Good things are better shared, and this card brings the people to share them with. It's a card of friendship, reunions, and marking a win together.
reversed: The party has gone a bit sideways. It might be too many late nights and too much wine, fun that's turned into a way to avoid things. Gossip shows up here, or a falling out in a friend group, or that painful feeling of seeing everyone else together without you. In love readings, the old meaning is a third person getting between two people. Look at which friendships actually feed you and which ones just fill time. Too much of a good time can leave a hangover, literal or social. Watch the drinking, the gossip, and who's being left out.
sitWith: Which friends make you feel most like yourself? Who would you call first with good news?
inASpread: Alongside the Four of Wands or the Ten of Cups, this points to a wedding, a party, or a happy family event. With the Seven of Swords nearby, someone in the circle may not be as loyal as they seem. It makes a lovely outcome card, the kind where things end with people you care about raising a glass.
imagery: Three young women in bright dresses dance in a circle and lift their cups high in a toast, with fruit and gourds from the harvest scattered at their feet. It's a party after the hard work is done, and they're celebrating together.

waite.upright: The conclusion of any matter in plenty, perfection and merriment; happy issue, victory, fulfilment, solace, healing.
waite.reversed: Expedition, dispatch, achievement, end. It signifies also the side of excess in physical enjoyment, and the pleasures of the senses.
waite.picture: Maidens in a garden-ground with cups uplifted, as if pledging one another.
waite.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911)

symbols.meaning: Friendship, celebration, and shared joy.
Community and mutual support, everyone included.

symbols.symbol: Fruit and gourds at their feet
symbols.meaning: Harvest and good fortune ready to enjoy.
Festivity and a happy occasion.

history: In Waite's picture, maidens in a garden-ground lift their cups as if pledging one another, and he reads it as a happy issue, healing, and the conclusion of any matter in plenty. Reversed, he notes the side of excess in physical enjoyment. The older pip had only three cups grouped together, and Smith turned it into one of the deck's most joyful scenes.
numerologyAstrology: Three is growth through others, the first community after the pair. Mercury in Cancer, good talk around a full table, rules its decan, and its Book T title is the Lord of Abundance.

upright.love: Your social circle supports the relationship, which counts for a lot. Meeting someone through friends, or celebrating with a partner and your circle. A single reader might find love at a party or a group outing.
upright.work: A team win, a launch party, or colleagues who have become real friends. Waite's happy issue fits a project that ends well. Networking and collaboration bring good results, so say yes to the drinks after work.
upright.money: Enough to celebrate, or money coming through friends and community. Share the good fortune and enjoy it. Spending on celebrations, or money shared among friends. Enjoy it, and set a limit before the night starts.
upright.advice: Gather your people and celebrate what's gone right. Joy is better when it's shared.
upright.asAPerson: Sociable, fun, and loyal to friends. They enjoy you, and part of the appeal is how well you fit into each other's circles.

yesNo.why: There's reason to celebrate. Good company and good news make this a yes.

reversed.love: Waite's reversed reading points to excess in physical enjoyment, so watch where the fun is leading. Gossip, a third person interfering, or partying that's hurting the relationship. Couples may need more time alone and less time in the group.
reversed.work: Cliques, office gossip, or a celebration that goes too far. Keep professional lines clear. Decisions may really be made over after-work drinks, and missing them can cost you. Keep your head down and your comments kind.
reversed.money: Overspending on nights out, gifts, or social pressure. Set a spending limit before the next plans get made. Lending to friends who rarely pay back strains the money and the friendship. Set a budget for fun and stick to it.
reversed.advice: Enjoy yourself without overdoing it, and step back from gossip. Choose friends who still show up when the party's over. Watch the excess and the gossip.
reversed.asAPerson: Fun but shallow, a gossip, or someone who loves a crowd more than closeness. Their attention to you may be social more than serious. Fun, and sometimes a bit too much.

yesNo.why: Excess or outside interference is spoiling things. Too much excess or drama right now.

waiteNote.upright: Waite reads the three dancing women as “the conclusion of any matter in plenty, perfection and merriment”, meaning things ending well and happily. He adds happy issue (a good outcome), victory, fulfilment, solace (comfort), and healing. In practice it's friends, celebrations, and good news shared.
waiteNote.reversed: Reversed, Waite gives expedition and dispatch, both meaning speed and getting things done, plus achievement and end. He adds “the side of excess in physical enjoyment”, meaning overdoing food, drink, or pleasure. In practice it's partying too hard, gossip, or a friendship circle that's gone off.

imageryHistory: Marseille-pattern decks drew the Three of Cups as three cups in a decorative arrangement, and Book T describes a hand holding lotuses with flowers overhanging the cups. Smith painted three young women in a garden raising their cups together among fruit and flowers, the picture Waite describes as maidens pledging one another.

mathers.title: Three of Cups
mathers.reversed: Expedition of business, Quickness, Celerity, Vigilance.
mathers.source: S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Tarot: Its Occult Signification, Use in Fortune-Telling, and Method of Play (1888)

goldenDawn.title: The Lord of Abundance
goldenDawn.printed: THE LORD OF ABUNDANCE
goldenDawn.source: Golden Dawn "Book T", printed as "Liber LXXVIII: A Description of the Cards of the Tarot" in The Equinox I:8 (1912)

waiteAdditional.upright: Unexpected advancement for military man.
waiteAdditional.reversed: Consolation, cure. end of the business.
waiteAdditional.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911), Part III section 4, "Some Additional Meanings of the Lesser Arcana"

olderMeanings.note: Mathers reads success, triumph, victory, and a favourable issue, and reversed, expedition of business, quickness, and celerity (speed). Book T calls it the Lord of Abundance.

name: Four of Cups
upright: Meh. That's the feeling of the Four of Cups, the flat spell where nothing appeals and even good things don't quite land. Maybe you're bored with your routine, a little sulky, or quietly wondering if this is all there is. Some of that is healthy, a pause to work out what you want next. The trouble is that something new is being held out right beside you, and arms-crossed isn't a great way to receive it. You're bored or fed up, and it's easy to miss what's right in front of you. Look up from what's wrong long enough to notice what's being offered.
reversed: You're starting to sit up and look around. After a stretch of feeling stuck or uninterested, something has caught your attention again, or you've finally admitted what you were missing. Now and then it runs the other way, pulling back even further from people and plans so you can sort out your feelings in private. Either version means you've stopped just stewing. Pay attention to what you find yourself curious about. Coming out of a slump can feel awkward at first. Say yes to one small new thing and see where it leads.
sitWith: What might be sitting right next to you that you haven't noticed? What's being offered to you right now that you haven't really looked at?
inASpread: The cloud hand in this card is often answered by an Ace nearby, especially the Ace of Cups, which suggests the offer is real and worth taking. With the Hermit or the Four of Swords, the mood is withdrawal, and it may need time before anything shifts. As a starting position, it describes someone who is bored or checked out, which colors how they'll see the rest of the spread. With the Eight of Cups, the boredom may be turning into a wish to leave.
imagery: A young man sits under a tree with his arms crossed, frowning at three cups on the grass, while a hand reaches out of a cloud offering him a fourth that he doesn't seem to notice. He's so wrapped up in what he already has, or doesn't want, that he can't see what's being handed to him.

waite.upright: Weariness, disgust, aversion, imaginary vexations, as if the wine of this world had caused satiety only; another wine, as if a fairy gift, is now offered the wastrel, but he sees no consolation therein. This is also a card of blended pleasure.
waite.reversed: Novelty, presage, new instruction, new relations.
waite.picture: A young man is seated under a tree and contemplates three cups set on the grass before him; an arm issuing from a cloud offers him another cup. His expression notwithstanding is one of discontent with his environment.
waite.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911)

symbols.symbol: Man under a tree with arms crossed
symbols.meaning: Closed off, bored, or brooding.

symbols.symbol: Three cups standing on the grass
symbols.meaning: What he already has and doesn't value.

symbols.symbol: Hand from a cloud offering a fourth cup
symbols.meaning: Another wine, as if a fairy gift, which he doesn't even see.
Stillness and withdrawal, perhaps a real need for rest.

history: Waite reads this card as weariness, disgust, and aversion, as if the wine of this world had caused satiety only. He also calls it a card of blended pleasure, the same phrase the Golden Dawn used for its title, the Lord of Blended Pleasure. Where the Marseille pip showed only four cups, Smith drew a young man under a tree ignoring the cup being offered to him.
numerologyAstrology: Four is stability that can turn stale. The Moon in Cancer rules its decan, moods circling inward.

upright.love: Boredom, apathy, or a sense that nothing anyone offers is quite right. Someone may be reaching out and you're too withdrawn to notice. Boredom in a relationship, or not noticing someone who's interested. Look up, because someone may be offering more than you realize.
upright.work: Going through the motions, turning down offers out of habit, or feeling uninspired. Look up, because something new may be on the table. Feeling stuck, bored, or unmotivated at work. An offer or idea may be sitting there that you haven't taken seriously, so give it a second look.
upright.money: Ignoring opportunities because you're fed up or distracted. Review offers you dismissed too quickly. Ignoring an opportunity because you feel flat. Review what's actually available before saying no. A side offer or a small raise may be worth more than it looks.
upright.advice: Notice what's being offered before you wave it away. Rest if you need to, then look again.
upright.asAPerson: Withdrawn, apathetic, or hard to reach. Unhappiness with themselves may be the issue more than lack of interest in you. Withdrawn, a little grumpy, and deep in thought.

yesNo.why: You may be missing the offer in front of you. You're not in the mood to see the good in it yet.

reversed.love: Coming out of a slump and ready to try again, or noticing someone who was there all along. Novelty and new relations are Waite's reversed meanings. Waking up to someone you'd overlooked, or new interest in a relationship. Singles may feel ready to meet people again.
reversed.work: Fresh motivation, a new direction, or finally accepting the offer. Waite gives new instruction, so a course or mentor may help. Boredom lifts once a task has a clear point to it. Take the offer seriously this time.
reversed.money: Seeing an opportunity you had ignored. Act on it now that you're paying attention. Noticing an opportunity you'd missed. Reply to the email, book the meeting, or fill in the form you've been ignoring.
reversed.advice: Say yes to the fresh cup. Your interest is coming back for a reason. Call back the person whose offer you ignored.
reversed.asAPerson: Someone waking up to new possibilities, possibly including you. They're more open than they were. Coming out of their shell.

yesNo.why: You're starting to see the offer. Interest is coming back.

waiteNote.upright: Waite gives weariness, disgust, aversion (turning away), and “imaginary vexations”, meaning troubles you've made up in your head. He says it's as if the world's wine had only made the man satiated, too full to enjoy more, so he doesn't even see the new cup being offered. He also calls it a card of blended pleasure, meaning happiness mixed with dissatisfaction.
waiteNote.reversed: Reversed, Waite gives novelty, presage (a sign of something coming), new instruction, and new relations. In practice the reversal is waking up from the slump and noticing what's on offer. A reader takes it as new interests, new people, and saying yes again.

imageryHistory: Marseille-pattern decks drew four cups in a simple pattern, and Book T describes four cups, the two upper ones overflowing into the two lower ones. Smith painted a young man sitting under a tree, arms crossed, staring at three cups on the grass while a hand from a cloud offers him a fourth, the offered cup that Waite says he can't see.

mathers.title: Four of Cups
mathers.source: S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Tarot: Its Occult Signification, Use in Fortune-Telling, and Method of Play (1888)
mathers.remarks: The following cards might show what the displeasure or anxiety was about; the preceding cards, whence it originated.

goldenDawn.title: The Lord of Blended Pleasure
goldenDawn.printed: THE LORD OF BLENDED PLEASURE
goldenDawn.source: Golden Dawn "Book T", printed as "Liber LXXVIII: A Description of the Cards of the Tarot" in The Equinox I:8 (1912)

waiteAdditional.upright: Contrarieties.
waiteAdditional.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911), Part III section 4, "Some Additional Meanings of the Lesser Arcana"

olderMeanings.note: Mathers reads ennui (boredom), displeasure, discontent, and dissatisfaction, and reversed, new acquaintance, conjecture, sign, and presentiment. Book T calls it the Lord of Blended Pleasure, the phrase Waite borrows.

name: Five of Cups
upright: Something has been lost, and it hurts. The Five of Cups is grief and disappointment: a breakup, a missed chance, a plan that fell through, a loss you're still mourning. The figure in black can't look away from the spilled cups, and that's natural for a while. There are still two cups standing behind them, though, and a bridge back to the house. When you're ready, and not before, turn around and see what's still there. Grief needs its time, and there's no shortcut through it.
reversed: The worst of it is passing. You can glance back at the two cups still standing now, and maybe take a first step toward that bridge. This is acceptance and forgiveness, the first day you think about the loss and don't cry. Other times this is grief you've pushed down and kept to yourself because you felt you should be over it by now. There's no deadline on this, and moving on doesn't mean it didn't matter. Healing sometimes arrives as a phone call from an old friend or a relative. Let people back in, and be careful of plans made in a rush to feel better.
sitWith: What's still standing that you haven't let yourself notice?
inASpread: Paired with the Three of Swords, the grief is sharp and fresh, often about love. When the Six of Cups sits beside it, the sadness is tangled up with memories and missing how things used to be. If Pentacles like the Five or the Ten follow, the loss may be about money or security, and the two standing cups are the resources you still have.
imagery: A figure in a long black cloak stands with head bowed over three spilled cups, while two cups still stand upright behind them, and across the river a bridge leads to a house. All their attention is on what spilled, with what remains and the way home just out of view.

waite.upright: It is a card of loss, but something remains over; three have been taken, but two are left; it is a card of inheritance, patrimony, transmission, but not corresponding to expectations; with some interpreters it is a card of marriage, but not without bitterness or frustration.
waite.reversed: News, alliances, affinity, consanguinity, ancestry, return, false projects.
waite.picture: A dark, cloaked figure, looking sideways at three prone cups; two others stand upright behind him; a bridge is in the background, leading to a small keep or holding.
waite.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911)

symbols.meaning: Grief and mourning.
What's been lost and can't be undone.

symbols.symbol: Two cups still standing behind him
symbols.meaning: Something remains over: three taken, two left.

symbols.symbol: Bridge leading to a small keep
symbols.meaning: A way back home when you're ready to turn around.
Tears and feeling separating him from home.

history: Waite says plainly that this is a card of loss, but something remains over: three cups taken, two left. He adds readings of inheritance that falls short of expectations and marriage with some bitterness. The older fortune-tellers he quotes, oddly, called it generally favourable and a happy marriage.
numerologyAstrology: Five brings the shake-up and the loss. As the Lord of Loss in Pleasure, Mars in Scorpio, it's what happens when desire runs hot and something gets spilled.

upright.love: Heartbreak, regret, or grieving a relationship that ended. It hurts, and there are still people standing by you, the two cups you haven't turned to see. Let yourself feel it, and notice who's still there for you.
upright.work: A setback, a lost opportunity, or a project that failed. Grieve it, then look at what's still intact. A rejected application or a project that went to someone else fits here. Ask for feedback so the next attempt goes better.
upright.money: Loss or an inheritance that disappoints, as Waite notes. What remains is still worth protecting. A financial loss or disappointment. Focus on what you still have and rebuild from there. Count what's left before deciding the whole plan failed.
upright.advice: Let yourself mourn properly, then turn around slowly. Not everything is gone.
upright.asAPerson: Grieving, regretful, or stuck in sadness. Their feelings toward you may be tangled with loss. Sad, regretful, and dwelling on the past.

yesNo.why: There's loss here, though not everything is lost.

reversed.love: Moving on after grief, or reconnecting with someone from the past. Return and alliances appear in Waite's reversed list, so an old connection may resurface. Friends who stood by you during the loss become closer. You're ready to heal.
reversed.work: Recovery after a setback, or accepting what happened and finding a new path. Old contacts may help. Recovering from a setback, or learning from a mistake. Pick up what's left and move forward. What went wrong last time is useful information for the next try.
reversed.money: Recovering from a loss, or family money news connected to ancestry or a relative's return. Waite lists both among the reversed meanings. Rebuild slowly. A relative or old friend may offer practical help, so let them.
reversed.advice: Pick up the cups that are still standing. Forgiveness helps you walk on.
reversed.asAPerson: Healing, reconnecting, or ready to move on. Don't be surprised if they come back into your life. Healing and moving on.

yesNo.why: Recovery is underway. Things lean toward yes as the grief eases.

waiteNote.upright: Waite calls it a card of loss where something remains: three cups are spilled, but two still stand. It's also a card of inheritance, patrimony (what's passed down from parents), and transmission, though not what was expected. Some interpreters read it as marriage, but “not without bitterness or frustration”. In practice it's grief with something still worth turning around for.
waiteNote.reversed: Reversed, Waite gives news, alliances, affinity, consanguinity (blood relations), ancestry, and return. He adds false projects, meaning plans that won't work. In practice it's moving on from grief, often through family or old connections coming back.

imageryHistory: Marseille-pattern decks showed five cups arranged with ornament, and Book T describes a hand holding lotuses whose flowers are falling to either side. Smith drew a figure in a black cloak with head bowed over three spilled cups, two cups still standing behind him, and a bridge leading to a small house across the river.

mathers.title: Five of Cups
mathers.reversed: Arrival, Return, News, Surprise, False projects.
mathers.source: S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Tarot: Its Occult Signification, Use in Fortune-Telling, and Method of Play (1888)

goldenDawn.title: The Lord of Loss in Pleasure
goldenDawn.printed: THE LORD OF LOSS IN PLEASURE
goldenDawn.source: Golden Dawn "Book T", printed as "Liber LXXVIII: A Description of the Cards of the Tarot" in The Equinox I:8 (1912)

waiteAdditional.upright: Generally favourable; a happy marriage; also patrimony, legacies, gifts, success in enterprise.
waiteAdditional.reversed: Return of some relative who has not been seen for long.
waiteAdditional.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911), Part III section 4, "Some Additional Meanings of the Lesser Arcana"

olderMeanings.note: Mathers reads union, junction, marriage, and inheritance, and reversed, arrival, return, news, surprise, and false projects. Waite keeps the inheritance and marriage threads with a bitter edge, and Book T calls it the Lord of Loss in Pleasure.

name: Six of Cups
upright: The Six of Cups is nostalgia, the sweet pull of the past. An old friend gets in touch, you drive past your childhood home, a song takes you straight back to being fourteen. It's about innocence and simple kindness, the sort of gift a child gives without thinking twice. It can also mean time spent with children, or playing like one again. Some of what you loved back then might be worth bringing forward. Waite's own reading adds new relationships, new knowledge and new surroundings, so the past can open a door to something fresh. There's sweetness in it, and a reminder of who you were before things got complicated.
reversed: The past has too strong a hold. Rose-colored glasses are part of it: measuring everything now against how good it was before, or repeating a pattern you learned young. Another reading is finally leaving home, literally or otherwise, and growing up in a way you'd put off. Some readers see old childhood hurts coming up to be dealt with here. Visit the past if you need to, then come back to the present. Looking back can become a way of hiding from the present. Keep the good memories and live in today.
sitWith: What from your younger years would you like to have back? What did you love as a child that you could bring back into your life?
inASpread: Alongside the Five of Cups, it's grief and nostalgia together, missing someone or something that's gone. Near the Knight or Page of Cups, it can mean an old flame coming back, and the real question is whether you want the person or the memory. If it closes the spread, expect something from the past to resurface. Next to a court card, it can mean someone from your past returning.
imagery: In an old village courtyard, a boy hands a smaller girl a cup filled with white flowers, while an older figure walks away in the background and more flower-filled cups stand around them. It feels like a scene from childhood, safe and simple, a gift given for no reason at all.

waite.upright: A card of the past and of memories, looking back, as—for example—on childhood; happiness, enjoyment, but coming rather from the past; things that have vanished. Another reading reverses this, giving new relations, new knowledge, new environment, and then the children are disporting in an unfamiliar precinct.
waite.reversed: The future, renewal, that which will come to pass presently.
waite.picture: Children in an old garden, their cups filled with flowers.
waite.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911)

symbols.symbol: Older child offering a cup of flowers to a smaller one
symbols.meaning: Innocent kindness, nostalgia, and simple gifts.

symbols.symbol: White star-shaped flowers in the cups
symbols.meaning: Fond memories kept fresh.
Home, childhood, and the past, the old garden of Waite's description.

symbols.symbol: Figure walking away in the background
symbols.meaning: Grown-up concerns moving off, leaving the children safe for now.

history: Waite pictures children in an old garden with cups filled with flowers and calls it a card of the past and of memories. He notes another reading that flips this into new relations, new knowledge, and new surroundings, with the children playing in an unfamiliar precinct. Reversed, he gives the future and renewal, the opposite of looking back.
numerologyAstrology: Six brings back balance after the loss of five, this time through memory and kindness. Book T calls it the Lord of Pleasure, set in the Sun in Scorpio: warmth found by going deep.

upright.love: An old flame getting back in touch, a childhood sweetheart, or a relationship with an easy, familiar sweetness. Small thoughtful gestures mean more than big ones right now. Couples may enjoy remembering how they met.
upright.work: Returning to an old workplace, reconnecting with former colleagues, or work involving children, teaching, or care. Skills from years ago come in handy. A hobby from childhood may turn into paid work. Old contacts may bring new opportunities.
upright.money: A gift from family, an inheritance, or money connected with your hometown. Pleasant memories is all Waite's extra notes say, and a small windfall from the past fits that mood. Gifts, family money, or spending on things that bring back good memories. Be generous within your means.
upright.advice: Let a happy memory remind you what you actually enjoy. Kindness without an agenda goes a long way. Get in touch with an old friend this week.
upright.asAPerson: Sweet, nostalgic, gentle, and a little innocent. Their feeling toward you is fond and protective, possibly rooted in shared history. Kind, sentimental, and nostalgic.

yesNo.why: Yes, especially where old ties or the past are involved. The past brings something good.

reversed.love: Living in the past, comparing a new partner to an old one, or an ex who keeps reappearing. Waite's reversed reading points to the future, so it may be time to look forward. Checking an ex's social media keeps the old story going. Make one new plan that has nothing to do with the past.
reversed.work: Clinging to how things used to be done, or refusing to grow up in a role. Learn from the past without living there. Stuck in old ways, or moving on from a past job. Look forward. The way it used to be done may not suit the team you have now.
reversed.money: Relying on family money too long, or nostalgia spending. An inheritance to fall in quickly is the reversed note Waite records, so family finances may shift. Waiting on an inheritance or a family loan can stall your own plans. Focus on the future.
reversed.advice: Keep the memory and put down the rose-tinted glasses. What's ahead needs your attention now. Live in today.
reversed.asAPerson: Stuck in the past, childish, or idealizing what used to be. They may love a memory of you more than who you are now.

yesNo.why: Looking back won't give you the answer. The next step is ahead.

waiteNote.upright: Waite calls it a card of the past and of memories, like looking back on childhood, with happiness and enjoyment that come “rather from the past”, from things that have vanished. Another reading turns this around: new relations, new knowledge, and a new environment. In practice it's nostalgia, childhood, old friends, and simple kindness.
waiteNote.reversed: Reversed, Waite gives the future, renewal, and “that which will come to pass presently”, meaning soon. In practice modern readers take it as being stuck in the past, or finally leaving it behind. The reversal often points forward, away from memory.

imageryHistory: Marseille-pattern decks drew six cups in two columns, and Book T describes a hand with six lotus flowers bending over the cups. Smith painted two children in an old garden, one handing the other a cup filled with white flowers, the scene Waite describes as children in an old garden.

mathers.title: Six of Cups
mathers.upright: The Past, passed by, Faded, Vanished, Disappeared
mathers.reversed: The Future, that which is to come, Shortly, Soon.
mathers.source: S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Tarot: Its Occult Signification, Use in Fortune-Telling, and Method of Play (1888)
