mathers.remarks: Shows either that what precedes it is past, has occurred already; or if R., what is going to happen.

goldenDawn.title: The Lord of Pleasure
goldenDawn.printed: THE LORD OF PLEASURE
goldenDawn.source: Golden Dawn "Book T", printed as "Liber LXXVIII: A Description of the Cards of the Tarot" in The Equinox I:8 (1912)

waiteAdditional.upright: Pleasant memories.
waiteAdditional.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911), Part III section 4, "Some Additional Meanings of the Lesser Arcana"

olderMeanings.note: Mathers reads the past, passed by, faded, vanished, and disappeared, and reversed, the future, that which is to come, shortly, soon. Waite's reading of memories and the future reversal come directly from that older pairing, and Book T calls it the Lord of Pleasure.

name: Seven of Cups
upright: Too many options, and most of them are daydreams. The Seven of Cups shows a person faced with a sky full of possibilities, some wonderful, some dangerous, none of them quite real yet. It's about imagination and wishful thinking, and the risk of getting lost in what might be instead of choosing something. Not every shiny cup is a good idea, and one of them has a snake in it. Pick one and test it against real life. Daydream for a bit, then choose one and check if it holds up.
reversed: The clouds are clearing. The fantasy is giving way, and you're seeing your options for what they really are, which makes it far easier to choose. Or it goes the other way, and you're so swamped by choices that you freeze. Waking up from an illusion about a person or a plan fits here too. Clarity can be a little disappointing at first, but you can stand on it. Clarity often arrives when you stop keeping every option open. Pick one and put your energy behind it.
sitWith: Which of these options would you still want if nobody knew about it?
inASpread: Next to the Moon, the Seven of Cups warns strongly of illusion, deception, or fooling yourself. When practical cards like the Eight of Pentacles or the Emperor come after it, you can watch a dream being turned into a plan. As a starting position it often describes someone full of ideas who hasn't committed to any of them yet.
imagery: A dark figure stands with their back to us facing seven cups floating in the clouds, each holding something different: a castle, jewels, a laurel wreath, a dragon, a snake, a glowing veiled figure, and a head. Some are tempting and some are frightening, and all of them are made of cloud.

waite.upright: Fairy favours, images of reflection, sentiment, imagination, things seen in the glass of contemplation; some attainment in these degrees, but nothing permanent or substantial is suggested.
waite.reversed: Desire, will, determination, project.
waite.picture: Strange chalices of vision, but the images are more especially those of the fantastic spirit.
waite.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911)

symbols.meaning: Strange chalices of vision, as Waite puts it: fantasies and choices.

symbols.symbol: Castle, jewels, and a laurel wreath
symbols.meaning: Dreams of security, wealth, and victory.

symbols.symbol: Snake and dragon in two of the cups
symbols.meaning: Temptation and fear hiding among the options.
The hidden self, or a mysterious choice nobody can see clearly.
Seen from behind, dazzled by the options.

history: Waite calls them strange chalices of vision and says they show fairy favours, sentiment, and imagination, with nothing permanent or substantial suggested. Smith filled the seven cups with a castle, jewels, a wreath, a dragon, a snake, a head, and a shrouded glowing figure, making it one of the most detailed pips in the deck. The older pip had only the seven cups.
numerologyAstrology: Seven tests your judgment, this time among fantasies. Venus in Scorpio rules its decan, and its Golden Dawn title is the Lord of Illusionary Success: desire promising more than it delivers.

upright.love: Too many options, daydreaming about someone you barely know, or an idealized picture of a partner. Waite's images of reflection fit love that lives mostly in your head. Endless options on dating apps can make it hard to commit to anyone. Look at what's real.
upright.work: Plenty of ideas and possibilities with no clear winner. Pick two or three and test them against real facts. Busy work can hide the fact that nothing important is moving. Talk to someone already doing the job you're dreaming about. Write each option down with what it would really take, and the fantasy ones fall away.
upright.money: Get-rich-quick dreams, or too many options competing for the same money. Check what's solid before committing anything. Crypto tips and schemes sold by friends need a hard look. Focus on one realistic plan. Lottery thinking is the risk here.
upright.advice: Choose one cup and look inside it closely. Not everything that glitters in the clouds is real. Sleep on any decision that looks perfect.
upright.asAPerson: Dreamy, imaginative, and hard to pin down. Their feeling toward you may be more fantasy than fact so far. They may promise more than they can deliver, without meaning harm.

yesNo.why: It depends on which choice you make and whether it's real. Too many options to know yet.

reversed.love: Clarity arriving after confusion, or a decision finally made. Desire, will, and determination, Waite's reversed meanings, turn wishing into choosing. Seeing someone clearly, or choosing what you really want. Commit.
reversed.work: Focus returns, and you commit to one path. Clear goals make the next step obvious. Making a decision, or focusing on one goal. Act. The fog lifts once you pick a goal and give it a deadline, so name the one project you'll finish first.
reversed.money: Seeing through illusions and making a practical plan. Cut out what isn't real. Dropping a scheme that was never going to pay is a relief. Cancel the courses and apps that only cost money. A realistic budget replaces the wish list, and savings start to grow once the plan stays the same for a few months.
reversed.advice: Decide, and then act on it. Determination turns a dream into a project. Decide and commit.
reversed.asAPerson: Someone who has sorted out what they want and is ready to commit. They see you more clearly now. Focused and clear.

yesNo.why: Clarity makes the choice easier. Once you choose, yes.

waiteNote.upright: Waite gives fairy favours (gifts that aren't quite real), images of reflection, sentiment, imagination, and “things seen in the glass of contemplation”, visions seen while daydreaming. He adds that there may be some success in these, “but nothing permanent or substantial”. In practice it's too many options, wishful thinking, and daydreams that need a reality check.
waiteNote.reversed: Reversed, Waite gives desire, will, determination, and project. In practice it's choosing one dream and putting your will behind it. A reader takes it as clarity after confusion.

imageryHistory: Marseille-pattern decks showed seven cups in a pattern, and Book T describes the cups arranged as two descending triangles above a point. Smith painted a figure seen from behind facing seven cups floating in the clouds, filled with a castle, jewels, a wreath, a dragon, a snake, a head, and a veiled glowing figure, which Waite calls chalices of vision.

mathers.title: Seven of Cups
mathers.source: S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Tarot: Its Occult Signification, Use in Fortune-Telling, and Method of Play (1888)

goldenDawn.title: The Lord of Illusionary Success
goldenDawn.printed: THE LORD OF ILLUSIONARY SUCCESS
goldenDawn.source: Golden Dawn "Book T", printed as "Liber LXXVIII: A Description of the Cards of the Tarot" in The Equinox I:8 (1912)

waiteAdditional.upright: Fair child; idea, design, resolve, movement.
waiteAdditional.reversed: Success, if accompanied by the Three of Cups.
waiteAdditional.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911), Part III section 4, "Some Additional Meanings of the Lesser Arcana"

olderMeanings.note: Mathers reads idea, sentiment, reflection, and project, and reversed, plan, design, resolution, and decision. That lines up with Waite's reversal of will and determination, and Book T calls it the Lord of Illusionary Success.

name: Eight of Cups
upright: Walking away from something that no longer fills you up. The Eight of Cups is the quiet decision to leave a job, a relationship, a town, or a way of life, even when nothing is obviously wrong with it. The cups are stacked neatly, and still there's a gap, something missing that you can't ignore anymore. It's a sad card and a brave one. You're choosing what matters over what's comfortable. Walking away doesn't mean it was worthless; it means you've outgrown it.
reversed: You know it's time to go and you're not going. Fear of the unknown, guilt, or plain habit may be keeping you in something that stopped working a while ago. Other times it means trying one more time before you leave, which can be the right call. There's also the drifter, moving from one thing to the next and always leaving before anything gets deep. Staying out of habit or fear rarely brings the joy back. Be honest about whether you're recommitting or just avoiding the goodbye.
sitWith: What are you still holding on to that stopped feeding you a while ago?
inASpread: Walking away with the Hermit nearby is a real retreat, time alone to figure out what matters. After the Five of Cups, the Eight means finally leaving a loss behind instead of standing over it. It ends a reading with a departure, and usually one that's for the best. After the Four of Cups, the boredom has turned into a decision to leave.
imagery: A cloaked figure with a walking stick heads away from eight neatly stacked cups toward bare mountains, under a moon that is both full and crescent at once. The cups are carefully arranged with a gap in the stack, and he's leaving them anyway.

waite.upright: The card speaks for itself on the surface, but other readings are entirely antithetical—giving joy, mildness, timidity, honour, modesty. In practice, it is usually found that the card shews the decline of a matter, or that a matter which has been thought to be important is really of slight consequence—either for good or evil.
waite.reversed: Great joy, happiness, feasting.
waite.picture: A man of dejected aspect is deserting the cups of his felicity, enterprise, under-taking or previous concern.
waite.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911)

symbols.meaning: A man of dejected aspect deserting the cups of his felicity, in Waite's phrase.

symbols.symbol: Eight cups stacked with a gap
symbols.meaning: Something is missing despite everything you've built.
Instinct guiding a hard choice at night.
The harder road toward something that means more.

history: A dejected man deserts the cups of his felicity or previous concern, and Waite admits other readings give the opposite: joy, mildness, modesty. In practice, he says, it usually shows the decline of a matter, or that something thought important is of slight consequence. Book T gives it the title Lord of Abandoned Success.
numerologyAstrology: Eight moves you on after the seven's illusions. Saturn in Pisces, hard limits inside the dreamiest sign, is the decan, which is why walking away becomes the answer.

upright.love: Leaving a relationship that no longer fulfills you, even if nothing is dramatically wrong. It takes courage to walk away from something that looks fine from outside. Single readers may be stepping back from dating to figure out what you really want.
upright.work: Waite notes something thought important may turn out to be of slight consequence. Quitting a job, leaving a career path, or walking away from a project that stopped mattering. It takes courage, and the reasons are sound if the work has gone hollow.
upright.money: Walking away from a comfortable income for something more meaningful. Plan the transition before you leave. Letting go of an investment or a way of earning that no longer pays off in money or meaning. Accept the loss and put your resources toward something that fits who you are now.
upright.advice: Trust the feeling that it's time to go. Pack what you need and take the harder road. Walk away from what's hollow.
upright.asAPerson: Restless, searching, emotionally withdrawn. Pulling away to find themselves is likely. They may need time alone before they can commit.

yesNo.why: It's time to walk away from this. Something here needs to be left behind first.

reversed.love: Fear of leaving keeps you in something that isn't working, or drifting back and forth. Oddly, Waite reverses it into great joy and feasting, so staying may also work out. Afraid to leave, or trying one more time with someone. Be honest about whether things can really change, and whether you're staying for love or for fear of being alone.
reversed.work: Staying in a role you've outgrown out of fear, or aimless wandering. Decide one way or the other. An exit plan kept in a drawer for years may be worth dusting off. Set a date to review whether it's improving, and stick to it.
reversed.money: Clinging to security you don't need, or leaving without a plan. Balance meaning with practicality. Holding on to a losing investment because you've already put so much in. Past spending isn't a reason to keep spending.
reversed.advice: Be honest about why you're staying or going. Fear is a bad reason for either. Decide if you're staying for love or fear.
reversed.asAPerson: Indecisive, avoidant, or someone who keeps leaving and coming back. They may not know what they want. Torn between staying and going.

yesNo.why: Staying could work out, as long as fear isn't the reason. You're not sure yet, and that's the honest answer.

waiteNote.upright: Waite says the surface meaning is plain, a man walking away from his cups, though other old readings are the opposite: joy, mildness, timidity (shyness), honour, and modesty. His practical rule is that the card shows the decline of a matter, or that something thought important turns out to be of slight consequence. In practice it's leaving something that no longer satisfies, even if it once did.
waiteNote.reversed: Reversed, Waite gives great joy, happiness, and feasting, the opposite of the upright's quiet leaving. Modern readers usually take it as being afraid to walk away, or trying one more time. So hold both: a return to enjoyment, or staying out of fear.

imageryHistory: Marseille-pattern decks drew eight cups in a pattern, and Book T describes a hand holding lotus stems with only two flowers bending over the cups. Smith painted a man in red walking away at night toward rocky hills, leaving eight stacked cups behind him under an eclipsed moon, a man deserting the cups of his former happiness, as Waite puts it.

mathers.title: Eight of Cups
mathers.upright: A fair Girl, Friendship, Attachment, Tenderness
mathers.source: S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Tarot: Its Occult Signification, Use in Fortune-Telling, and Method of Play (1888)

goldenDawn.title: The Lord of Abandoned Success
goldenDawn.printed: THE LORD OF ABANDONED SUCCESS
goldenDawn.source: Golden Dawn "Book T", printed as "Liber LXXVIII: A Description of the Cards of the Tarot" in The Equinox I:8 (1912)

waiteAdditional.upright: Marriage with a fair woman.
waiteAdditional.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911), Part III section 4, "Some Additional Meanings of the Lesser Arcana"

olderMeanings.note: Mathers gives a fair girl, friendship, attachment, and tenderness, and reversed, gaiety, feasting, joy, and pleasure. Book T calls it the Lord of Abandoned Success, which is much closer to today's reading of walking away.

name: Nine of Cups
upright: The Nine of Cups says you're likely to get what you want, and to enjoy it when you do. It's contentment, comfort, pleasure, and a sense of having enough. The man on the bench isn't out chasing anything; he's sitting back and enjoying what he has. If you're asking whether something will work out, this is a warm yes. This is the card people hope to see: a wish coming true and a sense of being satisfied. Let yourself enjoy it without guilt.
reversed: You got the thing, and it isn't making you as happy as you expected. The reversed Nine can mean chasing pleasures that don't satisfy, or putting too much faith in money and comfort. There's also a smug side, showing off or acting like you've made it. It may point to a wish that hasn't come true yet, or to learning that contentment has to come from inside. Ask what you're actually hungry for. Getting what you wanted can feel strangely flat if it wasn't what you needed. Look at what would satisfy you more deeply.
sitWith: If your wish came true tomorrow, what do you hope it would feel like?
inASpread: When the Nine of Cups lands as the outcome, it's the classic wish card answer, a yes. Surrounded by the Sun or other happy Cups, the good news is confirmed, while the Four of Pentacles or the Devil nearby can turn the pleasure into clinging or overindulgence. With the Star or the Sun, it's one of the happiest combinations in the deck.
imagery: A well-fed man sits on a wooden bench with his arms folded and a satisfied grin, and behind him nine golden cups are lined up on a curved, cloth-draped shelf. He looks very pleased with himself, and he has reason to be.

waite.upright: Concord, contentment, physical bien-être; also victory, success, advantage; satisfaction for the Querent or person for whom the consultation is made.
waite.reversed: Truth, loyalty, liberty; but the readings vary and include mistakes, imperfections, etc.
waite.picture: A goodly personage has feasted to his heart's content, and abundant refreshment of wine is on the arched counter behind him, seeming to indicate that the future is also assured. The picture offers the material side only, but there are other aspects.
waite.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911)

symbols.symbol: Contented man seated with arms folded
symbols.meaning: Satisfaction and a little pride in what he has.

symbols.symbol: Nine cups on an arched counter behind him
symbols.meaning: Plenty in reserve; Waite says it seems to show the future is also assured.

symbols.symbol: Blue cloth draped over the counter
symbols.meaning: Comfort on display, and perhaps something kept out of view.
A secure seat in his own success.

history: Long called the wish card by fortune-tellers, it shows what Waite calls a goodly personage who has feasted to his heart's content. He adds that the picture offers the material side only, but there are other aspects. Lord of Material Happiness was its Golden Dawn title.
numerologyAstrology: Nine is the peak before the final ten. Jupiter in Pisces, generous luck in the sign of dreams, rules its decan, which is why wishes come true here.

upright.love: Contentment, a wish fulfilled, or a relationship that simply feels good. If you've hoped for something specific, this card says it may well happen. Getting what you wished for in love, or a relationship that feels satisfying and easy. Anyone unattached may meet someone who fits their wish list, and couples enjoy comfort and pleasure together.
upright.work: Success, satisfaction, and a job well done. Waite's victory, success, and advantage fit a deal that closes in your favor. Achieving a goal, getting the job you wanted, or feeling proud of your work. Take a day to enjoy it before setting the next target.
upright.money: Comfort and plenty, with enough to enjoy life. Treat yourself, and keep some in reserve on that counter. A bonus or a good sale may cover something you've wanted for a while. Share the good meal, since this card enjoys company.
upright.advice: Enjoy what you've got and let yourself be pleased. Make your wish plainly, because this card grants them.
upright.asAPerson: Content, generous, a little self-satisfied, and fun to be around. They're happy with you and see no reason to hide it. They enjoy good food, good company and being the host.

yesNo.why: The wish card says yes. What you hoped for is likely to happen.

reversed.love: A wish granted that doesn't feel as good as expected, or smugness getting in the way. Oddly, Waite's reversed list starts with truth, loyalty, and liberty before adding mistakes and imperfections. Getting what you wanted and finding it doesn't satisfy, or being too comfortable to grow. Couples may need more depth, and single readers may be chasing a checklist over a real connection.
reversed.work: Complacency after a success, or results that look good only on the surface. Check the numbers beneath the shine. Success that feels hollow, or resting on your laurels. Look for work that satisfies more deeply than a title.
reversed.money: The old notes Waite quotes give good business for the reversal, so the money may be fine even if the mood isn't. Overindulgence, or spending on things that don't make you happy. Look at what really brings you comfort and cut the rest.
reversed.advice: Ask whether what you wished for is what you still want. Satisfaction has to come from inside you; the shelf can only hold so much. Ask what would satisfy you deeply.
reversed.asAPerson: Smug, indulgent, or materialistic, though possibly more loyal than they seem. Their happiness may depend on having things just so. Smug, overindulgent, or restless under the comfort.

yesNo.why: The wish may come in a different form. What you want may not be what you need.

waiteNote.upright: Waite gives concord, contentment, and physical bien-être, a French phrase meaning bodily well-being. Victory, success, and advantage follow, with satisfaction for the person asking. In practice this is the wish card: comfort, pleasure, and getting what you wanted.
waiteNote.reversed: Reversed, Waite gives truth, loyalty, and liberty (freedom), then admits the readings vary and include mistakes and imperfections. In practice modern readers take it as smugness, overindulgence, or a wish granted that doesn't satisfy. A reader asks whether the comfort is real or just surface.

imageryHistory: Marseille-pattern decks drew nine cups in rows, and Book T describes a hand holding lotuses with a flower over each cup and water pouring out. Smith painted a well-fed man sitting with arms crossed and a satisfied smile, nine cups lined up on a curved counter behind him, the figure who has feasted to his heart's content in Waite's words.

mathers.title: Nine of Cups
mathers.upright: Victory, Advantage, Success, Triumph, Difficulties surmounted
mathers.source: S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Tarot: Its Occult Signification, Use in Fortune-Telling, and Method of Play (1888)

goldenDawn.title: The Lord of Material Happiness
goldenDawn.printed: THE LORD OF MATERIAL HAPPINESS
goldenDawn.source: Golden Dawn "Book T", printed as "Liber LXXVIII: A Description of the Cards of the Tarot" in The Equinox I:8 (1912)

waiteAdditional.upright: Of good augury for military men.
waiteAdditional.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911), Part III section 4, "Some Additional Meanings of the Lesser Arcana"

olderMeanings.note: Mathers reads victory, advantage, success, triumph, and difficulties surmounted, and reversed, faults, errors, mistakes, and imperfections. Waite keeps that reversal, and Book T calls it the Lord of Material Happiness.

name: Ten of Cups
upright: The happy ending. The Ten of Cups is love that lasts, family harmony, and feeling at home with the people who matter most. Think marriage, a family gathering, a settled home, or just a stretch of real peace in your relationships. The Nine was personal satisfaction; the Ten is joy that's shared. It's the kind of happiness you can build a life on. This is emotional fulfillment: the people you love, a home that feels safe, and a sense that it's enough. Enjoy it and let others enjoy it with you.
reversed: The picture-perfect family isn't quite so perfect. Maybe there's tension at home, distance between partners, or values that don't match. Some of the strain comes from chasing an ideal of family life that doesn't fit who you really are. In harder cases it points to a broken home, or feeling cut off from people you love. Look for the real connection underneath the picture you think you're supposed to have. Talk honestly about what's not working so the happiness can be real.
sitWith: What does home feel like when it's at its best?
inASpread: Readers often pair this card with the Four of Wands and the Two of Cups as signs of marriage or family milestones. In a spread otherwise full of Swords, it may be describing the home life that the stress is threatening, the thing worth protecting. As the final card, it's about as good as it gets. Reversed beside the Five of Cups, family tension may be spoiling a happy occasion.
imagery: A couple stands with their arms around each other, raised toward a rainbow of ten cups in the sky, while two children dance beside them and a cozy house sits by a river. It's a family that loves each other and a home to share.

waite.upright: Contentment, repose of the entire heart; the perfection of that state; also perfection of human love and friendship; if with several picture-cards, a person who is taking charge of the Querent's interests; also the town, village or country inhabited by the Querent.
waite.reversed: Repose of the false heart, indignation, violence.
waite.picture: Appearance of Cups in a rainbow; it is contemplated in wonder and ecstacy by a man and woman below, evidently husband and wife. His right arm is about her; his left is raised upward; she raises her right arm. The two children dancing near them have not observed the prodigy but are happy after their own manner. There is a home-scene beyond.
waite.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911)

symbols.symbol: Rainbow of ten cups across the sky
symbols.meaning: Emotional fulfilment, which the couple contemplate in wonder.
Shared joy and gratitude.
They haven't noticed the prodigy, Waite says, but they're happy in their own way.

symbols.symbol: House among trees and a stream
symbols.meaning: Home and family harmony.

history: Waite describes the couple as evidently husband and wife, gazing at a rainbow of cups while their children dance without noticing it. He reads it as contentment and repose of the entire heart, the perfection of human love and friendship. Where the Marseille pip showed ten cups in rows, Smith drew one of the deck's happiest family scenes.
numerologyAstrology: Ten completes the suit of feeling. Mars in Pisces rules the decan, and the title Lord of Perfected Success belongs to it: action finally bringing dreams to rest.

upright.love: Lasting happiness, family, a home together, or the relationship you've hoped for. In Waite's words, it is the perfection of human love and friendship. Couples may talk about marriage, children, or moving in, and single readers may meet someone who wants the same kind of life.
upright.work: Harmony at work, a team that feels like family, or balance between career and home. Waite also mentions someone taking charge of your interests. A family business, or working from home, can suit you well. Your values and your job line up, so enjoy it.
upright.money: Enough for a secure and happy home. Money serves the family rather than ruling it. Financial security for the family, or money spent on home and loved ones. It's a good time to plan for long-term stability.
upright.advice: Notice the rainbow over your own life and say thank you for it. Protect the people who make it feel like home. Enjoy the people you love.
upright.asAPerson: Family-minded, loving, and loyal. They see a lasting future with you and would like to build a home. They'll want to meet your family early.

yesNo.why: This is a happy, lasting yes. Happiness is lasting here.

reversed.love: A picture-perfect family that isn't happy underneath, or disagreements about home and children. Repose of the false heart, indignation, and violence are the reversed meanings, so take any sign of real harm seriously. Tension at home, disconnection, or clashing values in a relationship. Couples need honest talk, and single readers may be chasing a picture of family that doesn't fit them.
reversed.work: A team that looks harmonious and isn't, or work pulling you away from home. Address the tension before it spreads. Work-life imbalance, or a workplace with hidden tension. Protect your time at home and set boundaries.
reversed.money: Family money arguments, or spending to keep up appearances at home. Honest conversations are needed. Sit down together and make a plan. Money kept secret from a partner tends to become the real argument.
reversed.advice: Stop performing happiness and talk about what's really wrong. Real closeness can survive the truth. Talk honestly at home.
reversed.asAPerson: Someone putting on a happy face while struggling inside. They may want a family life they can't quite create. Struggling to keep up appearances.

yesNo.why: The picture isn't as happy as it looks. There's strain under the surface.

waiteNote.upright: Waite gives contentment and “repose of the entire heart”, meaning a heart completely at rest, and the perfection of that state, along with perfection of human love and friendship. Next to several court cards it can mean someone looking after your interests, and it can also mean your hometown or country. In practice it's lasting happiness, family love, and a sense of being home.
waiteNote.reversed: Reversed, Waite gives “repose of the false heart”, a peace that isn't real, along with indignation (anger at unfairness) and violence. In practice it's tension at home, a family that looks happy from outside, or values clashing. A reader treats it as the home life needing honest attention.

imageryHistory: Marseille-pattern decks drew ten cups in a pattern, and Book T describes a hand holding lotuses whose flowers pour water into all the cups until they all run over. Smith painted a couple with arms around each other and raised in greeting, two children dancing beside them, a house by a river, and ten cups in a rainbow overhead.

mathers.title: Ten of Cups
mathers.upright: The Town wherein one resides, Honour, Consideration, Esteem, Virtue, Glory, Reputation
mathers.source: S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Tarot: Its Occult Signification, Use in Fortune-Telling, and Method of Play (1888)

goldenDawn.title: The Lord of Perfected Success
goldenDawn.printed: THE LORD OF PERFECTED SUCCESS
goldenDawn.source: Golden Dawn "Book T", printed as "Liber LXXVIII: A Description of the Cards of the Tarot" in The Equinox I:8 (1912)

waiteAdditional.upright: For a male Querent, a good marriage and one beyond his expectations.
waiteAdditional.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911), Part III section 4, "Some Additional Meanings of the Lesser Arcana"

olderMeanings.note: Mathers reads the town where one lives, honour, consideration, esteem, and reputation, and reversed, combat, strife, and dispute. Waite keeps the hometown thread, and Book T calls it the Lord of Perfected Success.

name: Page of Cups
upright: The Page of Cups brings a happy surprise. It can be a sweet message, a new crush, or a creative idea that shows up unannounced, like the fish in his cup. As a person, he's gentle, dreamy, sensitive, and a bit young at heart in the nicest way. He also stands for listening to your intuition and letting yourself be a little silly and open. Don't dismiss the odd little idea just because it seems unlikely. Something tender or imaginative is trying to get your attention. Follow the odd idea or the soft feeling and see where it leads.
reversed: Feelings are running the show in a less charming way. It can look like sulking, oversensitivity, or getting hurt by small things. Creative ideas may feel blocked, or you may be escaping into daydreams instead of dealing with real life. Sometimes it's a message that disappoints, or a crush that turns out to be mostly fantasy. Take the feeling seriously without letting it take over. Feelings can get hurt easily right now, yours or someone else's. Check that affection being offered is sincere before you trust it fully.
sitWith: What small, surprising feeling or idea came up lately that you brushed off? Who could you share it with, just to see what they say?
inASpread: When the Page of Cups turns up near the Ace or Two of Cups, a new romance or friendship may be starting sweetly. Among Swords, it can be the soft, sensitive part of you that's getting drowned out by overthinking. Good news of a personal kind is likely if it's the outcome, often something small that means a lot. Reversed near the Seven of Cups, daydreams may be standing in for action.
imagery: A young man in a tunic printed with lotus flowers stands by the sea, looking with mild surprise at a fish poking its head out of the cup in his hand. Something unexpected has popped up out of the water, the way a feeling or idea surfaces out of nowhere.

waite.upright: Fair young man, one impelled to render service and with whom the Querent will be connected; a studious youth; news, message; application, reflection, meditation; also these things directed to business.
waite.reversed: Taste, inclination, attachment, seduction, deception, artifice.
waite.picture: A fair, pleasing, somewhat effeminate page, of studious and intent aspect, contemplates a fish rising from a cup to look at him. It is the pictures of the mind taking form.
waite.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911)

symbols.symbol: Fish rising out of the cup
symbols.meaning: The pictures of the mind taking form, in Waite's words: a surprising idea or feeling.

symbols.symbol: Page gazing calmly at the fish
symbols.meaning: Curiosity and openness to the unexpected.
Gentleness and creative imagination.
Feeling and intuition moving just under the surface.

history: Waite pictures a fair, pleasing page of studious and intent aspect watching a fish rise from a cup to look at him, and calls it the pictures of the mind taking form. The fortune-tellers he quotes call it a good augury, and also a young man unfortunate in love. The French name in Marseille packs is Valet de Coupe.
numerologyAstrology: As Earth of Water in the Golden Dawn scheme, the Page is feeling taking its first solid shape. Pages bring news and beginnings.

upright.love: A sweet message, a shy admirer, or a new crush that surprises you. Feelings are tender and a little dreamy, which is part of the charm. Single readers may get a surprise note from someone, and couples can enjoy a playful, gentle phase.
upright.work: A creative idea out of nowhere, a study opportunity, or news about a project. Waite gives application, reflection, and meditation directed to business. Follow your imagination, and share the idea with someone who can help it grow.
upright.money: Small, pleasant surprises, or money through creative work. Let an unusual idea have a trial run. Selling art, crafts or writing on a small scale can go well. Enjoy it, and keep it small until it's proven.
upright.advice: Stay open to what surprises you and follow the odd idea. Playfulness can lead somewhere real. Follow the tender feeling.
upright.asAPerson: Gentle, imaginative, sensitive, and a little shy. They're sweet on you and may show it in quirky ways. Often younger, or new to relationships, they wear their heart openly.

yesNo.why: A gentle yes, with a surprise. Something sweet is coming.

reversed.love: Emotional immaturity, fantasy crushes, or someone playing with feelings. Seduction and deception are on Waite's reversed list. Emotional immaturity, mixed messages, or a charming person who isn't sincere. Take your time before you trust someone new.
reversed.work: Creative block, or ideas that never get past daydreaming. Ground the idea in a plan. Finish something small to build confidence. Criticism may sting more than usual, so take the useful part and leave the rest.
reversed.money: Impulsive spending on a whim, especially on pretty things. Wait before buying and see if you still want it tomorrow. Impulse spending on feelings, or a deal that seems too sweet. Be careful and read the details.
reversed.advice: Separate fantasy from fact before acting on feelings. A daydream isn't a promise. Check the feeling is real.
reversed.asAPerson: Moody, clingy, or seductive in a way that isn't sincere. Their interest may be more about attention than you. Moody, oversensitive, and sometimes deceptive.

yesNo.why: There's too much fantasy and not enough ground. Feelings are too unsettled right now.

waiteNote.upright: Waite describes a fair young man who wants to help, someone you'll be connected with, and a studious youth. He adds news, message, application (hard work), reflection, and meditation, also turned toward business. In practice it's a sweet message, a creative idea, or a young, gentle person.
waiteNote.reversed: Reversed, Waite gives taste, inclination (a leaning toward something), attachment, seduction, deception, and artifice, meaning clever tricks. In practice it's feelings that aren't quite honest, emotional immaturity, or a charming person who isn't sincere.

imageryHistory: The Marseille-pattern Valet of Cups is a standing youth holding a cup. Smith painted a young man in a flowered tunic by the sea, looking at a fish that pokes its head out of his cup, which Waite says shows pictures of the mind taking form.

mathers.title: Knave of Cups
mathers.upright: A fair Youth, Confidence, Probity, Discretion, Integrity
mathers.source: S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Tarot: Its Occult Signification, Use in Fortune-Telling, and Method of Play (1888)

goldenDawn.title: The Princess of the Waters; the Lotus of the Palace of the Floods
goldenDawn.printed: THE PRINCESS OF THE WATERS; THE LOTUS OF THE PALACE OF THE FLOODS
goldenDawn.source: Golden Dawn "Book T", printed as "Liber LXXVIII: A Description of the Cards of the Tarot" in The Equinox I:8 (1912)

waiteAdditional.upright: Good augury; also a young man who is unfortunate in love.
waiteAdditional.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911), Part III section 4, "Some Additional Meanings of the Lesser Arcana"

olderMeanings.note: Mathers calls him the Knave of Cups and reads a fair youth, confidence, probity (honesty), discretion, and integrity, and reversed, a flatterer, deception, and artifice. Waite keeps the deception reversal almost word for word.

name: Knight of Cups
upright: Here's the romantic of the deck. The Knight of Cups follows his heart and arrives with an offer: a proposal, a date, a creative opportunity, a heartfelt gesture. He moves slowly and gracefully, led by feeling more than logic. He's charming, imaginative, and sincere, the one who writes you a poem or plans the thoughtful surprise. Follow what moves you, and bring something beautiful with you when you do. Someone is coming toward you with an offer, and it's heartfelt. Say yes to romance, beauty, and following your feelings.
reversed: The romance goes a little wrong. He can turn moody or jealous, or promise more than he delivers, all lovely words that don't lead anywhere. It may point to being in love with the idea of someone more than the actual person. An offer you were hoping for may simply not come through. Pay attention to what's happening underneath the charm. Charm without follow-through leaves people hurt. Check whether the promise has anything solid behind it.
sitWith: What offer are you hoping for, and would you know it if it came?
inASpread: Paired with the Two of Cups or the Lovers, he makes a proposal or new romance very likely. Beside the Seven of Cups or the Moon, his offer may be more fantasy than substance. Expect an offer, a gesture, or a message from the heart when he comes last.
imagery: A knight with little wings on his helmet and heels rides a white horse at a slow walk, holding out a golden cup as though offering it, with a river ahead of him. He isn't charging anywhere; he's the romantic who arrives gently with a gift.

waite.upright: Arrival, approach—sometimes that of a messenger; advances, proposition, demeanour, invitation, incitement.
waite.reversed: Trickery, artifice, subtlety, swindling, duplicity, fraud.
waite.picture: Graceful, but not warlike; riding quietly, wearing a winged helmet, referring to those higher graces of the imagination which sometimes characterize this card. He too is a dreamer, but the images of the side of sense haunt him in his vision.
waite.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911)

symbols.meaning: The higher graces of the imagination, which Waite links with this card.
Riding quietly rather than charging, a gentle approach.
An offer, a proposal, or an overture of love.
Feeling carrying him forward.

history: Waite describes him as graceful but not warlike, riding quietly in a winged helmet, sometimes a dreamer haunted by the images of the senses. He reads the card as arrival, approach, advances, and propositions. His Sola Busca counterpart is labeled Natanabo, after Nectanebo, the Egyptian pharaoh remembered in legend as a magician.
numerologyAstrology: Knights are the movers of their suit, and as Fire of Water in the Golden Dawn scheme he is feeling set in motion by desire, which is why he brings offers.

upright.love: A romantic proposal, a declaration of feelings, or a charming admirer on the way. Waite's meanings are advances and propositions, so expect someone to make a move. Those looking for love may be asked out, and couples may enjoy a romantic gesture or talk about the next step.
upright.work: An offer arrives, often creative or artistic, sometimes through a messenger or agent. It's a proposal worth considering seriously. An appealing offer, a creative opportunity, or work that follows your heart. Say yes if it feels right, and check the details before you sign.
upright.money: A pleasant offer, or money through art, charm, or a proposal. One old reading Waite includes promises a visit from a friend bringing unexpected money. An offer that looks good on paper. Take your time and make sure it's solid before you commit money.
upright.advice: Follow your heart, and check the offer is real. Romance is lovely with its feet on the ground.
upright.asAPerson: Romantic, charming, idealistic, and a bit of a dreamer. They're openly smitten with you and may say so with flowers or poetry.

yesNo.why: A heartfelt offer is on its way. An offer is coming, and it's a good one.

reversed.love: Empty promises, moodiness, or a charmer with no follow-through. Trickery, duplicity, and fraud are what Waite lists for the reversal. Lavish attention followed by silence is a pattern to watch for. Watch actions more than words.
reversed.work: An offer that falls through, or plans that sound lovely and can't be delivered. Read the fine print and get commitments in writing. Creative projects may overpromise on timing. Ask for references before you commit to a partner.
reversed.money: Scams, flattering sales pitches, or offers too good to be true. Check who benefits before you agree. A friend's investment pitch deserves the same checks as a stranger's. Walk away if you're unsure. Anyone pressing you to decide on the spot is a red flag.
reversed.advice: Look past the charm to the facts. Actions matter more than beautiful words. Check before you say yes.
reversed.asAPerson: Unreliable, moody, or manipulative in a soft-spoken way. Their romance may be an act, or a fantasy they can't live up to. Their apologies are lovely and rarely change anything.

yesNo.why: The offer may not be what it seems. Check the details before saying yes.

waiteNote.upright: Waite gives arrival and approach, sometimes of a messenger, plus advances, proposition, demeanour (manner), “invitation”, and incitement, meaning encouragement to act. In practice it's someone arriving with an offer, often romantic. A reader takes it as a proposal, a charming person, or an offer to follow your heart.
waiteNote.reversed: Reversed, Waite gives trickery, artifice, subtlety, swindling (cheating people out of money), duplicity (two-facedness), and fraud. In practice it's a charming offer that isn't what it seems, or empty promises. A reader treats it as a warning to check before saying yes.

imageryHistory: The Marseille-pattern Cavalier of Cups is a rider on horseback carrying a cup. Smith painted him in armor with a winged helmet and heels, riding a white horse at a slow walk, holding his cup out, and Waite says the wings point to the gifts of imagination this card can carry.

mathers.title: Knight of Cups
mathers.reversed: Duplicity, Abuse of Confidence, Fraud, Cunning.
mathers.source: S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Tarot: Its Occult Signification, Use in Fortune-Telling, and Method of Play (1888)

goldenDawn.title: The Lord of the Waves and the Waters; the King of the Hosts of the Sea
goldenDawn.printed: THE LORD OF THE WAVES AND THE WATERS; THE KING OF THE HOSTS OF THE SEA
goldenDawn.source: Golden Dawn "Book T", printed as "Liber LXXVIII: A Description of the Cards of the Tarot" in The Equinox I:8 (1912)

waiteAdditional.upright: A visit from a friend, who will bring unexpected money to the Querent.
waiteAdditional.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911), Part III section 4, "Some Additional Meanings of the Lesser Arcana"

olderMeanings.note: Mathers reads arrival, approach, and advance, and reversed, duplicity, abuse of confidence, fraud, and cunning, nearly the same as Waite. Mathers adds, from Etteilla, that this card shows the arrival of whatever card follows it.

name: Queen of Cups
upright: She's the friend you call at two in the morning, the one who actually listens. The Queen of Cups is compassion with a backbone: caring, intuitive, and steady enough to sit with someone else's pain without being swept away by it. Notice she sits right at the water's edge but stays on dry land. In a reading she can be a real person, often a mother figure, counselor, or healer, or the part of you that already knows how to comfort. Trust what you're sensing about people right now. She feels deeply and stays steady, which makes her a safe place for others.
reversed: When she's reversed, the caring spills over its banks. Maybe you're soaking up everyone else's moods until you can't tell which feelings are yours, or giving so much that there's nothing left. It can turn into martyrdom, or caring for others as a way to feel needed. Some readers also see insecurity and moodiness here, a need for constant reassurance. Your own heart needs looking after too, and nobody else is going to do it for you. Taking on everyone's feelings leaves no room for your own. Care for yourself first so your kindness doesn't run dry.
sitWith: Whose feelings are you carrying that don't belong to you? What is your intuition telling you that you haven't acted on?
inASpread: Beside the Empress or the Six of Cups, she brings a strong theme of caregiving, family, and tenderness. In a spread heavy with Swords, she's the emotional intelligence the situation is missing, or the person who can help. The answer, if she's the outcome, comes through compassion and listening to your gut. With the High Priestess, intuition is very strong.
imagery: A queen sits on a throne at the edge of the sea, gazing at an ornate, closed cup with handles shaped like angels, while little sea creatures decorate her throne. Hers is the only closed cup in the suit, as if what she feels and knows is kept safe inside.

waite.upright: Good, fair woman; honest, devoted woman, who will do service to the Querent; loving intelligence, and hence the gift of vision; success, happiness, pleasure; also wisdom, virtue; a perfect spouse and a good mother.
waite.reversed: The accounts vary; good woman; otherwise, distinguished woman but one not to be trusted; perverse woman; vice, dishonour, depravity.
waite.picture: Beautiful, fair, dreamy—as one who sees visions in a cup. This is, however, only one of her aspects; she sees, but she also acts, and her activity feeds her dream.
waite.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911)

symbols.symbol: Ornate lidded cup held in both hands
symbols.meaning: Feelings kept private and treasured; unlike the open cups elsewhere in the suit, hers is closed.
Emotional depth, on the border between land and sea.
Imagination and a loving nature.

symbols.symbol: Shells and pebbles at her feet
symbols.meaning: Small treasures washed up from the deep.

history: Waite calls her beautiful, fair, and dreamy, as one who sees visions in a cup, and then adds that this is only one of her aspects: she sees, but she also acts, and her activity feeds her dream. He reads her as loving intelligence and the gift of vision. On the Sola Busca Queen of Cups the lettered name is Polisena, that is, Polyxena.
numerologyAstrology: Queens hold their element within. As Water of Water, she is feeling in its purest form, deep, receptive, and intuitive.

upright.love: Deep, compassionate love and emotional safety. You understand what your partner feels before they say it, and they feel held by you. A caring, intuitive partner, or deep emotional connection. Couples feel understood, and single readers attract people with their warmth.
upright.work: Caring professions, counseling, the arts, or a manager who leads with empathy. Waite's gift of vision fits someone who reads people well. Art, music or writing may pay off if you give it proper time. Trust your read on people.
upright.money: Money handled with intuition and kindness, such as giving to causes or supporting family. Trust your gut about an offer. Using money to care for people, or trusting your gut about finances. Be generous and also look after yourself.
upright.advice: Listen to your intuition and treat your feelings as information. Care for yourself as gently as you care for others. Trust your intuition.
upright.asAPerson: Compassionate, intuitive, nurturing, and a little mysterious. Their feeling for you is deep, tender, and protective. People tend to tell them their secrets.

yesNo.why: Your heart already knows, and it says yes. The feeling is warm on both sides.

reversed.love: Moodiness, emotional overwhelm, or losing yourself in someone else's needs. Waite admits the reversed accounts vary, from a good woman to one not to be trusted. Emotional exhaustion, codependency, or drama. Take care of yourself first.
reversed.work: Absorbing everyone's stress at work, or decisions made on mood alone. Protect your time and set limits. Burnout from caring for everyone, or emotions clouding judgment. Set boundaries. You don't have to fix everyone's feelings to do your job well.
reversed.money: Emotional spending or being too generous to people who take advantage. Look at who benefits. Buying things to soothe a bad mood can add up quietly. Look after your own needs. Lending to someone who never repays is a pattern worth breaking.
reversed.advice: Put a boundary around your own feelings before helping anyone else. You can't pour from a cup with the lid stuck on. Fill your own cup first.
reversed.asAPerson: Moody, clingy, or emotionally manipulative, or simply overwhelmed. Their feelings may run too high to be steady. Emotionally drained, or manipulative when hurt.

yesNo.why: Emotions are clouding things. Emotions are too tangled right now.

waiteNote.upright: Waite describes a good, fair woman, honest and devoted, who will help you. “Loving intelligence, and hence the gift of vision” means her love makes her wise and intuitive. He adds success, happiness, wisdom, virtue, and calls her a perfect spouse and a good mother. In practice she's compassion, intuition, and emotional steadiness.
waiteNote.reversed: Reversed, Waite says the accounts vary: a good woman, or a distinguished woman who can't be trusted, or a perverse (contrary, wrong-headed) woman, and then vice, dishonour, and depravity, meaning moral corruption. In practice it's feelings overflowing into drama or manipulation, or caring so much you lose yourself.

imageryHistory: The Marseille-pattern Queen of Cups is a crowned queen seated with a cup. Smith seated her on a throne at the edge of the sea, carved with water spirits, gazing at an ornate covered cup unlike any other in the suit, which Waite says shows her seeing visions in a cup.

mathers.title: Queen of Cups
mathers.upright: A fair Woman, Success, Happiness, Advantage, Pleasure
mathers.reversed: A Woman in good position, but intermeddling, and to be distrusted; Success, but with some attendant trouble.
mathers.source: S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Tarot: Its Occult Signification, Use in Fortune-Telling, and Method of Play (1888)

goldenDawn.title: The Queen of the Thrones of the Waters
goldenDawn.printed: THE QUEEN OF THE THRONES OF THE WATERS
goldenDawn.source: Golden Dawn "Book T", printed as "Liber LXXVIII: A Description of the Cards of the Tarot" in The Equinox I:8 (1912)

waiteAdditional.upright: Sometimes denotes a woman of equivocal character.
waiteAdditional.reversed: A rich marriage for a man and a distinguished one for a woman.
waiteAdditional.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911), Part III section 4, "Some Additional Meanings of the Lesser Arcana"

olderMeanings.note: Mathers reads a fair woman, success, happiness, advantage, and pleasure, and reversed, a woman in good position but intermeddling and not to be trusted. Waite keeps both threads, the devoted woman and the one not to be trusted.

name: King of Cups
upright: The King of Cups keeps his head while feeling everything. His throne floats on rough water and he sits there calm, cup in hand, which is emotional maturity in a nutshell: he feels the waves and doesn't let them steer. He's the counselor, the doctor with a good bedside manner, the dad who stays calm in the emergency room. Often he's a real person like that, or your own ability to handle a stormy situation kindly and with a cool head. Diplomacy works better than force here. He's calm on the surface of stormy water, steady without being cold. Handle the situation with both feeling and good sense.
reversed: The calm cracks, or it was never really calm to begin with. He can be moody, cold, or bottling things up until they come out all at once. There's also the manipulative king, who uses feelings, his or yours, to get what he wants, or guilt-trips people into line. For you, it may mean you're struggling to keep your own reactions in check. Something has been pushed below the surface, and it's worth finding out what. Drinking or other escapes can be how the pressure gets let out. Find a safe place to let them out before they spill onto someone else.
sitWith: What do you do with feelings you don't want anyone to see? What would staying calm and kind look like in this situation?
inASpread: The King of Cups next to the King of Swords gives you head and heart working as a team. With the Seven of Swords or the Moon nearby, his calm face might be hiding something, so watch for emotional games. When he closes a spread, a situation that could have become a mess gets handled steadily and wisely. With the Emperor, it's leadership balanced with care.
imagery: A king sits on a stone throne that floats on a rough sea, holding a cup in one hand and a short scepter in the other, with a fish leaping on one side and a ship sailing on the other. The water around him is choppy, and he stays calm.

waite.upright: Fair man, man of business, law, or divinity; responsible, disposed to oblige the Querent; also equity, art and science, including those who profess science, law and art; creative intelligence.
waite.reversed: Dishonest, double-dealing man; roguery, exaction, injustice, vice, scandal, pillage, considerable loss.
waite.picture: He holds a short sceptre in his left hand and a great cup in his right; his throne is set upon the sea; on one side a ship is riding and on the other a dolphin is leaping. The implicit is that the Sign of the Cup naturally refers to water, which appears in all the court cards.
waite.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911)

symbols.symbol: Throne set on the open sea
symbols.meaning: Calm control amid emotional waters.
Feeling and authority held together.

symbols.symbol: Leaping dolphin on one side and a ship on the other
symbols.meaning: Emotion and practical life kept in balance.
Creativity and emotional wisdom worn close.

history: Waite describes his throne as set upon the sea, with a ship riding on one side and a dolphin leaping on the other, and notes that the sign of the Cup refers to water, which appears in all the court cards of the suit. He reads him as a man of business, law, or divinity, responsible and creative. Sola Busca's King of Cups carries the name Lucio Cecilio.
numerologyAstrology: Kings rule their element from outside. As Air of Water in the Golden Dawn scheme, he is feeling governed by thought: calm, diplomatic, and wise.

upright.love: A mature, emotionally steady partner who doesn't panic when things get stormy. Love that feels safe, kind, and patient. Anniversaries and quiet time at home matter to this partner. Single readers may be drawn to someone older or wiser.
upright.work: Calm leadership, diplomacy, or success in law, medicine, counseling, or the arts. Waite's creative intelligence and equity fit someone trusted to mediate. Mediating a conflict at work plays to your strengths. Keep your head and lead with empathy.
upright.money: Balanced, sensible choices and generous support for others. Stay steady, and avoid decisions made in the heat of a feeling. Sensible, calm financial decisions. Don't let emotions drive your spending, and take advice from someone steady.
upright.advice: Stay calm when the water gets rough. Feel it fully and act with a clear head. Listen fully before you answer.
upright.asAPerson: Wise, kind, diplomatic, and emotionally mature. He cares about you deeply and shows it through steady support.

yesNo.why: Calm wisdom leads to a good outcome. A steady hand will get you there.

reversed.love: Moodiness masked by calm, or emotional manipulation. A dishonest, double-dealing man is how Waite reads the reversal. Guilt may be used to settle arguments. Talk openly and don't let resentment build.
reversed.work: A boss who plays favorites or someone hiding their real motives. Watch out for manipulation. A moody boss, or emotions affecting decisions. Stay professional and write things down. Keep your own feelings out of written replies until you've cooled down.
reversed.money: Financial dishonesty or considerable loss, as Waite warns, often through someone who seemed trustworthy. Check every figure carefully. Emotional spending, or a dishonest adviser. Check credentials and get a second opinion.
reversed.advice: Don't bottle up feelings or let anyone manipulate yours. Honesty keeps the sea calm. Say what's bothering you while it's still small.
reversed.asAPerson: Charming but deceptive, or emotionally volatile under a calm surface. Their care may come with hidden motives. Moody, cold, or manipulative.

yesNo.why: Emotions or motives aren't sound here. Emotions are getting in the way.

waiteNote.upright: Waite describes a fair man of business, law, or divinity (religion), responsible and willing to help you. He adds equity (fairness), art and science, and the people who work in them, plus creative intelligence. In practice he's calm, wise, and emotionally mature, someone who keeps his head when feelings run high.
waiteNote.reversed: Reversed, Waite gives a dishonest, double-dealing man, plus roguery, exaction (demanding too much), injustice, vice, scandal, pillage (looting), and considerable loss. In practice it's emotions bottled up until they leak out badly, or someone using charm to manipulate. A reader treats it as a warning about a person or about your own buried feelings.

imageryHistory: The Marseille-pattern King of Cups is a crowned king seated with a cup. Smith set his throne on a stone block in the middle of a rough sea, with a ship on one side and a dolphin leaping on the other, a short sceptre in one hand and a great cup in the other.

mathers.title: King of Cups
mathers.upright: A fair Man, Goodness, Kindness, Liberality, Generosity
mathers.reversed: A Man of good position, but shifty in his Dealings, Distrust, Doubt, Suspicion.
mathers.source: S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Tarot: Its Occult Signification, Use in Fortune-Telling, and Method of Play (1888)

goldenDawn.title: The Prince of the Chariot of the Waters
goldenDawn.printed: THE PRINCE OF THE CHARIOT OF THE WATERS
goldenDawn.source: Golden Dawn "Book T", printed as "Liber LXXVIII: A Description of the Cards of the Tarot" in The Equinox I:8 (1912)

waiteAdditional.upright: Beware of ill-will on the part of a man of position, and of hypocrisy pretending to help.
waiteAdditional.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911), Part III section 4, "Some Additional Meanings of the Lesser Arcana"

olderMeanings.note: Mathers reads a fair man, goodness, kindness, liberality, and generosity, and reversed, a man of good position but shifty in his dealings, distrust, doubt, and suspicion. Waite's dishonest, double-dealing reversal grows out of that.

name: Ace of Swords
upright: Suddenly you can see it. The Ace of Swords is the moment the fog clears and the truth of a situation is obvious, or the moment a sharp new idea lands. It favors honest conversations, clear decisions, study, and saying the thing plainly. Truth cuts, and that's partly the point here. A clean cut often heals faster than a slow one. The sword points straight up, which is the whole idea: one aim, no wobbling. Write down the decision in a single sentence and see if it still holds tomorrow.
reversed: The thinking is muddled. A key piece of information may be missing, or you're trusting something that isn't true, or going round in circles in your own head. Words can come out harsher than you meant, since this sword cuts both ways. Now and then it's an idea that isn't ready yet, or clarity you're reaching privately before you can share it. Give it time and get the facts straight before you act. Pushing harder rarely clears a foggy head. Step away, sleep on it, and come back to the facts.
sitWith: What do you already know is true here that you haven't said plainly? If you had to say the truth of this in one sentence, what would it be?
inASpread: Beside Justice or the King of Swords, the Ace points to a decision made on hard facts, maybe a legal or official one. With the Moon or the Seven of Cups, the clear view is being blurred by illusion or wishful thinking. In a spread where Swords keep coming up, it often marks the one moment of real clarity in a stressful stretch. Next to the Eight of Wands, a message or decision arrives quickly and changes the picture.
imagery: A hand comes out of a cloud gripping an upright sword, its tip passing through a golden crown hung with an olive branch and a palm, above bare gray mountains. The sword cuts straight through, and the crown and branches say clear thinking can win the day.

waite.upright: Triumph, the excessive degree in everything, conquest, triumph of force. It is a card of great force, in love as well as in hatred. The crown may carry a much higher significance than comes usually within the sphere of fortune-telling.
waite.reversed: The same, but the results are disastrous; another account says—conception, childbirth, augmentation, multiplicity.
waite.picture: A hand issues from a cloud, grasping a sword, the point of which is encircled by a crown.
waite.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911)

symbols.symbol: Hand from a cloud gripping a sword
symbols.meaning: A sudden, clear idea that arrives with force.
Waite says the point is encircled by a crown: victory of the mind, and perhaps something higher.

symbols.symbol: Olive branch and palm hanging from the crown
symbols.meaning: Peace on one side, triumph on the other; a clear decision can bring either.
Yod-shaped sparks of insight coming down.
Cold, high ground where thinking is sharp and unsoftened.

history: The Marseille Ace of Swords already showed a hand from a cloud raising a sword through a crown hung with branches, and Smith kept the design close to that older model. Waite calls it a card of great force, in love as well as in hatred, and says the crown may carry a much higher meaning than fortune-telling usually reaches. Reversed, he lists the same force with disastrous results.
numerologyAstrology: As the one of its suit, the Ace is the first clean cut of thought. Golden Dawn tradition calls it the Root of the Powers of Air, mind and speech before they split into argument.

upright.love: A moment of truth: an honest talk that clears the air, or finally seeing the relationship for what it is. Clarity helps, even when it stings a little. Single people may finally be honest about what they want in a partner, and that makes the search easier. Couples can clear up a long misunderstanding with one frank talk.
upright.work: A breakthrough idea, a sharp decision, or winning an argument on the merits. Put your case in writing while your head is this clear. Pitches, exams, interviews, and anything that rewards a sharp mind go well. Say the idea plainly and let it stand on its merits.
upright.money: Cut through confusion with hard numbers. A clear plan or a firm no to a bad deal protects you. Set one clear rule, such as a savings amount or a spending cap, and stick to it. Clarity about the numbers stops the low hum of worry.
upright.advice: Say the true thing plainly. Decide, and cut away what's muddying the picture. Keep it short and true.
upright.asAPerson: Sharp, direct, intellectually honest, sometimes blunt. Their interest in you shows up as candor and a lot of good questions. They value honesty over comfort.

yesNo.why: The truth is on your side and the path is clear. Clear thinking gives a clear answer.

reversed.love: Harsh words, confusion, or the truth used as a weapon. Arguments go in circles when nobody is really listening. Texts get misread and tone gets lost, so have the important talks face to face. Half the story may be missing, so ask the second question.
reversed.work: Muddled thinking, a decision made in haste, or a clever idea that goes nowhere. Get a second opinion before you act. Emails fired off in frustration tend to backfire under this card. Draft it, wait an hour, and read it again before sending.
reversed.money: Misinformation or a rash call based on half the facts. Slow down and check the source. An angry message about a bill can make things worse, so wait a day before sending it. A small error on a form or statement may be worth fixing now while it's cheap.
reversed.advice: Wait until your head clears before cutting anything. Force applied to a muddle only makes a bigger mess. Get the facts first, then speak.
reversed.asAPerson: Cutting, argumentative, or mentally scattered. What they say to you may be sharper than what they mean. Their words can land harder than their intentions.

yesNo.why: The thinking behind this is clouded right now. The picture is still too muddy to call.

waiteNote.upright: Waite gives triumph, “the excessive degree in everything”, conquest, and the triumph of force, meaning power pushed as far as it goes. He calls it a card of great force “in love as well as in hatred”, so it cuts whichever way it's swung. In practice it's a breakthrough: a clear idea, a decision, or the truth said plainly.
waiteNote.reversed: Reversed, Waite says the results are “disastrous”, the same force turned against you. He adds a second, very different tradition from other writers, conception and childbirth, augmentation (growth), and multiplicity. In practice readers take it as clarity blocked or force misused: muddled thinking, harsh words, or a plan pushed through too hard.

imageryHistory: In Marseille-pattern decks the Ace of Swords already showed a single sword whose point passes through a crown. Book T describes the Golden Dawn card as an angelic hand grasping a sword that supports a crown hung with the olive of peace and the palm of suffering, with six drops falling from the point. Smith drew the same crown, olive branch, and palm over bare grey peaks, and six golden drops falling from the blade.

mathers.title: Ace of Swords
mathers.reversed: Embarrassment, Foolish and Hopeless Love, Obstacle, Hindrance.
mathers.source: S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Tarot: Its Occult Signification, Use in Fortune-Telling, and Method of Play (1888)

goldenDawn.title: The Root of the Powers of the Air
goldenDawn.printed: THE ROOT OF THE POWERS OF THE AIR
goldenDawn.source: Golden Dawn "Book T", printed as "Liber LXXVIII: A Description of the Cards of the Tarot" in The Equinox I:8 (1912)

waiteAdditional.upright: Great prosperity or great misery.
waiteAdditional.reversed: Marriage broken off, for a woman, through her own imprudence.
waiteAdditional.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911), Part III section 4, "Some Additional Meanings of the Lesser Arcana"

olderMeanings.note: Mathers reads triumph, fecundity, fertility, and prosperity, and reversed, embarrassment, foolish and hopeless love, obstacle, and hindrance. Book T calls it the Root of the Powers of Air, the whole suit of the mind in one card.

name: Two of Swords
upright: You're stuck between two options and you've decided not to decide. The Two of Swords is a stalemate, a truce with yourself where you keep things balanced by refusing to look. The blindfold is the telling part: some of this is avoidance, not knowing because knowing would mean choosing. Between two people, it's a standoff where nobody wants to budge. Sooner or later your arms get tired. Crossed arms protect the heart, and they also keep everything out. The calm here is real, but it's being held in place by effort.
reversed: The blindfold is slipping. You may be flooded with information and more confused than ever, or finally admitting what you'd been refusing to see. A decision may finally get made, often a hard one, a choice between two things you didn't want. Feelings you'd walled off can come bursting through. It's uncomfortable, and it's movement. A choice that's been dodged for a long time can arrive all at once. Take the decision in small steps if the whole thing feels too big.
sitWith: If you took the blindfold off, which option would you already be leaning toward? What would you notice if you let yourself feel this instead of balancing it?
inASpread: The Two of Swords with the Two of Pentacles or the Seven of Cups doubles the indecision; there are too many balls in the air and no choice being made. With the High Priestess, the answer is already inside you, waiting to be admitted. If this is where the spread ends, the stalemate will continue unless someone moves. With the Justice card, a fair decision is possible once all the facts are on the table.
imagery: A woman in white sits blindfolded on a bench by the sea, holding two long swords crossed over her chest, with rocky islands behind her and a thin crescent moon above. She's shut out what she can see and locked her arms over her heart, and the sword balance holds only as long as she doesn't move.

waite.upright: Conformity and the equipoise which it suggests, courage, friendship, concord in a state of arms; another reading gives tenderness, affection, intimacy. The suggestion of harmony and other favourable readings must be considered in a qualified manner, as Swords generally are not symbolical of beneficent forces in human affairs.
waite.reversed: Imposture, falsehood, duplicity, disloyalty.
waite.picture: A hoodwinked female figure balances two swords upon her shoulders.
waite.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911)

symbols.meaning: Waite's hoodwinked figure: not looking at what she'd rather not see.

symbols.symbol: Two crossed swords held at the shoulders
symbols.meaning: A standoff, balanced but tense and tiring to hold.

symbols.symbol: Calm sea with rocks behind her
symbols.meaning: Feelings kept still on the surface, with hazards underneath.
Intuition available, if she'd take the blindfold off.

history: Waite reads the card as balance and friendship, even concord in a state of arms, and then warns that any gentle reading must be taken cautiously because Swords are rarely kind forces in human affairs. Smith drew a blindfolded woman on a stone bench by the sea, arms crossed over two swords, where the older pip had only two crossed blades with a flower between them. Golden Dawn papers call it the Lord of Peace Restored.
numerologyAstrology: Two is balance, and here it is balance held by refusing to move. Its decan is the Moon in Libra, moods hidden under a need to keep the peace.

upright.love: A stalemate, avoiding a hard conversation, or refusing to choose between two people. The truce holds only as long as nobody looks. A couple may stay polite for months rather than raise the subject of children, money, or moving. If you're dating, you may be torn between two options or unwilling to let anyone close enough to choose.
upright.work: A decision you keep postponing, or two options that look equally good. More information would break the deadlock. Mediation, negotiation, or a truce between colleagues can hold for now. Write down what each option costs, since the answer may be clearer on paper.
upright.money: Frozen by a choice, leaving money idle while you wait. Gather facts and pick one path. Open the statements you've been avoiding, since the blindfold is part of the problem. Pick a simple default choice and adjust later if you need to.
upright.advice: Take the blindfold off and look at both options honestly. Choosing is uncomfortable; staying stuck costs more. A decision you can revise is better than none.
upright.asAPerson: Guarded, diplomatic, conflict-avoidant. Their heart stays shielded behind those crossed arms for now. Calm on the surface and working hard to stay that way.

yesNo.why: The choice hasn't been faced, so the answer is stuck. Nobody has chosen yet, so the matter waits.

reversed.love: The truth comes out and the stalemate breaks, or you're overwhelmed by too many feelings at once. Old secrets may surface. Someone may have been less than honest, and it's coming out now. Couples may finally have the argument they'd been avoiding, which can clear the air if it stays fair.
reversed.work: Information overload, pressure to decide, or deception coming to light. Falsehood and duplicity, Waite's reversed meanings, may be at work. A delayed decision may be made for you if you don't make it yourself. Watch for duplicity in a deal, and get promises in writing.
reversed.money: A hidden cost or dishonest detail surfaces. Deal with it directly instead of freezing again. A hidden fee, a dishonest seller, or an account you forgot about can surface. Look at the full statement before you agree to anything new.
reversed.advice: Once you can see, act. Don't let the flood of new information push you back into hiding. Look at what's in front of you.
reversed.asAPerson: Indecisive to the point of anxiety, or not being straight with you. Loyalty may be split. They may be telling each side what it wants to hear.

yesNo.why: Hidden facts or split loyalties muddy this. There's deception or confusion in the way.

waiteNote.upright: Waite lists conformity and “the equipoise which it suggests”, meaning a balance held on purpose, with courage, friendship, and “concord in a state of arms”, a truce where both sides keep their weapons. Another reading he gives is tenderness, affection, and intimacy. He warns that Swords are generally “not symbolical of beneficent forces”, so the harmony is qualified. In practice it's a stalemate or a truce kept by not looking.
waiteNote.reversed: Reversed, Waite gives imposture (pretending to be someone you aren't), falsehood, duplicity, and disloyalty. In practice readers take it as the truce breaking down: lies coming out, information flooding in, or a decision forced at last.

imageryHistory: In Marseille-pattern decks the Two of Swords was just two blades and some decoration, with no figures. Book T describes two crossed swords held by angelic hands with a white rose of five petals at the crossing. Smith painted a blindfolded woman seated by the sea with two swords crossed over her chest and a crescent moon above, the hoodwinked figure Waite describes.

mathers.title: Deuce of Swords
mathers.source: S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Tarot: Its Occult Signification, Use in Fortune-Telling, and Method of Play (1888)
mathers.remarks: R. If confirmed by the other cards may simply mean that the friends are not of much use to the inquirer in the matter under consideration.

goldenDawn.title: The Lord of Peace Restored
goldenDawn.printed: THE LORD OF PEACE RESTORED
goldenDawn.source: Golden Dawn "Book T", printed as "Liber LXXVIII: A Description of the Cards of the Tarot" in The Equinox I:8 (1912)

waiteAdditional.upright: Gifts for a lady, influential protection for a man in search of help.
waiteAdditional.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911), Part III section 4, "Some Additional Meanings of the Lesser Arcana"

olderMeanings.note: Mathers reads friendship, valour, firmness, and courage, and reversed, false friends, treachery, and lies. Book T calls it the Lord of Peace Restored, and Waite's additional meanings give dealings with rogues for the reversal.

name: Three of Swords
upright: It hurts, and this card doesn't pretend otherwise. The Three of Swords is heartbreak: a breakup, a betrayal, a loss, words that cut deep, or finding out something you'd rather not know. The rain behind the heart is grief coming down. There's nothing to fix in the first moment of this kind of pain, only to let it be real. Hearts do heal, but not by skipping this part. Tears are useful here, since they're how grief moves through. Give it a set time each day if it's swamping everything else.
reversed: The rain is easing off. You're starting to recover from a heartbreak, maybe forgiving, maybe just finding you can talk about it without falling apart. The other possibility is grief you've pushed down and refuse to feel, which tends to keep the swords in longer. Or you keep reopening the hurt by replaying what happened. Let the pain out so it can go. Replaying the moment it happened keeps the swords in place. Write it down once, completely, and then put the page away.
sitWith: What hurt are you still carrying that needs to be grieved? Who could you tell about this hurt without having to explain yourself?
inASpread: Next to the Lovers or the Three of Cups, it can point to a love triangle or betrayal by someone close. Followed by the Star or the Six of Swords, it tells a story of healing after heartbreak. In the outcome position it's hard to hear, and honest: some pain is coming, and you'll come through it. With the Ten of Cups reversed, the pain is inside the family or the home.
imagery: A red heart floats against a gray sky of storm clouds and rain, pierced straight through by three swords. It's one of the plainest pictures in the deck, and it means exactly what it looks like.

waite.upright: Removal, absence, delay, division, rupture, dispersion, and all that the design signifies naturally, being too simple and obvious to call for specific enumeration.
waite.reversed: Mental alienation, error, loss, distraction, disorder, confusion.
waite.picture: Three swords piercing a heart; cloud and rain behind.
waite.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911)

symbols.meaning: Heartbreak in its plainest form; Waite calls the design too obvious to need explaining.
Grief and a heavy mind hanging over everything.
Tears that let the pain move through.
