history: Smith's heart pierced by three swords is one of the clearest borrowings from the fifteenth-century Sola Busca deck, whose Three of Swords shows a very similar image. Waite lists removal, absence, division, and rupture, and says the design is too simple and obvious to need explaining. Its title in the Golden Dawn system is the Lord of Sorrow.
numerologyAstrology: Three is usually growth, but in the suit of the mind it is the first real wound. Its decan is Saturn in Libra, hard reality breaking into a relationship.

upright.love: Heartbreak, betrayal, a painful truth, or a separation. It hurts, and pretending otherwise won't make it heal faster. On your own, you may still be grieving an old love, and that's worth honoring before starting fresh. Honest words can hurt without ending things, so listen for what the other person is actually asking.
upright.work: Painful criticism, rejection, or a falling-out with colleagues. Let yourself feel it, then look at what's true in it. A project you cared about may be cancelled, or a team may split. Take a day to be upset before you decide what to do next.
upright.money: A loss that stings emotionally as much as financially. Don't make big decisions from the hurt. A painful expense, like a vet bill or a family emergency, can drain savings. Pay what has to be paid and leave the rest of the budget alone for a while.
upright.advice: Let yourself grieve honestly. Pain named out loud heals faster than pain hidden. Nothing needs to be solved today.
upright.asAPerson: Someone hurting, or someone whose honesty cuts deep. A broken heart may still be riding along into any new bond. They've been hurt and may be quiet about it.

yesNo.why: This one comes with hurt. The heart is hurting, so the answer is painful.

reversed.love: Recovering from heartbreak, or reopening the wound by replaying the argument in your head. Waite's reversed meanings are distraction, confusion, and mental alienation, which fits a mind that won't let the hurt settle. The sharpest part is over, and you can talk about it without crying. Couples may start to rebuild after a rupture if both are honest about what happened.
reversed.work: Moving past harsh criticism or a falling-out, slowly. The sting fades faster once you stop rehearsing what you should have said. Criticism stings less once you take out what's useful and ignore the tone. A falling-out may be patched with one plain apology.
reversed.money: Recovering from a loss, with some confusion still around the figures. Sort the paperwork out and learn from it without punishing yourself. Errors in the paperwork may be adding confusion to a loss. Sit down with the documents and put things in order one line at a time.
reversed.advice: Stop pressing on the bruise. Talk to someone and let it close. Put away the old messages you keep rereading.
reversed.asAPerson: Healing from grief, or clinging to old pain because it feels familiar. They may be guarded with you and slowly opening. Slowly letting people back in.

yesNo.why: Healing is underway, but the wound is still fresh. The wound is closing, but give it longer.

waiteNote.upright: Waite lists removal, absence, delay, division, rupture (a break), and dispersion (scattering). He says the design is “too simple and obvious to call for specific enumeration”, meaning the pierced heart speaks for itself. In practice it's heartbreak: a painful truth, a separation, or grief.
waiteNote.reversed: Reversed, Waite gives mental alienation (feeling cut off in your own head), error, loss, distraction, disorder, and confusion. In practice readers take it as a hurt that's healing slowly or one that won't settle, where the mind keeps going back over it.

imageryHistory: In Marseille-pattern decks the Three of Swords was a plain arrangement of blades with no figures. Book T describes three angelic hands holding swords, the central one cutting apart the rose so its petals fall. Smith's heart pierced by three swords under clouds and rain echoes the fifteenth-century Sola Busca Three of Swords, which also shows a heart run through by three blades; photographs of that deck reached the British Museum in 1907.

mathers.title: Three of Swords
mathers.upright: A Nun, Separation, Removal, Rupture, Quarrel
mathers.source: S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Tarot: Its Occult Signification, Use in Fortune-Telling, and Method of Play (1888)
mathers.remarks: R. May show simply that something is lost, or mislaid for a time.

goldenDawn.title: The Lord of Sorrow
goldenDawn.printed: THE LORD OF SORROW
goldenDawn.source: Golden Dawn "Book T", printed as "Liber LXXVIII: A Description of the Cards of the Tarot" in The Equinox I:8 (1912)

waiteAdditional.upright: For a woman, the flight of her lover.
waiteAdditional.reversed: A meeting with one whom the Querent has compromised; also a nun.
waiteAdditional.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911), Part III section 4, "Some Additional Meanings of the Lesser Arcana"

olderMeanings.note: Mathers reads a nun, separation, removal, rupture, and quarrel, and reversed, error, confusion, misrule, and disorder. Book T calls it the Lord of Sorrow, and every older source agrees on the pain.

name: Four of Swords
upright: After a battle, you lie down. The Four of Swords is recovery, a deliberate pause to get your strength back after a hard stretch: an illness, a breakup, a brutal month at work. The knight on the tomb is resting so completely that he looks like stone. This might mean an actual break, a few quiet days, or simply not making any big decisions for a while. Your mind needs to go quiet before it can think clearly again. Rest is part of the work here. A quiet week now can save a month of illness later.
reversed: Rest isn't happening, or it's happening the hard way. Push through exhaustion long enough and your body forces the issue with a cold, a crash, or a burnout you can't ignore. There's the three in the morning version too, lying down and still running through lists. On a brighter note, it sometimes means you're coming out of a long recovery and ready to rejoin the world. Pay attention to which one your body is telling you. Lying in bed scrolling the phone doesn't count as rest. Try one hour with no screens and see what your body asks for.
sitWith: What would it take for you to rest without feeling guilty about it? What could you take off your plate this week so you can recover?
inASpread: With the Hermit or the Hanged Man around it, the message to stop and step back is unmistakable. Put it next to the Eight of Wands or the Knight of Swords and you'll feel the pull between hurrying and healing. In a health reading, as an outcome, it points to recovery through rest. With the Nine of Swords, rest is the cure for anxiety that has run on too long.
imagery: The stone figure of a knight lies on a tomb with his hands folded in prayer, three swords hanging on the wall above him and one lying beneath, a stained glass window glowing in the corner. He's resting deeply, the way you do after a battle.

waite.upright: Vigilance, retreat, solitude, hermit's repose, exile, tomb and coffin. It is these last that have suggested the design.
waite.reversed: Wise administration, circumspection, economy, avarice, precaution, testament.
waite.picture: The effigy of a knight in the attitude of prayer, at full length upon his tomb.
waite.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911)

symbols.meaning: Waite says tomb and coffin suggested the design: rest so deep it looks like death.
Stillness, reflection, and quiet recovery.
A sheltered, peaceful place where someone keeps watch.

symbols.symbol: Three swords on the wall, one beneath
symbols.meaning: Battles hung up for now; one kept close in case it's needed.

history: Waite reads the card as vigilance, retreat, and a hermit's repose, and he says the meanings of tomb and coffin are what suggested the design of a knight's effigy lying in a church. Reversed, he gives wise administration, caution, and economy. In the Marseille deck it was simply four swords curved around a flower.
numerologyAstrology: Four brings stability, and in this suit that means a pause from strife. Jupiter in Libra, a generous and restoring truce, rules the decan of this Lord of Rest from Strife.

upright.love: Time apart to recover, or a quiet period in the relationship. Rest now makes reconnection possible later. Singles may want time alone after a breakup, and that's healthy. Couples might plan a quiet weekend in with no big conversations, just rest.
upright.work: A break, sick leave, or stepping back to recharge. You'll work better after the pause. Use your vacation days, or take a long lunch away from the desk. Big decisions can wait until you're fresh. Handing off one task can buy you the breather you need.
upright.money: Pause before any big move. A quiet period of saving and reviewing is wiser than action now. Hold off on large purchases and review your accounts calmly. A savings goal set now pays off when the quiet time ends.
upright.advice: Rest before you're forced to. Silence and sleep will do more than another push. Take a nap without apologizing.
upright.asAPerson: Withdrawn, reflective, recovering from something hard. They need space before they can be close again. They recharge alone.

yesNo.why: Rest first, then ask again. The timing calls for a pause.

reversed.love: Restlessness, pushing to reconnect too soon, or burnout from never stopping. Take the break you keep postponing. One partner may want space while the other wants closeness, so talk about what rest means to each of you. Rushing a reunion after a hard stretch can tire both of you out.
reversed.work: Returning to work before you're ready, or refusing to rest at all. Exhaustion will catch up. Burnout shows up as small mistakes, short temper, and poor sleep. Book the day off before the body books it for you.
reversed.money: Upside down, Waite's meanings turn practical: wise management, caution, economy, even a will or testament. Look after the paperwork. Update your will, check your beneficiaries, or put the paperwork in order. Frugality is good, though stinginess with yourself can cost you later.
reversed.advice: Slow down on purpose, before your body does it for you. Recovery can't be rushed. Stop before you drop.
reversed.asAPerson: Restless, burned out, or unable to be still. They may seek you out before they've recovered from something else. Wired and tired at once.

yesNo.why: Pushing on without rest won't bring a good result. Exhaustion is steering this, so wait.

waiteNote.upright: Waite lists vigilance, retreat, solitude, “hermit's repose”, exile, and tomb and coffin. He says these last two “have suggested the design”, which is why Smith drew a knight's effigy on a tomb. In practice it's rest after a hard stretch, recovery, or a deliberate pause.
waiteNote.reversed: Reversed, Waite turns practical: wise administration, circumspection (caution), economy, avarice, precaution, and testament (a will). In practice readers take it as rest refused or overdone, or careful planning after a quiet spell, depending on the cards around it.

imageryHistory: In Marseille-pattern decks the Four of Swords was a plain arrangement of blades with no figures. Book T describes two angelic hands holding four crossed swords with the white rose restored at the crossing. Smith drew a knight's effigy lying on a tomb with hands joined in prayer, three swords on the wall above him and one along the side of the tomb, under a stained glass window.

mathers.title: Four of Swords
mathers.source: S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Tarot: Its Occult Signification, Use in Fortune-Telling, and Method of Play (1888)
mathers.remarks: R. The cards near will show whether it is health or money that requires care.

goldenDawn.title: The Lord of Rest From Strife
goldenDawn.printed: THE LORD OF REST FROM STRIFE
goldenDawn.source: Golden Dawn "Book T", printed as "Liber LXXVIII: A Description of the Cards of the Tarot" in The Equinox I:8 (1912)

waiteAdditional.upright: A bad card, but if reversed a qualified success may be expected by wise administration of affairs.
waiteAdditional.reversed: A certain success following wise administration.
waiteAdditional.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911), Part III section 4, "Some Additional Meanings of the Lesser Arcana"

olderMeanings.note: Mathers reads solitude, retreat, abandonment, solitary, and hermit, and reversed, economy, precaution, and regulation of expenditure. Book T calls it the Lord of Rest from Strife, which is close to how most people read it now.

name: Five of Swords
upright: Somebody won this fight, and nobody feels good about it. The Five of Swords is conflict where winning matters more than being kind, the argument where you score every point and lose the friendship. You could be the one gathering the swords, or one of the people walking away. Bullying and dirty tactics come under this card, and so does knowing when a battle isn't worth it. Ask yourself what winning here would really cost. Walking away from a rigged game counts as a win. Save your strength for the fights that actually matter to you.
reversed: The dust is settling, and there may be a chance to make things right. This can mean apologizing, reaching out after a falling out, or finally letting an old grudge go. Or the resentment hasn't gone anywhere, and it's the argument you keep replaying in the shower. Sometimes it's regret, looking back at a win that wasn't worth it. Pride is usually the only thing standing in the way now. Someone may reach out to patch things up. Hear them out even if you're not ready to forgive yet.
sitWith: Is being right worth what it's costing you here? What would it cost you to lose this argument on purpose?
inASpread: The Five of Swords next to the Five of Wands turns everyday friction into a real, bruising fight. Beside the Two of Cups or Temperance, the conflict can be healed with some humility. Drawn last, it warns of a hollow win, or a loss to walk away from with your head up. With the Seven of Swords, someone is playing dirty and hoping nobody notices.
imagery: A smirking young man gathers up swords while two defeated figures walk away toward the water, two more swords lying on the ground, under a sky of jagged, torn clouds. He's won, and it cost him the people he was fighting with.

waite.upright: Degradation, destruction, revocation, infamy, dishonour, loss, with the variants and analogues of these.
waite.reversed: The same; burial and obsequies.
waite.picture: A disdainful man looks after two retreating and dejected figures. Their swords lie upon the ground. He carries two others on his left shoulder, and a third sword is in his right hand, point to earth. He is the master in possession of the field.
waite.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911)

symbols.meaning: Waite's disdainful man, the master in possession of the field: a win that costs respect.
The defeated, dejected and leaving.
Weapons dropped; conflict ended badly.
Tension and ill will in the air.

history: In Waite's scene a disdainful man is master in possession of the field, while two dejected figures retreat and leave their swords behind. His meanings are degradation, dishonour, and loss, and reversed he gives the same again with burial and funerals added. The Golden Dawn titled it the Lord of Defeat.
numerologyAstrology: Five breaks the rest of four and brings conflict back, and this time someone loses. Its decan is Venus in Aquarius, where cool detachment can make people careless of each other's feelings.

upright.love: An argument where someone wins at the relationship's expense, or cruel words that are hard to take back. Is being right worth this? Couples may be fighting to win rather than to understand each other. Anyone looking for love may meet someone charming who turns out to keep score.
upright.work: Workplace conflict, dirty tactics, or winning a battle and losing allies. Watch your methods. A rival may take credit or bend the rules to beat you. Document your work and pick which battles are worth your time.
upright.money: Gains made unfairly, or losing out to someone who plays dirty. Keep records and walk away from bad deals. A dispute over money can cost more in stress and fees than it's worth. Get advice before you escalate it.
upright.advice: Ask what this fight is really costing you. Sometimes walking away is the win. Ask whether winning is worth the price.
upright.asAPerson: Competitive, self-serving, maybe a sore winner or a bully. They may care more about winning than about you. Competitive, and sometimes sore when they lose.

yesNo.why: Any win here comes at too high a price. Someone will feel wronged, and that costs more later.

reversed.love: Wanting to make peace after a fight, or lingering resentment. An apology could change things. Hurt feelings may linger after a fight, and one sincere apology can soften them. Watch for pride on both sides.
reversed.work: Conflict winding down, or regret over how you handled it. Mend fences. After a team dispute, someone needs to go first and clear the air. Let it be you if you can. Let the next project be a chance to work together on better terms.
reversed.money: Recovering from a loss or settling a dispute. Let it go, even if you didn't get everything you wanted. Mediation is often cheaper and quicker than court. Chasing the rest may cost more than it returns.
reversed.advice: Reach out and make amends where you can. Pride isn't worth the distance. Say sorry for your part.
reversed.asAPerson: Remorseful, or still holding a grudge. They may want to reconcile but don't know how. Proud, and quietly sorry.

yesNo.why: The conflict still hangs over this. Old resentment is still in the way.

waiteNote.upright: Waite lists degradation, destruction, revocation (taking something back), infamy, dishonour, and loss, “with the variants and analogues of these”. In practice it's a fight won at a cost, bullying, or a win that leaves people hurt.
waiteNote.reversed: Reversed, Waite gives “The same”, adding burial and obsequies (funeral rites), so the loss is marked or mourned. In practice readers take it as the aftermath: regret, making amends, or resentment that lingers.

imageryHistory: In Marseille-pattern decks the Five of Swords was a plain arrangement of blades with no figures. Book T describes the rose torn apart and its petals falling as a central sword divides the others. Smith drew a smirking man gathering swords while two defeated figures walk away toward the water under a torn, windy sky, the disdainful man Waite describes.

mathers.title: Five of Swords
mathers.reversed: Losses Trouble (same signification, whether reversed or not.)
mathers.source: S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Tarot: Its Occult Signification, Use in Fortune-Telling, and Method of Play (1888)

goldenDawn.title: The Lord of Defeat
goldenDawn.printed: THE LORD OF DEFEAT
goldenDawn.source: Golden Dawn "Book T", printed as "Liber LXXVIII: A Description of the Cards of the Tarot" in The Equinox I:8 (1912)

waiteAdditional.upright: An attack on the fortune of the Querent.
waiteAdditional.reversed: A sign of sorrow and mourning.
waiteAdditional.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911), Part III section 4, "Some Additional Meanings of the Lesser Arcana"

olderMeanings.note: Mathers reads mourning, sadness, and affliction, and reversed, losses and trouble, noting that the meaning is the same either way. Book T calls it the Lord of Defeat.

name: Six of Swords
upright: You're leaving something hard behind and heading somewhere quieter. The Six of Swords is a transition, often a sad one, the move after a breakup, the new town, the slow recovery after a rough patch. Notice they're taking the swords with them; the hurt comes along for now. Still, the water ahead is calmer than the water behind. It can also mean an actual trip, especially over water. The boat moves slowly, and slow is fine. Each week puts a bit more distance between you and the worst of it.
reversed: The boat is stuck, or you keep rowing back. You may know you need to move on and feel unable to, or be carrying so much from the past that you can't really settle anywhere new. Unfinished business may be pulling you back, or a move keeps getting delayed. The crossing may just be rough, more turbulent than you hoped. Figure out what you can leave on the shore. Sometimes the thing holding the boat back is a conversation you haven't had. Say what needs saying and the crossing gets easier.
sitWith: What are you ready to leave behind, and what are you bringing with you? What would you leave on this shore if you could?
inASpread: Following the Three or Five of Swords, the Six shows you getting away from the pain toward something better. With the Eight of Cups or Death nearby, it's clearly an ending and a departure. Things get calmer from here, even if the change itself feels sad.
imagery: A ferryman poles a small boat across the water, carrying a woman wrapped in a cloak and a child, with six swords standing upright in the boat. The water is choppy on one side and smooth on the other, and they're heading toward the calm.

waite.upright: Journey by water, route, way, envoy, commissionary, expedient.
waite.reversed: Declaration, confession, publicity; one account says that it is a proposal of love.
waite.picture: A ferryman carrying passengers in his punt to the further shore. The course is smooth, and seeing that the freight is light, it may be noted that the work is not beyond his strength.
waite.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911)

symbols.meaning: Waite notes the freight is light and the work within his strength: help getting through.
Carrying grief and vulnerability to safety.

symbols.symbol: Six swords standing in the boat
symbols.meaning: Troubles brought along, but no longer wielded.

symbols.symbol: Rough water one side, smooth the other
symbols.meaning: Leaving turbulence behind for calmer waters.

history: A ferryman carries passengers across in a punt, and Waite notes that since the freight is light the work is not beyond his strength. His meanings are travel by water, route, and way, and reversed, confession, publicity, and in one account a proposal of love. Lord of Earned Success is the Golden Dawn's name for it.
numerologyAstrology: Six is recovery and balance after the defeat of five. Mercury in Aquarius holds its decan: clear thinking that finds the way out.

upright.love: Moving on from a painful chapter, together or apart. Calmer waters are ahead, even if the crossing is quiet and sad. Couples may be moving house or moving past a rough patch together. A single reader is leaving an old heartache behind, and the next chapter feels calmer.
upright.work: A transition to a better situation, or travel for work. Things get easier once you're moving. A new job, a transfer, or a change of team brings relief. Travel for work can go well, especially by water.
upright.money: Gradual improvement after hard times, one payment at a time. Stay the course. Debts shrink bit by bit as you keep making payments. Moving costs may be part of the picture, so budget for them. A cheaper place or a lower bill may be part of the move.
upright.advice: Keep moving toward calmer water. You don't have to have healed before you leave. Keep going, even slowly.
upright.asAPerson: Quiet, resilient, moving on from something painful. They're heading toward something better and may bring you along. Quiet, and carrying a past they don't discuss.

yesNo.why: Things are getting better, slowly. It leans yes, once you leave the trouble behind.

reversed.love: Unable to move on, or dragging old baggage into a new relationship. The past is holding you back. An ex may reappear, or someone might make a surprise confession of feelings. Talk through the last breakup with a friend before the next date.
reversed.work: Delays in a move or transition, or resisting change. Deal with what's holding you there. A planned move or transfer may be delayed by paperwork. Use the wait to finish what you'd leave behind. The new start is still coming, just later than planned.
reversed.money: Stuck in a financial rut, unable to get across to something better. Look for small ways to move forward. Unexpected costs may push back a move or a big change. Keep a buffer for the delay. Don't cancel the plan, only the date.
reversed.advice: Unload what you don't need before the crossing. Some things can stay behind.
reversed.asAPerson: Stuck, or unwilling to leave the past. Confession is part of the reversal, so they may have something to say. Stuck between where they were and where they want to be.

yesNo.why: The crossing is delayed. The past keeps pulling the boat back.

waiteNote.upright: Waite gives travel by water, route, way, envoy (a messenger), commissionary (someone sent on an errand), and expedient (a practical way out). In the picture the passengers' load is light, which he takes as a sign the trouble being left behind is bearable. In practice it's a transition, moving away from something hard toward calmer ground.
waiteNote.reversed: Reversed, Waite gives declaration, confession, and publicity, and says one account reads it as a proposal of love. In practice readers take it as a move that's stuck or delayed, or something private coming out into the open.

imageryHistory: In Marseille-pattern decks the Six of Swords was a plain arrangement of blades with no figures. Book T describes two angelic hands holding crossed swords with the rose restored at the center. Smith drew a ferryman poling a flat boat with a cloaked woman and a child toward a far shore, six swords standing upright in the boat, the water rough on one side and smooth on the other.

mathers.title: Six of Swords
mathers.source: S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Tarot: Its Occult Signification, Use in Fortune-Telling, and Method of Play (1888)

goldenDawn.title: The Lord of Earned Success
goldenDawn.printed: THE LORD OF EARNED SUCCESS
goldenDawn.source: Golden Dawn "Book T", printed as "Liber LXXVIII: A Description of the Cards of the Tarot" in The Equinox I:8 (1912)

waiteAdditional.upright: The voyage will be pleasant.
waiteAdditional.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911), Part III section 4, "Some Additional Meanings of the Lesser Arcana"

olderMeanings.note: Mathers reads envoy, messenger, voyage, and travel, and reversed, declaration, love proposed, revelation, and surprise. Book T calls it the Lord of Earned Success, a more hopeful title than the picture suggests.

name: Seven of Swords
upright: Someone isn't being entirely honest, and it might be you. The Seven of Swords is sneaking, lying, cutting corners, getting away with something. That might be a person going behind your back, or you doing things quietly because you know others wouldn't approve. There's also a more neutral side: strategy, working alone, choosing your battles cleverly. Look closely at who's taking what, and why. Working alone can be smart strategy, but check that it isn't just a way to avoid being questioned. Be the person whose story holds up.
reversed: The sneaking is catching up with someone. A secret may come out, or a person might confess and come clean. Or your conscience just won't let you get away with it any longer. Sometimes the lie is one you're telling yourself, about a person, a habit, or how much you can handle alone. The truth is lighter to carry in the end. Hearing the truth from a friend is easier than discovering it later. If someone offers honest advice, take a moment before defending yourself.
sitWith: Where are you telling yourself a story that isn't quite true?
inASpread: The Seven of Swords near the Moon or the High Priestess points strongly to something hidden or someone being dishonest. Justice in the same spread means a deception is likely to be exposed. If it's the outcome, keep your eyes open and your own dealings clean. Alongside the Two of Cups, look closely at honesty inside a partnership.
imagery: A man tiptoes away from a military camp with five swords in his arms, glancing back over his shoulder with a sly grin, while two swords stay stuck in the ground behind him. He thinks he's getting away with it.

waite.upright: Design, attempt, wish, hope, confidence; also quarrelling, a plan that may fail, annoyance. The design is uncertain in its import, because the significations are widely at variance with each other.
waite.reversed: Good advice, counsel, instruction, slander, babbling.
waite.picture: A man in the act of carrying away five swords rapidly; the two others of the card remain stuck in the ground. A camp is close at hand.
waite.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911)

symbols.symbol: Man tiptoeing off with five swords
symbols.meaning: Stealth and strategy, or simply getting away with something.
What he couldn't carry: the plan has a gap in it.
Waite says a camp is close at hand; the people he is slipping past.
Checking whether anyone saw, which says a lot about the plan.

history: The picture, as Waite gives it, is a man carrying five swords away rapidly while two stay stuck in the ground beside a camp, and he admits the card's import is uncertain because its meanings vary so widely. His list runs from design, hope, and confidence to quarrelling and a plan that may fail. The older Marseille pip gave no hint of theft at all, only seven blades arranged in a pattern.
numerologyAstrology: Seven asks you to prove yourself, and this card asks whether you'll do it honestly. Its Golden Dawn title, Lord of Unstable Effort, sits in the Moon in Aquarius: clever schemes built on shifting ground.

upright.love: Something is being kept quiet, whether a second contact on the phone or feelings not admitted. Look at what someone does when they think nobody is watching. Mixed signals or secretive behavior may be worth asking about calmly. If you're looking, you may meet someone who seems too good to be true, so take your time.
upright.work: Office politics, a colleague lifting your idea, or a workaround that bends the rules. Keep copies of your work and your emails. Protect your ideas and keep a paper trail. A clever strategy can work, as long as it's honest enough to explain out loud.
upright.money: Scams, sly fees, or the temptation to cut a corner on taxes or expenses. Whatever looks like a shortcut probably isn't one. Online deals, sly subscription fees, and investment tips from strangers need extra care. Change passwords and check your statements.
upright.advice: Be smart about strategy without sliding into sneakiness. If you'd hate to be caught doing it, skip it. Play smart, and play fair.
upright.asAPerson: Clever, evasive, good at telling people what they want to hear. Their interest in you may be real and still come with an angle. Clever, independent, and hard to pin down.

yesNo.why: Something about this isn't being done in the open. Something here isn't what it seems.

reversed.love: A secret surfaces or someone decides to come clean. Trust takes work to rebuild after that, and it can be rebuilt. Couples may have an honest talk after a secret comes out. Listen to the friend who tells you what they really think of the relationship.
reversed.work: Getting caught out, or choosing honesty before you are. Good advice and counsel are among the reversed meanings, so listen to the person telling you straight. Gossip or slander may be going around or slander, so stay calm and let the facts speak. A mentor's advice may save you from a mistake.
reversed.money: Money returned, a mistake admitted, or finally facing a debt you'd been dodging. It feels lighter once it's out. Money owed may come back, or you might own up to a mistake before it grows. Honest bookkeeping clears it.
reversed.advice: Tell the truth and take the advice you've been avoiding. Hiding costs more than confessing. Come clean and move on.
reversed.asAPerson: Someone owning up to a lie or giving up an old habit of dodging. With you, they may be trying to start over on honest terms. Finally ready to be honest.

yesNo.why: It turns on whether the truth comes out cleanly. The truth is coming out, and the answer depends on it.

waiteNote.upright: Waite lists design (a plan), attempt, wish, hope, confidence, and also quarrelling, “a plan that may fail”, and annoyance. He admits the card is “uncertain in its import” because its meanings vary so widely. In practice readers see a sneaky plan, strategy, or someone getting away with something.
waiteNote.reversed: Reversed, Waite gives good advice, counsel, instruction, slander, and babbling. In practice it's the scheme exposed, a confession, or advice worth listening to, with a warning about gossip.

imageryHistory: In Marseille-pattern decks the Seven of Swords was a plain arrangement of blades with no figures. Book T describes swords whose points just touch, with the rose held up by the hand holding the central sword. Smith drew a man tiptoeing away from a camp of tents with five swords in his arms and two left stuck in the ground, looking back over his shoulder.

mathers.title: Seven of Swords
mathers.reversed: Wise Advice, Good Counsel, Wisdom, Prudence, Circumspection.
mathers.source: S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Tarot: Its Occult Signification, Use in Fortune-Telling, and Method of Play (1888)
mathers.remarks: R. The cards which come next will show whether it will be good to follow the advice given or not. Also, the preceding cards will show from whom, and why, the advice comes.

goldenDawn.title: The Lord of Unstable Effort
goldenDawn.printed: THE LORD OF UNSTABLE EFFORT
goldenDawn.source: Golden Dawn "Book T", printed as "Liber LXXVIII: A Description of the Cards of the Tarot" in The Equinox I:8 (1912)

waiteAdditional.upright: Dark girl; a good card; it promises a country life after a competence has been secured.
waiteAdditional.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911), Part III section 4, "Some Additional Meanings of the Lesser Arcana"

olderMeanings.note: Mathers reads hope, confidence, desire, attempt, and wish, and reversed, wise advice, good counsel, wisdom, prudence, and circumspection. Book T calls it the Lord of Unstable Effort, which suits the half-finished plan in the picture.

name: Eight of Swords
upright: You feel trapped, and the trap is partly in your head. The Eight of Swords is the feeling of having no options, every direction blocked, nothing you can do. Look at the card, though, and the ropes are loose and the swords don't fully surround her. The prison here is fear, anxious thinking, or a story you've told yourself about being stuck. You have more choices than you think. Fear shrinks when you write it down. List every option, even the silly ones, and notice there's more than one.
reversed: You're starting to see the way out. The blindfold is loosening and the ropes are slipping, and you're realizing that a lot of what held you back was fear. That might mean leaving a situation, or just thinking about it differently for the first time in months. There's a harder version too, where you can see the gap in the swords and still insist there's no way through. Take one step and see if the ground holds. Getting out is a series of small moves.
sitWith: What story about yourself would you have to stop telling to feel free?
inASpread: Beside the Nine of Swords, the Eight is anxiety feeding on itself. With the Devil nearby, the trap may be a habit or relationship you keep choosing. A card like the Star or an Ace following it shows the blindfold coming off.
imagery: A woman stands blindfolded and loosely tied, surrounded by eight swords stuck in the muddy ground, with a castle on a hill in the distance. The bindings are loose and there's a gap in the swords, so she could walk out if she could see it.

waite.upright: Bad news, violent chagrin, crisis, censure, power in trammels, conflict, calumny; also sickness.
waite.reversed: Disquiet, difficulty, opposition, accident, treachery; what is unforeseen; fatality.
waite.picture: A woman, bound and hoodwinked, with the swords of the card about her. Yet it is rather a card of temporary durance than of irretrievable bondage.
waite.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911)

symbols.meaning: Trapped as much by what she can't see as by the ropes.

symbols.symbol: Swords planted around her with gaps
symbols.meaning: It reads as temporary durance rather than irretrievable bondage: there is a way out.
Her legs aren't tied; she could walk if she trusted herself.

symbols.symbol: Castle on the rocky hill behind
symbols.meaning: Safety isn't far, just out of her sight.

history: Waite describes a woman bound and hoodwinked among the swords, and adds that it is rather a card of temporary durance than of irretrievable bondage. His meanings are bad news, crisis, censure, conflict, and power in trammels. Book T's title for it is the Lord of Shortened Force.
numerologyAstrology: Eight usually brings power and movement, but here the power is tied up. It falls in Jupiter in Gemini, where too many thoughts and options build their own cage.

upright.love: Feeling stuck in a relationship, or so afraid of getting hurt that you won't move at all. The ropes are looser than they feel. Newly single, you may feel they've run out of chances, and that isn't the truth. Couples may feel stuck, so talk about what each of you would change.
upright.work: Boxed in by a boss, a contract, or your own belief that you have no options. List the exits, even the unlikely ones. Criticism or unfair blame at work can make you feel boxed in. Get advice from someone outside the situation.
upright.money: Debt or obligations that feel like a trap. One small change, like a phone call to the lender, starts to loosen it. Budgets can feel like a cage, so look for one flexible line. Call the bank before assuming there's no help available.
upright.advice: Lift the blindfold, one corner at a time. Your feet are free; take one step. Try one small move.
upright.asAPerson: Anxious, self-limiting, often waiting to be rescued. They may want to reach you but feel too tied up to do it. Anxious, and often more capable than they believe.

yesNo.why: Fear is doing most of the holding back here. Fear is stopping things for now.

reversed.love: Walking out of a dynamic that kept you small, or finally seeing it for what it was. Freedom feels shaky at first. Friends may notice you laughing again before you do. Couples may find a new way to talk that frees both of you.
reversed.work: New options appear, or you stop believing the story that you're stuck. The first move out is the hardest. A new role, a transfer, or quitting may open up. Expect the unexpected, since opportunities may come from surprising places.
reversed.money: A way through a money bind shows up: a payment plan, a new job, help you were too proud to ask for. Take it. Free debt advice services can see options you can't. Keep going even when the first steps feel slow.
reversed.advice: Keep going, even while it still feels scary. You're nearly out of the circle of swords. Keep moving toward the gap.
reversed.asAPerson: Someone regaining confidence after a hard stretch. They may come toward you now with more courage than before. Waking up to their own strength.

yesNo.why: The bindings are coming loose. The way out is opening up.

waiteNote.upright: Waite lists bad news, “violent chagrin” (strong distress), crisis, censure (blame), “power in trammels” (power held back by restraints), conflict, calumny (slander), and sickness. He adds that it's a card of “temporary durance”, a short confinement. In practice it's feeling trapped, often by fear or a story in your own head.
waiteNote.reversed: Reversed, Waite gives disquiet, difficulty, opposition, accident, treachery, “what is unforeseen”, and fatality. In practice readers take it as the ropes loosening and a way out coming into view, or as a trap you can see through and still hesitate to leave.

imageryHistory: In Marseille-pattern decks the Eight of Swords was a plain arrangement of blades with no figures. Book T describes four angelic hands holding eight swords with their points touching near the top. Smith painted a woman bound and blindfolded, standing in shallow water with eight swords planted around her and a castle on the cliff behind, the temporary confinement Waite writes about.

mathers.title: Eight of Swords
mathers.reversed: Treachery in the Past, Event, Accident, Remarkable Incident.
mathers.source: S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Tarot: Its Occult Signification, Use in Fortune-Telling, and Method of Play (1888)
mathers.remarks: R. Shows Treachery or Deceit in the past, and will be explained by the neighbouring cards.

goldenDawn.title: The Lord of Shortened Force
goldenDawn.printed: THE LORD OF SHORTENED FORCE
goldenDawn.source: Golden Dawn "Book T", printed as "Liber LXXVIII: A Description of the Cards of the Tarot" in The Equinox I:8 (1912)

waiteAdditional.upright: For a woman, scandal spread in her respect.
waiteAdditional.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911), Part III section 4, "Some Additional Meanings of the Lesser Arcana"

olderMeanings.note: Mathers reads sickness, calumny, criticism, and blame, and reversed, treachery in the past, event, accident, and remarkable incident. Book T calls it the Lord of Shortened Force, strength held back.

name: Nine of Swords
upright: It's three in the morning and your mind won't stop. The Nine of Swords is anxiety and dread, the nightmares and worst-case scenarios that feel huge in the dark. Guilt and shame feed it too, going over and over something you regret. Notice the swords hang on the wall and never touch her. Things often look very different in daylight, and talking to someone can help shrink them. Worry grows in the dark and shrinks in daylight. Keep a notebook by the bed to catch the thoughts so they don't loop.
reversed: The nights are getting a little easier. Maybe you've started to talk about your fears, get help, or see that some of what kept you up wasn't as bad as it seemed. The harder reading is anxiety so heavy and private that you're hiding how bad it really is. Facing the thing you've been dreading, in daylight, is often what finally lets you sleep. If it's this bad, tell someone you trust. Asking for help is a sign of strength here. If it's been weeks of poor sleep, talk to a doctor.
sitWith: What would you say to a friend who was losing sleep over this?
inASpread: Surrounded by other heavy Swords, especially the Eight or Ten, the anxiety is intense and may need real support. The Star or the Sun nearby shows fears easing with time. Even in the outcome spot, a lot of what this card dreads never actually happens. With the Four of Swords, rest is the remedy the worry needs.
imagery: A woman sits up in bed in the dark with her face in her hands, nine swords lined up on the black wall behind her, and a quilt covered in roses and zodiac signs across her lap. The swords aren't touching her; what keeps her awake is what she's thinking about.

waite.upright: Death, failure, miscarriage, delay, deception, disappointment, despair.
waite.reversed: Imprisonment, suspicion, doubt, reasonable fear, shame.
waite.picture: One seated on her couch in lamentation, with the swords over her. She is as one who knows no sorrow which is like unto hers. It is a card of utter desolation.
waite.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911)

symbols.symbol: Woman sitting up in bed, face in her hands
symbols.meaning: Utter desolation is Waite's phrase for it: the small-hours spiral.

symbols.symbol: Nine swords lined up on the black wall
symbols.meaning: Worries stacked high, hanging over her yet never touching her.

symbols.symbol: Quilt of roses and zodiac signs
symbols.meaning: Comfort and a larger order are right there in her lap, unnoticed.

symbols.symbol: Carving of a fight on the bed panel
symbols.meaning: Old conflicts replaying underneath the sleeper.

history: Waite describes one seated on her couch in lamentation, as one who knows no sorrow which is like unto hers, and calls it a card of utter desolation. His upright meanings are some of the bleakest in the book, while reversed he gives suspicion, doubt, reasonable fear, and shame. The Golden Dawn went further, titling it the Lord of Despair and Cruelty.
numerologyAstrology: Nine sits just short of the end, so the worry is at its peak. Mars in Gemini is its decan, a restless mind turning its weapons on itself.

upright.love: Lying awake over a relationship, guilt about something you said, or dread of what might happen. The mind at night paints things darker than they are. Singles might lie awake replaying a date or a message. Couples may carry guilt about something unsaid, and daylight talk helps.
upright.work: Stress that follows you home and into your sleep. Name the worst case to someone; out loud, it usually shrinks. Deadlines and fear of failure may be keeping you up. Make a short list of the actual tasks, then do the first one.
upright.money: Money worry that chews at you in the dark. Open the statements in daylight with a cup of coffee and a pen. Fear often makes money problems look bigger than they are. Write the actual numbers down, since the real total is usually smaller than the dread.
upright.advice: Tell someone what's keeping you up. Worries lose a lot of their size once they're said out loud. Talk to someone before bed.
upright.asAPerson: Anxious, guilt-prone, carrying a lot in silence. They may be losing sleep over you, or over something they haven't told you. Anxious, and often kinder to others than to themselves.

yesNo.why: Worry is doing the talking right now. Worry is driving this, and the facts may be better.

reversed.love: The worst of the worry starts to lift, or it goes underground where nobody can see it. Waite's reversed phrase, reasonable fear, asks you to sort the real threats from the imagined ones. A loved one could be hiding how anxious they really are, so check in gently. Shared fears often lose their grip once spoken.
reversed.work: Coming out of a stressful stretch, or hiding stress until it spills. Talk to a doctor or a friend if sleep has gone. Stress may be easing, or it's being hidden until it bursts. Tell your manager or a colleague if the load is too much.
reversed.money: The panic eases as the numbers get faced. Keep going with the practical steps. Facing the numbers helps the dread fade. A money counselor or a free budgeting tool can make it manageable. Small steps count, like one phone call or one bill paid.
reversed.advice: Check each fear against the facts, one at a time. Get support for the ones that turn out to be real. Say the fear out loud.
reversed.asAPerson: Someone quietly struggling, often more anxious than they let on. Slowly, they're finding their way out. Worried in private.

yesNo.why: Things are easing, though the worry still has a grip. The fear is easing, but slowly.

waiteNote.upright: Waite lists death, failure, miscarriage, delay, deception, disappointment, and despair. He describes the woman as one who “knows no sorrow which is like unto hers”, a card of utter desolation. In practice it's anxiety, sleepless nights, and worst-case thinking that feels bigger than the facts.
waiteNote.reversed: Reversed, Waite gives imprisonment, suspicion, doubt, “reasonable fear”, and shame. In practice readers take it as worry easing when shared, or fear that's hidden and growing, depending on the cards nearby.

imageryHistory: In Marseille-pattern decks the Nine of Swords was a plain arrangement of blades with no figures. Book T describes four hands holding eight swords falling apart, a fifth sword in the center, and no rose left at all. Smith drew a woman sitting up in bed with her face in her hands, nine swords laid across a black wall, and a quilt patterned with roses and astrological signs.

mathers.title: Nine of Swords
mathers.upright: An Ecclesiastic, a Priest, Conscience. Probity, Good Faith, Integrity
mathers.reversed: Wise distrust, Suspicion, Fear, Doubt, Shady character.
mathers.source: S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Tarot: Its Occult Signification, Use in Fortune-Telling, and Method of Play (1888)
mathers.remarks: R. The card following will show whom or what to distrust, &c..

goldenDawn.title: The Lord of Despair and Cruelty
goldenDawn.printed: THE LORD OF DESPAIR AND CRUELTY
goldenDawn.source: Golden Dawn "Book T", printed as "Liber LXXVIII: A Description of the Cards of the Tarot" in The Equinox I:8 (1912)

waiteAdditional.upright: An ecclesiastic, a priest; generally, a card of bad omen.
waiteAdditional.reversed: Good ground for suspicion against a doubtful person.
waiteAdditional.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911), Part III section 4, "Some Additional Meanings of the Lesser Arcana"

olderMeanings.note: Mathers reads an ecclesiastic, a priest, conscience, probity, good faith, and integrity, and reversed, wise distrust, suspicion, fear, doubt, and a shady character. Book T calls it the Lord of Despair and Cruelty, which is the reading Smith's picture carries.

name: Ten of Swords
upright: This is rock bottom. The Ten of Swords is a painful ending: a betrayal, a crushing loss, the moment you realize something is truly finished. It can look almost over the top, ten swords when one would do the job, and that's how it feels from the inside, like the end of the world. Look at the horizon, though. The worst has happened, and the sky is already getting lighter. The worst is out in the open now, and there's a strange relief in that. The only direction from here is up.
reversed: You're getting up off the ground, slowly. Recovery has started, the swords are coming out one at a time, and you're learning to live with what happened. The harder version is refusing to accept an ending, dragging out something that's already over, or bracing for a disaster that keeps not quite arriving. Once in a while it's a near miss, the worst avoided at the last minute. Let the old thing be finished so the morning can come. Getting up takes time, and nobody has to see you do it.
sitWith: Now that the worst has happened, what's one small thing you can do today? What has truly ended that you're still trying to fix?
inASpread: With the Tower or Death, the Ten of Swords marks a truly final ending with no going back. Followed by the Star, the Sun, or any Ace, it's the dawn after the darkest night. In a past position it often describes a betrayal or loss the person is still recovering from, which colors how they see everything that comes after. Reversed beside the Star, recovery is already underway, even if it doesn't feel like it yet.
imagery: A man lies face down by the water with ten swords driven into his back under a pitch-black sky, while a thin strip of yellow dawn breaks over calm water and distant hills. It's as bad as it gets, it's over, and the light is already coming.

waite.upright: Whatsoever is intimated by the design; also pain, affliction, tears, sadness, desolation. It is not especially a card of violent death.
waite.reversed: Advantage, profit, success, favour, but none of these are permanent; also power and authority.
waite.picture: A prostrate figure, pierced by all the swords belonging to the card.
waite.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911)

symbols.symbol: Figure face down with ten swords in his back
symbols.meaning: The full, undeniable end; Waite adds it is not especially a card of violent death.
The darkest point, when nothing more can go wrong.
The new day already breaking at the edge of the scene.
Quiet after the fight is over.
Some readers notice his fingers curled like the Hierophant's: grace even at the bottom.

history: Waite describes a prostrate figure pierced by all the swords of the card and takes care to say it is not especially a card of violent death. Oddly, his reversed meanings are advantage, profit, and success, with the warning that none of them is permanent. Golden Dawn tradition names it bluntly: the Lord of Ruin.
numerologyAstrology: Ten closes the suit, and in the suit of the mind that means a thought or situation that has run all the way out. Its decan is the Sun in Gemini, light arriving right after mental overload.

upright.love: A hard ending, a betrayal, or the moment you finally accept something is over. It's rock bottom, which also means the ground can't drop further. A person dating now may finally let go of hoping an ex will come back. Couples facing betrayal need honesty and time before any decision.
upright.work: A job lost, a project killed, or burnout that flattens you. Recovery starts from here, once you stop pretending you're fine. A layoff or a failed project hurts, and it also frees you from something that wasn't working. Take stock before you jump.
upright.money: A serious loss or debt reaching its peak. Stop the bleeding first, then rebuild slowly. Hitting the bottom of an account or a debt peak is frightening. Stop new spending, list what's owed, and call for advice.
upright.advice: Let it be over. Lie still for a moment, then turn toward the light at the edge. Rest now, and rebuild later.
upright.asAPerson: Someone at a low point, or someone who plays the martyr. They may feel too defeated right now to give much to anyone. Exhausted, and often more resilient than they look.

yesNo.why: This chapter is finished. This one ends in a painful no.

reversed.love: Getting up after a painful ending, slowly and a bit sore. Be careful not to reopen the wound by going back. Healing comes slowly after a hard breakup, and old wounds can reopen if you go back too soon. Couples may be rebuilding carefully.
reversed.work: Recovering from a setback and finding your feet. What Waite calls advantage and success here are real, if not permanent. Take on one manageable task to rebuild confidence. Don't mistake a temporary gain for a full recovery.
reversed.money: The worst of a loss is behind you and small gains return. Protect them. A little money comes back after a loss, so save it before spending. The recovery is real, and it's still early. Rebuild the emergency fund before anything else.
reversed.advice: Pull out one sword at a time. Healing takes more than a single day. Get up slowly.
reversed.asAPerson: Someone recovering from a crushing experience. They're rebuilding and may be cautious with you. Recovering, and careful not to fall again.

yesNo.why: Recovery has started but needs time. The worst is behind you, but it's not over yet.

waiteNote.upright: Waite says the card means “whatsoever is intimated by the design”, meaning what the picture shows, plus pain, affliction, tears, sadness, and desolation. He adds that it is “not especially a card of violent death”, so read it as an ending. In practice it's rock bottom, a painful finish, or betrayal.
waiteNote.reversed: Reversed, Waite gives advantage, profit, success, and favour, “but none of these are permanent”, along with power and authority. In practice readers take it as recovery after the worst, or an ending dragged out because it hasn't been accepted.

imageryHistory: In Marseille-pattern decks the Ten of Swords was a plain arrangement of blades with no figures. Book T describes swords falling away from each other with no rose, flower, or bud left anywhere. Smith drew a man lying face down on a shore pierced by ten swords under a black sky, while a band of yellow dawn light spreads along the horizon over calm water.

mathers.title: Ten of Swords
mathers.source: S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Tarot: Its Occult Signification, Use in Fortune-Telling, and Method of Play (1888)

goldenDawn.title: The Lord of Ruin
goldenDawn.printed: THE LORD OF RUIN
goldenDawn.source: Golden Dawn "Book T", printed as "Liber LXXVIII: A Description of the Cards of the Tarot" in The Equinox I:8 (1912)

waiteAdditional.upright: Followed by Ace and King, imprisonment; for girl or wife, treason on the part of friends.
waiteAdditional.reversed: Victory and consequent fortune for a soldier in war.
waiteAdditional.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911), Part III section 4, "Some Additional Meanings of the Lesser Arcana"

olderMeanings.note: Mathers reads tears, affliction, grief, and sorrow, and reversed, passing success and momentary advantage. Book T calls it the Lord of Ruin, and Waite's reversal keeps the same idea of a gain that won't last.

name: Page of Swords
upright: The Page of Swords has a thousand questions and wants answers to all of them. Think of the curious, restless mind: starting a course, researching a big decision, noticing everything going on around you. The wind is up in the card and so is his guard, so there's a watchful quality too, an eye out for trouble. The person behind this card is quick, clever, a little nosy, and happy to argue a point just for fun. Curiosity is your best tool right now, so use it. Watch for gossip, since the same sharp mind can slide into spying on others. Keep a notebook and write down what you learn.
reversed: The sharp mind goes looking for trouble. It can turn into gossip, sarcasm, or firing off a message you'll regret, words used as weapons without much thought behind them. Or it's all talk and no action, plenty of opinions and not much follow-through. Someone may be snooping, too, or passing on half-truths. Get the facts straight before you speak, and watch what you say about others. Rumors travel fast under this card, so don't be the one passing them on.
sitWith: What do you actually want to know here, if you're honest? What are you curious about that you haven't let yourself explore?
inASpread: When the Page sits near the Seven of Swords or the Moon, someone may be spying or spreading half-truths. With the Eight of Pentacles, it's a strong card for study and learning a new skill. Expect news, often by message or email, if it's the last card. With the Ace of Swords, a sharp idea or piece of news arrives.
imagery: A young person stands on uneven ground holding a sword up with both hands and looking over their shoulder, while the wind whips the clouds and trees and a flock of birds scatters overhead. Alert, restless, and ready to argue.

waite.upright: Authority, overseeing, secret service, vigilance, spying, examination, and the qualities thereto belonging.
waite.reversed: More evil side of these qualities; what is unforeseen, unprepared state; sickness is also intimated.
waite.picture: A lithe, active figure holds a sword upright in both hands, while in the act of swift walking. He is passing over rugged land, and about his way the clouds are collocated wildly. He is alert and lithe, looking this way and that, as if an expected enemy might appear at any moment.
waite.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911)

symbols.symbol: Sword held upright in both hands
symbols.meaning: Alert, curious, ready to defend an idea.
Collocated wildly, in Waite's odd phrase: a head full of racing thoughts.
A spot for watching and scouting.
Thoughts and messages on the move.
Waite has him looking this way and that, as if an enemy might appear.

history: Smith's page is, in Waite's words, a lithe figure walking swiftly over rugged land, looking this way and that as though expecting an enemy. His meanings are authority, overseeing, vigilance, spying, and examination, the qualities of a scout or inspector. Marseille packs name him the Valet d'Epee, the knave of swords.
numerologyAstrology: The Page is the student of the court, and the Golden Dawn makes this one Earth of Air: sharp ideas just starting to take practical form.

upright.love: Curiosity, lots of texts and questions, or someone sizing you up. Clear conversation matters more than grand gestures. Single people might be chatting with someone new and asking a lot of questions. Couples do well with open, curious talks about what each wants.
upright.work: Research, fact-checking, learning a new skill, or an audit. A watchful eye catches what others miss. Study, training, or an audit can go well if you stay alert. A younger colleague may bring a sharp insight.
upright.money: Read the terms and compare the numbers before committing. Knowledge protects you here. Research before you buy, and compare prices. A careful eye catches overcharges. Keep receipts and track your spending for a month to see where it goes.
upright.advice: Ask the questions nobody else is asking. Stay alert without turning suspicious. Stay curious and ask.
upright.asAPerson: Quick-witted, curious, a bit nosy, full of opinions. They're intrigued by you and want to figure you out. They notice everything.

yesNo.why: Get more information before you decide. More facts are needed first.

reversed.love: Gossip, snooping through phones, or sharp words that land harder than intended. Think before you send that message. A partner may be checking your phone or asking prying questions. Talk about trust directly instead of snooping back.
reversed.work: Rumors, someone prying into your business, or rushing in without preparing. Waite's reversed meanings name the unprepared state and the unforeseen. Unprepared meetings and hasty emails backfire. Check the facts before you speak up.
reversed.money: Acting on a tip without checking it. Pause and verify before handing over anything. A tip from a friend of a friend isn't research. Look the company up yourself instead of clicking the link. Scams often come dressed as insider news, so be wary of any message that rushes you.
reversed.advice: Mind your words and watch who's listening. Check facts before repeating them. Think before you talk.
reversed.asAPerson: Gossipy, defensive, or all talk. Be careful what you confide in them. Prying, and quick with rumors.

yesNo.why: The information here isn't reliable yet. The information is unreliable, so wait.

waiteNote.upright: Waite lists authority, overseeing, “secret service”, vigilance, spying, and examination, with the qualities that go with them. In practice it's a watchful, curious mind: study, research, or someone keeping an eye on things.
waiteNote.reversed: Reversed, Waite gives the “more evil side of these qualities”, meaning spying turned into prying, along with what is unforeseen and an unprepared state. He notes that sickness is also intimated. In practice readers take it as gossip, hasty words, or rushing in without preparation.

imageryHistory: The Marseille-pattern Valet of Swords is a standing youth holding a sword. Smith drew a lithe young man striding over rough ground with his sword held upright in both hands, clouds racing behind him and birds overhead, the swift, watchful figure Waite describes.

mathers.title: Knave of Swords
mathers.reversed: That which is unforeseen, Vigilance, Support.
mathers.source: S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Tarot: Its Occult Signification, Use in Fortune-Telling, and Method of Play (1888)

goldenDawn.title: The Princess of the Rushing Winds: the Lotus of the Palace of Air
goldenDawn.printed: THE PRINCESS OF THE RUSHING WINDS: THE LOTUS OF THE PALACE OF AIR
goldenDawn.source: Golden Dawn "Book T", printed as "Liber LXXVIII: A Description of the Cards of the Tarot" in The Equinox I:8 (1912)

waiteAdditional.upright: An indiscreet person will pry into the Querent's secrets.
waiteAdditional.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911), Part III section 4, "Some Additional Meanings of the Lesser Arcana"

olderMeanings.note: Mathers reads a spy, overlooking, and authority, and reversed, that which is unforeseen, vigilance, and support. Book T calls this court the Princess of the Rushing Winds.

name: Knight of Swords
upright: Full speed ahead. The Knight of Swords sees what he wants, forms an opinion, and charges straight at it, which is great when you need to act fast and awful when you need to listen. This card is quick thinking, ambition, and the drive to get something done right now, whether that's a deadline, a debate, or a hard conversation you've been putting off. Meet him as a person and he's sharp, confident, and blunt to the point of tactless. He'll get there first, though he may leave a few bruised feelings behind him. Speed is useful when you know where you're going. Check your map once before you ride.
reversed: The charge has lost its aim. You might be rushing into something without thinking it through, snapping at people, or pushing so hard you're heading for burnout. Plans may stall out too, all that drive with nowhere to go. In someone else, this is the bully or the know-it-all who won't let anyone else talk. Pull up the horse for a minute and check you're heading the right way. Slow down enough to hear the other side before you answer.
sitWith: Is the speed helping here, or just making you feel like you're doing something? What are you rushing toward, and have you checked it's still what you want?
inASpread: With the Eight of Wands or the Chariot, the Knight doubles the speed, and things will happen very fast. Beside tender Cups like the Queen or the Two, his bluntness can hurt someone, so choose your words carefully. In the final position, look for a swift move or a sudden confrontation. With the Tower, a sudden confrontation or upheaval comes fast.
imagery: A knight in armor charges forward on a galloping white horse with his sword raised high, while the wind bends the trees and tears at the clouds behind him. He's going flat out, straight at whatever's in front of him.

waite.upright: Skill, bravery, capacity, defence, address, enmity, wrath, war, destruction, opposition, resistance, ruin. There is therefore a sense in which the card signifies death, but it carries this meaning only in its proximity to other cards of fatality.
waite.reversed: Imprudence, incapacity, extravagance.
waite.picture: He is riding in full course, as if scattering his enemies. In the design he is really a prototypical hero of romantic chivalry. He might almost be Galahad, whose sword is swift and sure because he is clean of heart.
waite.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911)

symbols.meaning: Waite says he rides in full course, as if scattering his enemies.
Single-minded purpose, all edge and no brakes.

symbols.symbol: Trees and clouds bent by wind
symbols.meaning: The speed and force he brings disturb everything around him.
Thoughts racing faster than he can check them.

symbols.symbol: Butterflies and birds on the harness
symbols.meaning: Air symbols: the mind driving the horse.

history: Waite calls this knight a prototypical hero of romantic chivalry who might almost be Galahad, whose sword is swift and sure because he is clean of heart. His meanings still swing from skill and bravery to wrath, war, and ruin. Amone, a nod to Zeus Ammon, is the Sola Busca name for this Knight.
numerologyAstrology: The Knight is the court card that moves, and Fire of Air in the Golden Dawn scheme: thought driven by impulse, fast and forceful.

upright.love: Someone who pursues you head-on, or a relationship moving at full speed. Exciting, as long as you both look where you're going. If you're unattached, you may be swept up by someone confident and quick to act. Couples might be making a big decision fast, so pause long enough to agree.
upright.work: Ambition and fast action; a hard push toward a goal or a fight for a cause. Just make sure your facts are as quick as your mouth. Deadlines get met and debates get won. Make sure your speed doesn't run over your colleagues.
upright.money: Decisive moves pay off if they're researched. Speed without homework is how money gets lost. Quick moves can work if the research is done. Don't let urgency stand in for homework. Set a limit on how much you'll risk before you begin.
upright.advice: Charge at the goal, with your eyes open. Say what you mean, and mind who's standing in the way. Move fast, but look first.
upright.asAPerson: Driven, outspoken, brave, sometimes tactless. They come straight at you and don't play games. Bold, quick, and a bit blunt.

yesNo.why: Decisive action carries this, if you've done the thinking. Swift action favors a yes.

reversed.love: Harsh words said in a rush, or someone who charges in and then vanishes. Wait before replying in the heat of it. A new flame may rush in with big talk and then disappear. Couples may argue fast and hard, so take a breather before responding.
reversed.work: Rash decisions, steamrolling colleagues, or burning out from pace. Imprudence and extravagance are what Waite gives for the reversal. Taking on too much too fast can lead to burnout or mistakes. Slow the pace and double-check the details.
reversed.money: Impulsive trades or purchases made in a hurry. Sleep on it. Impulse buys and hurried investments may cost you. Give any purchase over a set amount a day to wait. Traders who chase every move tend to lose, and the same goes for shoppers chasing every sale.
reversed.advice: Rein in the horse before it bolts. Speed is useful only when it's aimed. Rein it in and slow down.
reversed.asAPerson: Aggressive, impatient, argumentative. They can hurt people without noticing they've done it. Rash, and sorry later.

yesNo.why: Haste is working against you here. Hurry is spoiling the outcome.

waiteNote.upright: Waite lists skill, bravery, capacity, defence, address (quick skill), enmity, wrath, war, destruction, opposition, resistance, and ruin. He says the card can point to death, but only “in its proximity to other cards of fatality”. In practice it's fast action, ambition, and a sharp mind in a hurry.
waiteNote.reversed: Reversed, Waite gives imprudence, incapacity, and extravagance. In practice readers take it as haste gone wrong: rash decisions, harsh words, or charging ahead without a plan.

imageryHistory: The Marseille-pattern Cavalier of Swords is a rider on horseback holding a sword. Smith drew him charging at full speed on a white horse, sword raised, with wind-torn clouds and bent trees behind him, and Waite compares him to a hero of romantic chivalry, perhaps Galahad.

mathers.title: Knight of Swords
mathers.upright: A Soldier, a man whose profession is arms, Skilfulness, Capacity, Address, Promptitude
mathers.source: S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Tarot: Its Occult Signification, Use in Fortune-Telling, and Method of Play (1888)

goldenDawn.title: The Lord of the Winds and the Breezes: the King of the Spirits of Air
goldenDawn.printed: THE LORD OF THE WINDS AND THE BREEZES: THE KING OF THE SPIRITS OF AIR
goldenDawn.source: Golden Dawn "Book T", printed as "Liber LXXVIII: A Description of the Cards of the Tarot" in The Equinox I:8 (1912)

waiteAdditional.upright: A soldier, man of arms, satellite, stipendiary; heroic action predicted for soldier.
waiteAdditional.reversed: Dispute with an imbecile person; for a woman, struggle with a rival, who will be conquered.
waiteAdditional.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911), Part III section 4, "Some Additional Meanings of the Lesser Arcana"

olderMeanings.note: Mathers reads a soldier, a man whose profession is arms, skilfulness, capacity, address, and promptitude, and reversed, a conceited fool, ingenuousness, and simplicity. Book T calls this court the Lord of the Winds and the Breezes.

name: Queen of Swords
upright: The Queen of Swords tells it like it is. She's clear, honest, independent, and very hard to fool, the friend who gives you the truth when everyone else is being polite. Often she's been through hard things, grief or loss, and come out wiser and sharper for it. In a reading, she asks you to set clear boundaries, speak plainly, and trust your own judgment. Her honesty is a form of kindness, even when it doesn't feel soft. Saying no clearly is a kindness to everyone involved. Say it once, calmly, and don't overexplain.
reversed: Her sharpness turns cold. You may be using words to wound, holding on to grudges, or shutting your feelings down so completely that you've grown bitter. She can be the critical, judgmental person who cuts others down, maybe behind their backs. Or feelings flood in and cloud that famous clear head. Look for where old hurt is making you hard. Notice when a sharp remark is really an old hurt talking.
sitWith: Where do you need a clear boundary, and what would you say to set it?
inASpread: Next to the Three of Swords or the Five of Cups, the Queen shows someone who has come through grief and grown stronger for it. Paired with the Queen of Cups, you get a good balance of head and heart. Closing a reading, she says the situation needs honesty and firm boundaries.
imagery: A queen sits on a throne in profile, her sword held straight up and her other hand raised as if to welcome or to warn, with clouds gathering below and a single bird high above. She's alone up there and clear-eyed, someone who has seen enough of life to know the truth when she hears it.

waite.upright: Widowhood, female sadness and embarrassment, absence, sterility, mourning, privation, separation.
waite.reversed: Malice, bigotry, artifice, prudery, bale, deceit.
waite.picture: Her right hand raises the weapon vertically and the hilt rests on an arm of her royal chair; the left hand is extended, the arm raised; her countenance is severe but chastened; it suggests familiarity with sorrow. It does not represent mercy, and, her sword notwithstanding, she is scarcely a symbol of power.
waite.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911)

symbols.meaning: Waite says her right hand raises the weapon vertically: judgment with no wobble.
Waite describes it raised: an open hand that welcomes and warns at once.

symbols.symbol: Butterflies and a winged cherub on the throne
symbols.meaning: The soul and change, carved into the seat of her authority.
A clear view from a lonely height.
Troubles beneath her; she has risen above them.

history: Waite describes her face as severe but chastened, suggesting familiarity with sorrow, and says she does not represent mercy and is scarcely a symbol of power. His meanings include widowhood, mourning, absence, and separation, and his extra notes simply call her a widow. The Sola Busca Queen of Swords is Olinpia, Olympias, the mother of Alexander the Great.
numerologyAstrology: As a Queen she holds the suit's element inward, and Water of Air in the Golden Dawn scheme: feeling passed through a clear mind, which is why her honesty has depth.

upright.love: Honest, grown-up love with clear boundaries, often after a loss. She'd rather be alone than be lied to. A single reader knows what they want and won't settle for less. Couples do well with honest talk and clear agreements.
upright.work: Clear communication, fair judgment, and the confidence to say no. Editors, analysts, and anyone who cuts through fluff do well under her. Editing, analysis, negotiation, and any job that needs a clear head go well. Speak plainly and keep emotions steady.
upright.money: Independent, well-reasoned decisions. Don't let sentiment talk you into a bad deal. Handling your own accounts after a separation fits this queen. Don't let guilt push you into lending money you can't spare. Read every contract as if you'll have to defend it later.
upright.advice: Speak plainly and kindly, and hold your line. Your experience has earned you that clarity. Be honest and kind at once.
upright.asAPerson: Perceptive, witty, independent, someone who has known grief and come through it wiser. She respects you most when you're straight with her. They may have been through divorce or loss and speak plainly because of it.

yesNo.why: The honest answer is a clear yes. Honesty points to yes.

reversed.love: Old hurt hardened into coldness, or words used to wound. Waite's reversed list includes malice, bigotry, and deceit. Bitterness from an old hurt may be spilling into a new relationship. Couples might hear harsh words, so call a timeout before it turns cruel.
reversed.work: Harsh criticism, a cold boss, or someone gossiping behind the scenes. Stay fair even if others don't. A critical boss or colleague may be difficult to please. Stay professional, and keep a record if the criticism turns unfair.
reversed.money: Decisions made from bitterness or distrust. Separate the old grudge from the present numbers. Distrust can make you miss a good deal, or stinginess can cost friends. An ex or a former business partner may be at the center of it.
reversed.advice: Keep your clarity and let a little warmth back in. Being right doesn't have to mean being cruel. Drop the grudge.
reversed.asAPerson: Cold, cutting, or quietly bitter, someone judging from old wounds. Her distance may have more to do with her history than with you. Cold, and hurting underneath.

yesNo.why: Bitterness is clouding the judgment here. Let the resentment cool before you decide.

waiteNote.upright: Waite lists widowhood, “female sadness and embarrassment”, absence, sterility, mourning, privation (going without), and separation. In practice readers see a woman who has known grief and come out clear-eyed and honest, with firm boundaries.
waiteNote.reversed: Reversed, Waite gives malice, bigotry, artifice (trickery), prudery, bale (harm), and deceit. In practice it's her clarity turned cold or cruel, bitterness, or harsh judgment.

imageryHistory: The Marseille-pattern Queen of Swords is a crowned queen seated with a sword. Smith seated her in profile on a throne carved with butterflies and a winged child's head, her sword upright in her right hand and her left hand raised as if in welcome, with clouds below her and a single bird high above.

mathers.title: Queen of Swords
mathers.reversed: A Bad Woman, ill-tempered and bigoted, Riches and Discord, Abundance together with Worry, Joy with Grief.
mathers.source: S. L. MacGregor Mathers, The Tarot: Its Occult Signification, Use in Fortune-Telling, and Method of Play (1888)
mathers.remarks: This is not necessarily to be taken by itself; it may signify that the person symbolised by the cards near it has just lost, or is likely soon to lose, wife or husband. In some instances it may merely signify that if two people are married, the one will die some time before the other, but not necessarily that the event will occur immediately.

goldenDawn.title: The Queen of the Thrones of Air
goldenDawn.printed: THE QUEEN OF THE THRONES OF AIR
goldenDawn.source: Golden Dawn "Book T", printed as "Liber LXXVIII: A Description of the Cards of the Tarot" in The Equinox I:8 (1912)

waiteAdditional.upright: A widow.
waiteAdditional.reversed: A bad woman, with ill-will towards the Querent.
waiteAdditional.source: A. E. Waite, The Pictorial Key to the Tarot (1911), Part III section 4, "Some Additional Meanings of the Lesser Arcana"

olderMeanings.note: Mathers reads widowhood, loss, privation, absence, and separation, and reversed, a bad woman, ill-tempered and bigoted, riches and discord, abundance together with worry, and joy with grief. Book T calls this court the Queen of the Thrones of Air.

name: King of Swords
upright: He's the clearest head in the room. The King of Swords deals in facts and fairness: the lawyer, the doctor, the judge, the advisor who tells you exactly where you stand. He doesn't let feelings make his decisions, which can seem cold, but it's also why people trust him in a crisis. He may be someone like that in your life, or your own need to think this through carefully and then make a firm call. Once you have the facts, decide. A firm decision made on good facts deserves to stand. Explain your reasoning once and then stop arguing it.
reversed: That sharp intellect gets turned on people. He can be manipulative, using logic and clever arguments to win at any cost, or an authority figure who abuses the position. There's also a cold, rigid version who talks down to others and leaves no room for anyone's feelings.
